Only with global.liveHomeAssistantToken: true: ExternalSecret battery-optimizer-home-assistant-live <- secret/battery-optimizer/home-assistant-live (service only, see Live battery control) Config ConfigMap battery-optimizer-config rendered from apps/battery-optimizer/files/ (tariff.yaml, service.yaml, and the climate shadow's climate.yaml, climate-mpc.yaml) Storage PVC battery-optimizer-data, 5 Gi, openebs-zfspv, mounted at /data (BATTERY_OPTIMIZER_DATA_DIR) Backup labels backup: battery-optimizer-zfs, backup/retain: quaterly; SnapshotSchedule battery-optimizer-zfs-backups (daily 06:00 UTC, keep 20) Alerts PrometheusRule/battery-optimizer (label release: monitoring) for the CronJob, PrometheusRule/battery-optimizer-service (long-term) for the service

docs.title: Design notes and gotchas
docs.text:
• Why daily with an 8 day HA window. HA's recorder keeps 10 days (purge_keep_days default, nothing overrides it). Rows older than that are gone for good, so the binding rule is "never more than 10 days between two successful runs". Daily with an 8 day lookback tolerates 7 missed runs. The window is deliberately shorter than the retention: the recorder purges nightly, so the oldest chunk of a 10 day window is partly or wholly gone and would raise a coverage gap every night (see the next note). Re-pulling is free because the HA extractor dedups against rows already in the store. Chunk width stays at the CLI default (86400 s); changing it on a live store mints new carry-in anchors.
  • Prometheus extraction is not deduplicated across runs, so the lookback is only 3 days (about 40 KB per day-part). The Prometheus archive has no retention limit, so there is no urgency.
  • Bootstrap. If /data/manifests holds no finished Prometheus extraction (empty PVC), the run extracts Prometheus from PROM_BOOTSTRAP_START (2024-01-01) instead of the 3 day lookback. A manifest is written only by a finished run, so an interrupted bootstrap retries from scratch.
  • Build cadence and window. build is content-addressed and write-once, and measured on the cluster every new extraction changes the dataset id (the part list changes), adding about 4.2 MB per run (~1.5 GB a year if built daily) while nothing consumes the dataset yet. The job therefore builds only on UTC days 01 and 02 of the month (BUILD_ON_DAYS), over the complete months [BUILD_START, first of this month); other days log build skipped. The newest partial month is not in the dataset until the month closes. There is no CLI-side garbage collection of superseded datasets. Run a manual build job if you need one off-cycle (steps 1-3 still run).
  • Permissions. No fsGroup (slow startup on openebs-zfspv). A fresh ZFS dataset is root:root 0755, so the fix-permissions init container chowns the volume root to 65532 (recursively only if the root is not already owned by 65532). See ci-runner-workspace-permission-denied.md.
  • Alerts use release: monitoring, not operator.prometheus.io/instance: prometheus-long-term. kube-state-metrics and kubelet series exist only in the main Prometheus; a rule labelled for prometheus-long-term would load but never fire.
  • No NetworkPolicy. An egress-only policy (DNS, HA 8123, long-term Prometheus 9090) ran from 0.2.1 until 0.3.0 and was removed on 2026-10-25: battery-optimizer is first-party software published from our own repository, and the repo keeps NetworkPolicies for workloads that are not under our control (LLM harnesses). Outside live its only credential is the read-only HA token and it has no actuation path; in live the HA client can send only the allowlisted Omnibattery writes (ADR-0007).
  • The two power signals come from a Gen1 Shelly EM over MQTT at 2 s; the counters still poll. shellyem-main (192.168.86.130) publishes shellies/shellyem-244CAB417668/emeter/{0,1}/power to mosquitto every 2 s (mqtt_update_period: 2) and HA consumes them via apps/home-assistant/config/integrations/shelly_em_mqtt.yaml. Since the 2026-10-27 cutover, grid_power and observed carry those IDs from the mqtt platform, measured as battery_optimizer_input_age_seconds{role="grid_power"} = 2.3 s (was 31.9 s). grid_energy and everything else still arrive over the native integration at 2.2 × 15 s = 33 s, which is correct for a monotonic counter consumed as 900 s deltas — a faster transport would add recorder rows without adding information. The device still carries a permanent error-level push_update_* repair, because CoIoT is multicast-only (peer: "") and nothing forwards it to the HA pod; that is a hygiene item, not a data problem. A faster transport initially looked unusable — the device reboot-looped — but that was mis-diagnosed: the loop needs MQTT and coiot.enabled: false and an HA setup_retry storm, so MQTT is safe as long as CoIoT stays enabled (planning/shelly-em-mqtt-implementation.md). Do not rename these entities or the device: friendly_name is a Prometheus label and part of the archive's series_key. Renaming also moves recorder history — if an ID must ever change hands again, use remove-then-promote (home-assistant-entity-id-handover.md).
  • Never disable CoIoT on that device, and treat HA restarts as a checked operation. With coiot.enabled: false the firmware stops serving /cit/*, HA's initialize() hangs on GET /cit/d, and the next HA restart drops all 14 shellyem-main entities into setup_retry. That happened on 2026-10-26 and cost ~48 min of history (18:02:35Z-18:50:34Z). Since the MQTT cutover the blast radius is narrower but not gone: grid_power and observed would keep working (they come from the broker), while grid_energy — what the dataset is actually built from — would be lost, and MQTT being permanently enabled means the reboot-loop co-factor is always present. Before any HA ConfigMap change (Reloader restarts the pod), verify GET /cit/d still answers 200. Recovery, correct endpoint and pitfalls: shelly-gen1-coiot-disabled-breaks-ha-setup.md.
  • grid_energy still takes ~20 poll timeouts a day; grid_power no longer does. The native /status REST poll occasionally exceeds DEVICE_IO_TIMEOUT = 10 s (~19.7 unavailable rows/day on metadata_id 182 over a 10-day window, dating back before MQTT existed), which flips the whole block to unavailable at T + 33 s + 10 s. In the Prometheus archive those become missing 60 s samples — the 2026-10-27 03:30Z run saw 4420 of ~4526 expected over 3 days and still reported violations=0. Watch for it if the coverage check below ever starts failing: the fix is to move the counters to MQTT too, which has so far not been worth the recorder cost.
  • tariff.yaml and service.yaml are vendored copies of config/ in the app repository (the image carries no config). Update both together; the tariff config hash is part of every dataset id. The CronJob mounts the same ConfigMap at /config and sets BATTERY_OPTIMIZER_SERVICE_CONFIG=/config/service.yaml, so build and extract read battery.commissioned_at and the battery counters from the same service.yaml as the service; set them there on installation day and nothing else needs changing.
  • Coverage gaps fail the Job. From 0.2.1 extract exits 3 when the run's manifest records a coverage gap (HA: empty_chunk, empty_chunk_after_window_filter, chunk_accounting_mismatch, no_rows_for_entity, no_rows_extracted:all; Prometheus: no_samples_extracted, no_series_chunks, series_without_samples_chunks). The data and manifest are kept, but the Job fails and BatteryOptimizerJobFailed fires, so a silent gap is no longer silent. The pipeline does not pass --allow-coverage-gaps (except for the one-off Prometheus bootstrap, whose 2024 history has known holes). If a window legitimately has no data, fix the window rather than opting out.

docs.title: Shadow service (Phase C)
docs.text: Item Value Workload Deployment battery-optimizer-service, 1 replica, strategy: Recreate, same image anchor as the CronJob Command battery-optimizer serve, port 8080: /health/live, /health/ready, /status, /plan, /metrics Config files/tariff.yaml + files/service.yaml (vendored from the app repo config/) in ConfigMap battery-optimizer-config, mounted at /config. service.yaml uses soc_source: simulated because Home Assistant has no battery entities yet HA token the same ExternalSecret as the pipeline, mounted as a file (BATTERY_OPTIMIZER_HA_TOKEN_FILE). Read-only, non-admin. With global.liveHomeAssistantToken: true the live user's token is mounted at the same path instead (Live battery control) Storage the same PVC battery-optimizer-data at /data (RWO on prusik, Recreate avoids two pods). The service writes only /data/service/v1/; the pipeline uses raw/, manifests/ and analysis/, so the paths never collide Resources requests 100m / 256Mi, memory limit 512Mi, no CPU limit (observed ~125-150 MiB RSS) Probes liveness and readiness on /health/live; generous startup probe. /health/ready returns 503 whenever an input is stale, which would remove the endpoint and stop the scrape exactly when the metrics matter, so alert on battery_optimizer_ready instead Service / scrape ClusterIP battery-optimizer:8080 (http); ServiceMonitor labelled operator.prometheus.io/instance: prometheus-long-term (job battery-optimizer, 30 s), so battery_optimizer_* lives in the long-term Prometheus for the multi-week comparison Alerts PrometheusRule/battery-optimizer-service (long-term Prometheus): BatteryOptimizerServiceDown, ServiceAbsent, NotReady (30 m), HomeAssistantDisconnected (10 m), GridPowerStale (15 m), PlanStale (1 h), SolveFailures, SinkWriteErrors, SolvesSkipped, HistoryStale, the climate shadow alerts (rules-service/climate-shadow.yaml) and the live control alerts (rules-service/actuator.yaml) Dashboard ConfigMap dashboards-battery-optimizer, Grafana folder battery-optimizer, datasource prometheus-long-term: Battery optimizer service, Battery optimizer climate shadow, Battery: plan vs actual, Battery: load forecast, Battery: model and actuation, Battery: temperature, Tariff prices and the six Climate: ... dashboards (see Dashboards per component)

docs.title: Dashboards per component
docs.text:
One dashboard per component KPI table of the app repository (docs/components/*.md, section "KPIs"). They share the ${datasource} variable (default prometheus-long-term), the tags battery-optimizer, energy and battery, and a dashboard-links block that lists every dashboard tagged battery, so the six battery dashboards link to each other (a new battery dashboard needs only the tag). Panel descriptions state each sign and every approximation.

Component Dashboard (uid) What it answers battery-optimizer Battery: plan vs actual (battery-plan-vs-actual), Battery optimizer service (battery-optimizer-shadow) day-ahead against final plan against actual; readiness, solves, shadow-vs-native cost battery-load-forecast Battery: load forecast (battery-load-forecast) forecast error of the two plans battery-model Battery: model and actuation (battery-model-actuation) commanded, planned and actual power (+ charge), clamped power and energy not delivered, SOC tracking error at the slot boundary, daily discharge/charge ratio. The commanded power is derived (charge: PD target - house load, since the PD target is a grid-import setpoint; discharge: - system discharge cap, a ceiling). There is no round-trip-efficiency metric: the panel is a discharge/charge ratio, and an "RTE estimate" line is drawn only while the SOC moved 3 points or less over the 24 h battery-thermal Battery: temperature (battery-temperature) measured against predicted temperature, derate factor and state, Omnibattery's limit settings, predicted achievable against actual charge power, MAE, RMSE and bias per lead (final, 1h, 3h), model status, parameters, last fit, refits and predictions by result; the HA sensor sensor.venus_internal_temperature and the hours above 35, 40 and 45 degC. Needs planning.thermal.mode: shadow (service 0.10.0); the error panels fill as slots close, the last-fit stat and the derate-error panels stay empty until a refit is accepted and a derate slot has closed tariff-prices Tariff prices (battery-tariff-prices) next-day publication (state, last flip time, hour per day), price and plan horizon, day-ahead lead, the PVPC price from sensor.esios_pvpc (current hour only; the forward curve is a sensor attribute, not a metric), daily cost native against counterfactual and their difference

The cost panels are delta() sums over the per-process-run gauges shadow_native_cost_eur and shadow_counterfactual_cost_eur (they restart at 0 with every pod, so a restart makes the day approximate). Since the battery is commissioned, native is the house with the battery as it ran and counterfactual the replayed shadow decisions: the pair is not a house with and without the battery. shadow has no actuator, so the actuator panels need dry_run or live.

Size. The ConfigMap holds all thirteen JSON files (about 460 KB). Client-side apply stores the whole object in the last-applied-configuration annotation, which is limited to 256 KiB, so the ConfigMap in templates/dashboards.yaml carries argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: ServerSideApply=true (as kanidm, pyroscope and tempo do). The object limit is 1 MiB, so there is room for roughly the same again; past about 800 KB split the climate files into a second ConfigMap dashboards-climate (a second template with the same label and ServerSideApply, its own file glob and target-directory annotation).

docs.title: Climate dashboards per component
docs.text:
The climate KPI tables of the app repository (docs/components/*.md, section "KPIs") follow the same pattern: one dashboard per component that has at least three meaningful KPI panels, shared dashboards with one titled row per component where it does not. All carry the tags battery-optimizer, energy and climate, the ${datasource} variable and a dashboard-links block "Climate dashboards" (every dashboard tagged climate, so a new climate dashboard needs only the tag; Battery optimizer climate shadow carries it too and keeps its own panels). A panel description states what is approximated. Where the headline KPI has no metric yet, the panel shows the measured side or a baseline and the closing text panel "Not yet measured" names the gap.

Component Dashboard (uid) What it answers climate-mpc Climate: comfort MPC (climate-mpc) plan production (runs by result, planned share), solver health (solves by status, not-optimal share, duration), top-offset share, degree-hours below 21 degC and the hall-kitchen against 23.5 degC as the rule delivered them thermal-model Climate: thermal model (climate-thermal-model) room-mean RMSE, skill and bias per lead (1, 6, 12, 24 h) and window against the preregistered limits, daily heat MdAPE, scored origins and valid weeks, measured room temperatures, gate status, refits cop-model Climate: COP model (climate-cop) the measured side: COP from the HeishaMon counters (24 h, 7 d, by mode), reported COP, lift in heat mode, starts and compressor hours (the d and e terms), heat and electricity per day. The model's own error is offline (hack/climate_cop.py) heat-pump-controller Climate: heat-pump controller (climate-heat-pump-controller) room temperature against setpoint and the section-B comfort criteria, rule activity (heating and hot-water hours against min_hours, starts, water target), kWh per heating degree-day, heater safety and tank cap outdoor-temperature Climate: outdoor temperature (climate-outdoor-temperature) the unit sensor and compressor frequency, trusted, unknown and duty shares from the compressor frequency, weather forecast archive fetches and age hp-consumption-forecast, boost-mode Climate: planned components (climate-planned), one row each planned, not built: the heat-pump load and a same-slot-yesterday baseline (MAE, bias) the forecast must beat; for boost the grid import against the 5.0 kW limit, battery SOC and charge power, tank maximum against 50 degC and the heater states

Decisions: the first five have at least three KPI panels with real series (the outdoor-temperature ones are compressor-frequency approximations, and its forecast-error KPI is not measured). The two planned components have no metric of their own, only preconditions and baselines, so they share one dashboard with a titled row each instead of two near-empty ones. The thermal-model dashboard repeats the accuracy panels of Battery optimizer climate shadow on purpose (that one stays the job-level view) and adds the preregistered limits as dashed lines.

Gaps (no metric exists): the MPC's planned comfort deficit and planned against actual heat-pump energy, the COP model's predicted COP and error, the outdoor temperature forecast error, the heat-pump consumption forecast error, boost activations and soak energy; the controller's decisions. The weather archive panels expose a real effect: while the weather.forecast_home entity does not answer, weather_forecast_fetches_total{result="failed"} grows and the MPC horizon holds the last reading.

Day-ahead and final plan (0.9.0). The service keeps, per 15-minute slot, the day-ahead plan (the first plan that covered the slot, usually made the previous afternoon) next to the final plan (the intent frozen when the slot opened) and scores both against what happened. The metrics are battery_optimizer_slot_*{plan="day_ahead|final"}, load_forecast_*_total{plan}, plan_revision_kwh_total and shadow_day_ahead_energy_kwh_total; they appear after the first slot opens and closes, and the day-ahead values after a restart are rebuilt from the plan files on the PVC (startup log day-ahead rebuilt plan_files=N slots=M). Home Assistant gets four more template sensors from /plan current_slot in apps/home-assistant/config/integrations/battery_optimizer_plan.yaml: sensor.battery_optimizer_day_ahead_power and sensor.battery_optimizer_day_ahead_soc (next to the planned power and SOC, which the Battery dashboard calls Final plan), and sensor.battery_optimizer_day_ahead_load / sensor.battery_optimizer_final_load (forecast house load in W). They keep the existing sign (+ discharging, - charging), are unknown while the slot has no such plan and unavailable when the service does not answer (a service older than 0.9.0 has no current_slot, so they stay unknown). The Battery dashboard (dashboard-battery, storage mode) charts them as Day-ahead plan, Final plan and Actual (power, SOC and house load).

Passive archives (0.3.0). The archive: block of service.yaml turns on two append-only collectors under /data/service/v1/: pvpc_snapshots/ (every state change of the PVPC price sensor, to measure when next-day prices really appear) and weather_forecasts/ (weather.get_forecasts for weather.forecast_home, hourly at HH:05 UTC). The weather query is the single call_service frame the HA guard lets through; every other service call is still refused in code. Watch battery_optimizer_pvpc_snapshots_total, battery_optimizer_weather_forecast_fetches_total{result} and battery_optimizer_archive_last_success_timestamp_seconds. There is no retention yet.

The shadow store (/data/service/v1/) is private household data and is covered by the same PVC snapshots. Read the comparison with battery-optimizer shadow-report from a pod or a copy of the store; comparison_basis stays no_battery_pre_commissioning until battery telemetry is mapped, and that basis does not satisfy exit gate C.

Checks without a port-forward:

kubectl --context=grigri -n battery-optimizer exec deploy/battery-optimizer-service -- \
  python -c "import urllib.request as u; print(u.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8080/health/ready').read().decode())"

docs.title: Climate shadow (track B2)
docs.text:
From 0.4.0 the service also runs the climate shadow (climate_shadow: in files/service.yaml): the thermal model and the price-blind comfort MPC of the app repository on live data. Every hour at HH:10 UTC, on its own worker thread, it reads, predicts, plans, records and scores. It is read-only and actuates nothing: the plan is written to the PVC and never sent anywhere, it uses no new credential, and the HA guard still refuses every service call but weather.get_forecasts. App-side reference: docs/service.md#climate-shadow-track-b2 and the preregistration docs/planning/climate-preregistration-2026-27.md in the app repository.

Input Source Room temperatures and setpoints (four thermostats), Aquarea outdoor sensor, outlet target, compressor frequency, heat / DHW / cool power consumed and produced, force-DHW switch, legacy AppDaemon enable and minimum hours, PVPC long-term Prometheus (hass_* series), 30 days fetched at the first run and then incrementally input_boolean.comfort_control_enable (regime), input_text.comfort_dhw_plan, input_boolean.comfort_away Home Assistant, through the existing read-only session; each may be absent. Until the comfort controller is deployed they do not exist and every record is regime legacy Outdoor forecast the service's own weather archive (weather_forecasts/, fetched at HH:05)

Failure isolation. A missing prior, site file or config, a Prometheus error or a solver failure is logged (climate shadow not loaded: ..., climate shadow run failed), counted, written as a climate_shadow_error event and retried the next hour. It never changes readiness and never touches the battery planner, which keeps solving every 15 minutes. A healthy job logs nothing; check /status.

Files.

Path In git? Content /config/climate.yaml, /config/climate-mpc.yaml yes, files/ (public in the app repo too) Comfort rooms, filters, MPC horizon and schedule. Keep them byte-identical to the app repository: their sha256 is part of every climate record's lineage /data/analysis/v1/climate-shadow/priors/<prior>/prior.json no, PVC only The season prior (model parameters fitted on household data), content-addressed and write-once; climate_shadow.prior names it /data/climate/site.yaml no, PVC only Private site file (coordinates, reference station). Never commit it or paste it anywhere /data/service/v1/climate_{decisions,scores,days,models}/ no The shadow's records, written by the service; covered by the PVC snapshots and just pull-store

The prior and the site file stay out of this public repository and out of Vault: they are not credentials, and the job reads them from the data directory only. They are copied onto the PVC once from the owner's workstation, which keeps them in ~/data/battery-optimizer-cluster (the just pull-store copy of the PVC).

Install or refresh the prior. In the app repository, on a clean checkout of the deployed commit, with BATTERY_OPTIMIZER_DATA_DIR=~/data/battery-optimizer-cluster:

uv run python hack/climate_shadow_prior.py --feature-set <climate feature set id> \
  --dataset ~/data/battery-optimizer-cluster/analysis/v1/<dataset id> --season S3
# prints the prior id and writes analysis/v1/climate-shadow/priors/<id>/prior.json

Copy it and the site file onto the PVC through the running pod (the image has tar; /data is the only writable path):

PRIOR=<id>; SRC=~/data/battery-optimizer-cluster
tar -C "$SRC" -cf - "analysis/v1/climate-shadow/priors/$PRIOR/prior.json" climate/site.yaml \
  | kubectl --context=grigri -n battery-optimizer exec -i deploy/battery-optimizer-service -c service -- \
      tar -xf - -C /data --no-same-owner

then set climate_shadow.prior: "<id>" in files/service.yaml and merge. A prior directory can stay on the PVC after it is replaced: only the configured one is loaded.

Go-live of the comfort controller. On the day the comfort controller takes over, set climate_shadow.go_live: "YYYY-MM-DD" (local date) in files/service.yaml and merge. Without it there is no new-window verdict (the first comfort record is only reported as a provisional date); the new window starts 7 days after go_live. Do not change the prior, the comfort rooms or climate-mpc.yaml around go-live: any of them starts a new lineage, which the gates evaluate apart.

Read the gate report (from the store on the PVC, no network; it prints private figures, keep the output local):

kubectl --context=grigri -n battery-optimizer exec deploy/battery-optimizer-service -c service -- \
  battery-optimizer climate-shadow-report            # add --format json for the raw report

Per window (legacy, new) it shows the valid heating days and weeks (6 weeks are needed, else every criterion is UNDETERMINED), each preregistered criterion with its value, threshold and PASS / FAIL / UNDETERMINED, RMSE, persistence RMSE, skill and bias at 1, 6, 12 and 24 h, the daily heat MdAPE, solver statuses and times and the top-offset share. /status (climate_shadow) shows the prior, model hash, last run, scoring queue, error, go-live and the two verdicts.

When to refit the prior. The weekly ua/q0 re-estimation runs inside the service; the prior stays fixed through both preregistered windows. Fit a new one for the next heating season, or earlier only when a model input changes: the outdoor sensor or the heat measurement, the comfort rooms or their thermostats. A change of the schedule, the water curve or the machine limits is an edit of climate-mpc.yaml (vendor it from the app repository), not a refit. Record either in the app repository's regime log.

Expected after a deploy. The first run happens at the next HH:10 (or at once if the pod starts after HH:10). battery_optimizer_climate_shadow_up is 0 until then and 1 afterwards; runs_total{result="planned"} and solves_total{status="optimal"} grow every hour; regime{regime="legacy"} is 1; the first refits_total is counted at the first run. Accuracy series (rmse_kelvin, skill_ratio, ...) appear once the first origins are scored, 24 to 48 h later, and the gates stay UNDETERMINED until 6 valid heating weeks are in a window.

Alerts (rules-service/climate-shadow.yaml): BatteryOptimizerClimateShadowDown (up == 0 for 2 h), ClimateShadowNoRun (no run for 2 h), ClimateShadowRunErrors (more than 2 errors in 6 h), ClimateShadowSolveFailures (infeasible or error solves) and ClimateShadowNoState (the climate series have gaps). Dashboard: Battery optimizer climate shadow (runs, solver, accuracy per horizon, valid weeks, gates, regime).

docs.title: Live battery control
docs.text:
ADR-0007 in the app repository (docs/adr/0007-live-battery-control.md, operations in docs/service.md#live-control-dry_run-and-live) adds mode: dry_run | live to files/service.yaml. The service then sets Omnibattery's direction switches, PD grid target and discharge cap through a narrow write allowlist; Omnibattery stays the only Modbus writer. The deployed mode is shadow until the owner changes it. The battery and its Omnibattery setup are in home-assistant-omnibattery.md.

Piece Where State Kill switch input_boolean.battery_optimizer_live apps/home-assistant/config/integrations/battery_optimizer.yaml Read by the service only. Created off; restores its last state across HA restarts (no initial:) Heartbeat input_datetime.battery_optimizer_heartbeat same file Written by every reconciled live tick (~30 s) Watchdog automation battery_optimizer_watchdog same file Every minute: kill switch on and heartbeat older than 5 min -> both direction switches and switch.omnibattery_weekly_full_charge_enabled off (the last in its own continue_on_error step, so an unavailable entity blocks nothing); also on the kill switch's off edge. Persistent notification battery_optimizer_watchdog (replaced, not stacked) Live token global.liveHomeAssistantToken in values.yaml (default false) Off: nothing rendered. On: ExternalSecret battery-optimizer-home-assistant-live, mounted in the service at /secrets/home-assistant/BATTERY_OPTIMIZER_HA_TOKEN instead of the read-only token. The pipeline keeps the read-only token Alerts rules-service/actuator.yaml See Alerts AC failsafe apps/esphome/config/smart-plug-v2-battery.yaml See ESPHome AC failsafe. Must be flashed by hand

Tokens. shadow and dry_run use the read-only battery-optimizer HA user. live uses the separate non-admin user battery-optimizer-live (group system-users, local only), whose long-lived token the owner keeps in pass. Home Assistant cannot restrict a token to entities, so the service's ha_guard allowlist is the restriction. Rendering fails when files/service.yaml says mode: live while global.liveHomeAssistantToken is false (ArgoCD then shows a ComparisonError and syncs nothing), so live never runs on the read-only token.

Watchdog in dry_run. dry_run keeps the kill switch on (rollout step 2) but sends no heartbeat, so the watchdog turns both direction switches off every minute and keeps its notification up. That is expected: nothing else should be driving the battery during the rehearsal. The heartbeat and kill-switch alerts exclude dry_run for that reason.

Omnibattery weekly full charge. switch.omnibattery_weekly_full_charge_enabled must stay off by default, and so must switch.omnibattery_weekly_full_charge_delay. When full_charge.mode: live the optimizer owns the weekly switch (it arms it for the periodic full charge), and the watchdog turns it off together with the direction switches, so a dead optimizer never leaves it armed.

docs.title: Live token in Vault
docs.text:
Once, before the first live rollout. Load the token from a 0600 file, never from the command line, and never print it:

export VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.internal.grigri.cloud
umask 077
TOKEN_FILE="$(mktemp)"
# Put only the battery-optimizer-live user's long-lived token in "$TOKEN_FILE", taken from
# `pass iot/hass-battery-optimizer-live` (no trailing newline).
vault kv put secret/battery-optimizer/home-assistant-live token=@"$TOKEN_FILE"
shred -u "$TOKEN_FILE"
vault kv metadata get secret/battery-optimizer/home-assistant-live   # check it exists, no value shown

The ExternalSecret only exists while the flag is on, so a missing Vault secret shows up at the live rollout: SecretSyncedError on battery-optimizer-home-assistant-live and the new service pod stuck in ContainerCreating. The kill switch is off at that point, so nothing reaches the battery; roll back.

docs.title: ESPHome AC failsafe
docs.text:
The battery holds its last charge or discharge command while Home Assistant is down (commissioning test: outages of 23 s to 10.5 minutes, no device timeout). The watchdog and the service's safe idle both need HA, so the battery's AC plug (Athom Smart Plug V2 "Battery", switch.smart_plug_v2_battery) carries a failsafe in its own device file. The shared packages/smart-plug-v2.yaml is unchanged:

  • after 5 minutes without a Home Assistant API client (api.connected with state_subscription_only, so a log viewer does not count; checked every 10 s), the relay turns off. The battery then only powers its backup port and stops charging or discharging to the house;
  • when HA reconnects, the relay turns back on, only if the failsafe turned it off. A global with restore_value remembers that across reboots; any relay turn-on clears it. A relay the owner switched off stays off;
  • relay_restore_mode: RESTORE_DEFAULT_ON: a reboot or OTA restores the last state, and ON when nothing was saved. A failsafe OFF is restored as OFF and switched on again when HA returns;
  • ESPHome's own api reboot_timeout (default 15 min) reboots the plug during a long HA outage. The relay stays off through it.

It also trips on a Wi-Fi loss of 5 minutes. When the AC comes back the inverter goes back to Bypass, and Omnibattery may report backup_mode for a few minutes; the optimizer holds safe idle meanwhile.

Flashing. Pushing changes only the ConfigMap that the ESPHome dashboard reads (Reloader restarts the esphome pod); the plug keeps its old firmware until it is flashed over OTA. Either use the dashboard at esphome.internal.grigri.cloud (smart-plug-v2-battery -> Install -> Wirelessly), or flash from apps/esphome/config (see its README.md):

cd apps/esphome/config
make requirements
KUBE_CONTEXT=grigri make secrets
make smart-plug-v2-battery.yaml   # esphome run: compile + OTA

The plug reboots once (a few seconds) and restores the relay ON. The failsafe firmware has been on the plug since 2026-11-03 (ESPHome 2026.10.1) and passed the hardware test on 2026-11-04. Flash while the battery is idle (direction switches off), then check switch.smart_plug_v2_battery is on.

Known limit. A manual relay ON (HA or the plug's button) during a long HA absence is undone within 10 s: the absence counter is only reset by an HA reconnect or a reboot, not by a manual turn-on. To force AC while HA stays down, power-cycle the plug, then press the button (5 more minutes of grace). Fix candidate: let a manual turn-on suspend the failsafe until HA reconnects.

Servers on the backup port. Since 2026-11-03 the backup port feeds the servers (~250 W) that host Home Assistant. A trip makes them run from the battery: at 50 % SOC that is roughly 8 h before the battery's own cutoff. An HA outage longer than that drains the battery and stops the servers; the plug then has to be switched on by hand (power-cycle + button).

docs.title: Failsafe test
docs.text:
Passed on the flashed firmware on 2026-11-04 (see the result below). Repeat it after any change to the failsafe or the plug's firmware. It takes ~15 minutes and Home Assistant is really stopped for ~6 minutes. The servers switch to battery power for the switchover and back, the same switchover the commissioning test passed with the TV (max ping gap 0.22 s).

Preconditions:

  • SOC above 30 %, battery in Bypass, Omnibattery balanced, backup-port load below the 500 W threshold.
  • Kill switch input_boolean.battery_optimizer_live off (both direction switches off), so the optimizer does not chase the battery while it is islanded. Note the time; turn it back on at the end.
  • A second way to reach the plug if HA misbehaves: the relay button, and the ESPHome logs from a workstation (apps/esphome/config: KUBE_CONTEXT=grigri make secrets, then make logs FILE=smart-plug-v2-battery.yaml; a log subscription is not a state subscriber, so it does not keep the relay on). Delete secrets.yaml afterwards.
  • The Kubernetes API must stay reachable from the workstation: the servers host HA and the cluster. Do not run it if a server reboot would be a problem.

Steps (T = the moment HA is gone; the scaling only with the owner's explicit go):

  1. Start the ESPHome logs and note switch.smart_plug_v2_battery = on, sensor.venus_inverter_state = Bypass, sensor.venus_ac_offgrid_power ≈ servers' load.
  2. Stop HA for real, following Stopping Home Assistant under ArgoCD: scale argocd/argocd-repo-server to 0 first, then home-assistant/home-assistant-hass to 0. T: the pod is gone and the plug logs the lost API connection (Reading failed CONNECTION_CLOSED). Lighter alternative: Settings → Devices & services → ESPHome → smart-plug-v2-battery-9d9516 → ⋮ → Disable drops only the plug's API connection and leaves HA running.
  3. ~T+5:00: the log shows Battery failsafe: no Home Assistant for 5 min, relay OFF. Within seconds the battery reports Backup Mode (Omnibattery keeps polling it over Modbus) and the servers keep running (check the Kubernetes API or a ping).
  4. T+6: restore HA first, then argocd-repo-server (same doc). Within ~10 s of the HA API reconnect the log shows Battery failsafe: Home Assistant is back, relay ON; the switch is on in HA and the inverter returns to Bypass within 5–33 s. The home-assistant app shows sync Unknown until Argo's next refresh (about 3 min); a hard refresh clears it.
  5. Manual-off check: with HA connected, turn switch.smart_plug_v2_battery off, wait 30 s: it must stay off (the failsafe only restores what it turned off). Turn it on again; the battery returns to Bypass.
  6. Turn the kill switch back on and check the optimizer takes control at the next 15-minute slot.

Pass: relay off at about T+5:00 (up to ~10 s early, see the result), back on within 20 s of the HA reconnect, manual off respected, servers never lost power. Fail or abort:

  • relay still on at T+6:00: the failsafe does not trip (likely api.connected still sees a state subscriber). Restore HA and treat the battery as unprotected against HA outages until fixed;
  • relay not back on 1 minute after HA is back: turn it on from HA; if HA cannot reach the plug, press the button once;
  • any server reboots during the switchover: put the servers back on mains and stop using the backup port until the switchover is understood.

Record the timings in this section and in the regime log of the optimizer repo.

Result 2026-11-04: PASS (HA really stopped, repo-server scaled to 0 as above; kill switch off 08:29:35, SOC 45 %, backup-port load ~220 W):

Event Time (UTC) Timing HA stopped / pod gone 08:32:31 / 08:32:34 T Plug relay OFF 08:37:25 4:52 after the plug lost the HA API connection, 4:51 after the pod was gone HA back (API connected) 08:38:48 HA down ~6:17 Plug relay ON 08:38:56 8 s after reconnect (limit 20 s) Inverter back in Bypass ~08:39:06 ~10 s after relay ON Manual OFF 08:40:09 respected for the 46 s observed, no failsafe restore Manual ON, then Bypass 08:41:05 ~7 s Kill switch ON, optimizer in control 08:41:44 discharging from 08:42:25 (~40 s)
  • The trip is a few seconds before T+5:00 measured from the pod being gone: the 5-minute counter starts when HA drops its state subscriptions, shortly before the TCP close. Not an early trip.
  • The servers never rebooted: no pod restarts, the Kubernetes API answered /readyz throughout. One Modbus sample at the switchover showed the backup output at 0 W for one ~6 s poll interval; that is the inverter's reading during the mode change, not a 6 s outage.
  • SOC 45 % -> 44 % (live discharge resumed, ~254 W).
  • Grid side (Shelly EM per-minute history, averages): ~450 W from the grid with the battery idle (kill switch off). During the trip the servers' ~220 W moved to the battery (grid minute 08:38 averaged 241 W), back to ~450 W after the relay came on. No visible import spike at reconnection (minute resolution only).

docs.title: Rollout: dry_run, then live
docs.text:
Preconditions (owner):

  • The HA helpers and the watchdog are deployed. Pushing them restarts Home Assistant through Reloader, so check the Shelly GET /cit/d first (see the CoIoT note above). In Developer tools, check that the three entity IDs exist without a _2 suffix and that the kill switch is off.
  • The ESPHome failsafe is flashed and tested (passed 2026-11-04).
  • Omnibattery: competing strategies off (configuration); the PD controller stays on balanced (number.omnibattery_pd_controller_max_power_change 800 W; an earlier version of this page asked for 2000 W, but the PD log shows 800 W since 2026-11-03 and it never bound). Note the backup threshold workaround.
  • At the time (2026-11-03) the system caps were 1000 W charge / 800 W discharge until go-live (steps 1-2 of the live phase), so in dry_run the charge clamping reflected the 1000 W cap minus the house load. Current values: 2500 W / 2500 W since go-live, see Entities.

dry_run (1-2 days):

  1. Update the image to the optimizer release with live control (Renovate PR, or by hand) and vendor its config/service.yaml changes (the actuation: section). Set mode: dry_run in files/service.yaml. Merge; ArgoCD rolls the pod.
  2. Check /status (mode: dry_run, an actuator block) and battery_optimizer_build_info{mode="dry_run"}.
  3. Turn the kill switch on. Nothing is sent; the watchdog keeps the switches off (see above).
  4. Review /data/service/v1/actuation/ and the battery_optimizer_actuator_* metrics: guard reasons, the mapping at every slot, setpoint churn, how often a charge is clamped, and the house-load estimate against the meter.

live, supervised:

Go-live steps first, with the battery idle. Above 800 W of discharge the Venus needs Premium mode, and with the system power limits on the PD target is bounded by the system caps (ADR-0007 commissioning findings):

  1. Turn both Allow switches (switch.venus_battery_allow_charge, switch.venus_battery_allow_discharge) off, then switch Premium mode on in the Marstek app. Change nothing else in the app.
  2. Set number.omnibattery_system_max_charge_power and number.omnibattery_system_max_discharge_power to 2500 W (2026-11-03: 1000 / 800 W). The Venus's own number.venus_max_charge_power / _max_discharge_power are already 2500 W; check them.

Then:

  1. Put the live token in Vault (above).
  2. Turn the kill switch off.
  3. In one commit: mode: live in files/service.yaml (the app also requires planning.soc_source: entity for live) and global.liveHomeAssistantToken: true in values.yaml. Merge.
  4. Check kubectl --context=grigri -n battery-optimizer get externalsecret (both SecretSynced), the new pod running, /status mode: live, and battery_optimizer_build_info{mode="live"}.
  5. Turn the kill switch on while watching the grid meter. Verify: writes confirmed (battery_optimizer_actuator_writes_total{result="ok"}), the heartbeat entity advancing about every 30 s, a slot change in each direction, the import staying under 4500 W while charging, and the charge and discharge reaching up to 2500 W (minus the house load for a charge).
  6. Watchdog test: pause ArgoCD auto-sync for the app, scale the Deployment to 0, and within about 6 minutes see both direction switches go off, the battery_optimizer_watchdog notification and BatteryOptimizerHeartbeatStale. Scale back to 1 and resume auto-sync. (Run these kubectl writes only with the owner's explicit go.)
  7. Graceful stop: delete the pod (ArgoCD recreates it) and check that the actuation records show a safe idle with reason shutdown before the restart, and that the new pod holds safe idle until its first fresh plan.

Only then leave it unattended. HA host power loss is still untested (app repo TODO-5.4); the AC failsafe is the layer that does not depend on HA.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
1. Turn input_boolean.battery_optimizer_live off. This is immediate: the service sets safe idle once and stops writing, and the watchdog repeats the safe idle in HA. In an emergency, also turn the Allow switches off on the Battery dashboard, or the battery's AC plug.
  2. In one commit: mode: shadow (or dry_run) in files/service.yaml and global.liveHomeAssistantToken: false. Merge. ArgoCD prunes the live ExternalSecret and its Secret and the pod restarts on the read-only token. The flag cannot go off while the mode is still live (rendering fails).
  3. Restore Omnibattery's native configuration by hand: safe idle leaves the PD target and the discharge cap at their last values, so set them back before switching a direction on. Decide whether the 2500 W system caps and Premium mode stay (both Allow switches off while changing them).
  4. To retire the live user for good: delete its long-lived token in HA (the user's profile, as an admin) and vault kv metadata delete secret/battery-optimizer/home-assistant-live.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
rules-service/actuator.yaml, long-term Prometheus. The actuator_* series exist only in dry_run and live; the HA-side rules read hass_* and only fire while the kill switch is on.

Alert Fires when BatteryOptimizerActuatorAlert (critical) actuator_alert == 1 for 2 m: a write was not confirmed after its retries BatteryOptimizerActuatorSafeIdle in control and the guard has held safe idle for 30 m (actuator_guard_reason says why) BatteryOptimizerImportOverCap (critical) guard reason import_over_cap: import above 4700 W while charging BatteryOptimizerHeartbeatFailures a heartbeat write failed in the last 10 m BatteryOptimizerHeartbeatStale (critical) the heartbeat entity is older than 5 m while the kill switch is on (not in dry_run); fires with the service down BatteryOptimizerKillSwitchOnNotLive the kill switch has been on for 15 m while the service is not live or dry_run (or is down) BatteryOptimizerChargePowerHigh measured battery charge above 2600 W for 2 m (the go-live caps are 2500 W): a cap or battery_ac_power_sign is wrong BatteryOptimizerChargeClamped battery_optimizer_actuator_clamped_watts > 1000 for 30 m (sized for the 2500 W caps). Unconfirmed metric name from the unreleased optimizer change; check it against the released /metrics

docs.title: Omnibattery backup cooldown workaround
docs.text: number.venus_backup_offgrid_threshold is 500 W (default 50 W) because of upstream bug ffunes/Omnibattery#660 (backup_mode latched after the grid returns while the backup port has a load). The fix is ffunes/Omnibattery#723. Once a release with #723 is installed, set the threshold back to 50 W and check that the status returns to balanced within 5 minutes with a load on the backup port in Bypass. Side effects of the high threshold and the full procedure: home-assistant-omnibattery.md.

docs.title: Battery settings: where they are and how to read them
docs.text: The battery is a Marstek Venus E V3 driven by Omnibattery (v1.5.1b1 at the time of writing). Settings sit in three places: the device (Marstek app), Omnibattery's own entities in Home Assistant, and the optimizer's files/service.yaml. All reads below are read-only.

docs.title: Entities
docs.text:
Entity Value on 2026-11-04 Set by number.venus_max_discharge_power 2500 W (range 800-2500) The device: Marstek app Premium mode. Never written by us number.venus_max_charge_power 2500 W The device. Never written by us number.omnibattery_system_max_charge_power 2500 W The owner, in the Omnibattery settings number.omnibattery_system_max_discharge_power varies per slot Rewritten by the optimizer every slot: the per-slot discharge cap (actuation.entities.max_discharge_power; 0 = unlimited) number.omnibattery_pd_target_grid_power varies per slot Written by the optimizer: the grid-import target switch.omnibattery_system_power_limits on Written by the optimizer number.omnibattery_max_contracted_power 5000 W The owner

Owned by the owner and read-only for the optimizer:

  • select.omnibattery_pd_tuning_profile (balanced) and the PD controller numbers (kp 0.35, kd 0.3, deadband 40 W, direction hysteresis 60 W, max power change 800 W). How they act, the baseline and the change log: Omnibattery PD controller settings log. Integration source: https://github.com/ffunes/omnibattery.
  • The temperature limit: switch.omnibattery_temp_charge_limit and its numbers. The owner toggles it; the optimizer only reads it.

Optimizer-side knobs live in the deployed apps/battery-optimizer/files/service.yaml, actuation: block:

Key Value Meaning import_cap_w 4500 Upper bound of the PD grid-import target (the meter trips at 5 kW) import_guard_margin_w 200 Margin the guard keeps below the import cap discharge_margin_w 100 Import kept while discharging, never export. 100 W since 2026-11-05 (owner decision, optimizer 0.14.0, with planning.discharge_margin_bound: true). Steady-state error is about +-40 W (the PD deadband); export comes from 1-4 s transients when a large load stops while the battery is cap-pinned. 50 W gave brief exports min_discharge_cap_w 100 Smallest per-slot discharge cap written max_discharge_cap_w 2500 Largest per-slot discharge cap written neutral_pd_target_w 0 PD grid target in a planned idle

docs.title: Device facts and Omnibattery configuration
docs.text:
Item Value Venus E V3 firmware EMS 148, VMS 117, BMS 114 (as of commissioning, 2026-11-03) Marstek app Manual mode, empty schedule, no meter configured, Premium mode on (see the go-live steps). Never change it while Omnibattery runs Grid sensor The Shelly EM, channel 1 SOC window 20-95 % Contracted power 5000 W. The meter trips instantly, so charge targets stay at most 4500 W (import_cap_w)

Every Omnibattery feature that competes with the optimizer is off: predictive charging, charge delay, capacity protection, hourly balance and the weekly full charge. The weekly full charge is the one exception: full_charge.mode is shadow today, so its switches stay off; with live the optimizer arms it itself (see Live battery control).

docs.title: How to read them
docs.text:
1. Prometheus (prometheus-long-term) exports HA switch states (hass_switch_state), sensors and, verified 2026-11-06, the Omnibattery and Venus number entities: hass_number_state (unitless, such as kp and kd, e.g. hass_number_state{entity="number.omnibattery_pd_controller_kp"}) and the unit-suffixed hass_number_state_w, _s, _percent, _celsius, _kwh and _h. The select entities have no value series, only hass_state_change_total, hass_entity_available and hass_last_updated_time_seconds. Prometheus therefore gives what changed and when; the settings log gives why.
  2. select values and attributes (min/max): run a short Python inside the optimizer pod. It uses the pod's own HA token file (BATTERY_OPTIMIZER_HA_TOKEN_FILE) and URL (BATTERY_OPTIMIZER_HA_URL, a ws URL: the script converts it to http and strips /api/websocket) with GET /api/states. The token never leaves the pod and is never printed. Use a GET only, never a POST with it. Save the script as hastates.py and pipe it on stdin:
kubectl --context=grigri -n battery-optimizer exec -i deploy/battery-optimizer-service -c service -- python - < hastates.py

import os,json,urllib.request,re
tok=open(os.environ['BATTERY_OPTIMIZER_HA_TOKEN_FILE']).read().strip()
base=os.environ['BATTERY_OPTIMIZER_HA_URL'].rstrip('/')
base=re.sub(r'^ws',r'http',base); base=re.sub(r'/api/websocket$','',base)
req=urllib.request.Request(base+'/api/states',headers={'Authorization':'Bearer '+tok})
st=json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req,timeout=20))
pat=re.compile(r'^(number|select|switch|sensor)\.(omnibattery|venus)_.*(discharg|max_charge|power_limit|force_mode|work_mode|user_mode|manual|contracted|pd_|max_power|backup|premium|rs485|allow|set_charge|set_discharge|ac_power|battery_power|status)')
for s in sorted(st,key=lambda s:s['entity_id']):
  if pat.search(s['entity_id']):
    a=s.get('attributes',{})
    print(s['entity_id'],'=',s['state'],a.get('unit_of_measurement',''),('min=%s max=%s'%(a.get('min'),a.get('max'))) if 'max' in a else '', a.get('options','') if s['entity_id'].startswith('select') else '')
  1. The optimizer's own view, on port 8080 in the pod: /status (the actuator, thermal and full_charge blocks) and /plan. /metrics has battery_optimizer_actuator_desired_*, battery_optimizer_actuator_observed_* and battery_optimizer_actuator_house_load_watts.
kubectl --context=grigri -n battery-optimizer exec deploy/battery-optimizer-service -c service -- \
  python -c "import urllib.request;print(urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8080/status').read().decode())"
  1. Planned against actual discharge, caps, PD target and house load over 24 h, hourly, as Prometheus query_range calls run inside the pod (same exec -i ... python - < promr.py pattern):
import urllib.request,urllib.parse,json,sys,time
end=int(time.time()); start=end-24*3600
qs={'plan_dis':'sum(increase(battery_optimizer_shadow_planned_energy_kwh_total{direction="discharge"}[1h]))',
    'act_dis':'sum(increase(battery_optimizer_shadow_actual_battery_energy_kwh_total{direction="discharge"}[1h]))',
    'plan_w':'avg_over_time(max(battery_optimizer_slot_battery_power_watts{plan="final"})[1h:1m])',
    'maxdis':'avg_over_time(max(battery_optimizer_actuator_desired_max_discharge_watts)[1h:1m])',
    'pdt':'avg_over_time(max(battery_optimizer_actuator_desired_pd_target_watts)[1h:1m])',
    'load':'avg_over_time(max(battery_optimizer_actuator_house_load_watts)[1h:1m])',
    'obs':'avg_over_time(max(battery_optimizer_actuator_observed_battery_power_watts)[1h:1m])',
    'soc':'max(hass_sensor_battery_percent{entity="sensor.venus_battery_soc"})',
    'grid':'avg_over_time(max(hass_sensor_power_w{entity="sensor.shellyem_grid_power"})[1h:1m])'}
data={}
for k,q in qs.items():
  u='http://prometheus-long-term.monitoring:9090/api/v1/query_range?'+urllib.parse.urlencode({'query':q,'start':start,'end':end,'step':3600})
  r=json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(u))['data']['result']
  data[k]={int(t):float(v) for t,v in r[0]['values']} if r else {}
ts=sorted(set().union(*[d.keys() for d in data.values()]))
print('hourUTC '+' '.join('%8s'%k for k in qs))
for t in ts:
  print(time.strftime('%d %H:%M',time.gmtime(t)),' '.join('%8.2f'%data[k][t] if t in data[k] else '%8s'%'-' for k in qs))
  1. Grafana (folder battery-optimizer), by dashboard uid: battery-plan-vs-actual, battery-load-forecast, battery-model-actuation, battery-temperature, battery-tariff-prices, and the service dashboard battery-optimizer-shadow.

kubectl exec into the service pod is read-only use here. Never print or copy the token, and never reuse it for a write: writes are the actuator's job, through its allowlist.

docs.title: Omnibattery PD controller settings log
docs.text:
Policy (owner decision 2026-11-06). The optimizer analyses the PD response and recommends values. The owner sets them by hand in HA, and every change gets a row in the log below with date, old -> new, why and result. The optimizer does not write PD settings today. A later step may let it, which would need an ADR-0007 amendment in the app repo plus bounded allowlist entries and tests.

How the settings act (integration source at commit 2c94da9, manifest 1.5.0):

  • Cycles run on each grid-sensor change plus a 2 s timer. Event-triggered cycles closer than pd_min_cycle_interval are dropped; the timer is not. The timer resets the throttle clock, so a dropped update waits up to about 2 s for the next cycle (see loop timing).
  • The grid is filtered with an EMA of tau 2 s, which snaps on jumps over 200 W.
  • Load-down guard (corrects the earlier text, 2026-11-07). A load-down is corrected by the _apply_discharge_ceiling guard (control/residual_load.py, Omnibattery 1.5.1b1), not by the feedforward. After the rate limiter the guard caps the discharge at grid + battery AC power - target, so a step is removed in one cycle. Three events matched its prediction within 1-2 W. kp, kd and max_power_change do not decide load-downs.
  • Nothing happens within deadband of the target.
  • Feedforward (not the load-down path, see the guard above): an error jump above max(5 x deadband, 400 W) that is confirmed on the next sample (80 %) issues one deadbeat command, bypassing the rate limit. It has a 10 s cooldown, and an opposite-sign step within 30 s is treated as a pulsing load.
  • Otherwise incremental PD: Kp is applied per 2 s, the derivative is filtered, and the change is clamped by max_power_change per 2 s.
  • direction_hysteresis gates charge/discharge flips.
  • Selecting a pd_tuning_profile overwrites only kp, kd and max_power_change. Profiles:
Profile kp kd max_power_change (W) very_smooth 0.22 0.15 400 smooth 0.30 0.25 600 balanced 0.35 0.30 800 aggressive 0.55 0.45 1200 very_aggressive 0.75 0.45 2000

Editing a number by hand makes the select show custom. To revert, write the numbers, not the profile. - relay_cooldown must stay 0: it holds discharge at 100 W or more after demand falls, which causes export.

Baseline (2026-11-06):

Entity Value Profile balanced kp 0.35 kd 0.30 deadband 40 W max_power_change 800 W direction_hysteresis 60 W pd_min_cycle_interval 1.0 s pd_min_charge_power 0 pd_min_discharge_power 0 pd_relay_cooldown 0 no_pd_command_delay 0

Since 2026-11-06 09:30 UTC the profile select reads custom, because kp no longer matches a profile row (see the change log).

Baseline measurement: 2 s HA history, 2026-11-03 to 2026-11-06, about 66 h, all at the baseline settings.

  • Steady discharge error, grid minus target: std about 24 W, p1/p99 about -50/+60 W. No limit cycle.
  • Charge at the 4500 W cap: p99 about +105 W over target.
  • End-to-end dead time 1-4 s. It was first attributed to the feedforward confirm plus Modbus write and inverter ramp; that was wrong for load-downs (the discharge-ceiling guard corrects them, see the correction above). The parts are the grid meter's update lag, the cycle wait (loop timing), the Modbus write and the inverter ramp. Gains cannot remove it.
  • Export comes almost only from load-down steps while the battery is pinned at its per-slot cap: 2-4 s below 0 W, worst about -290 W and about 0.27 Wh per event. That is about 0.05 Wh per discharge hour at the 100 W margin, well below the 5 Wh/day BatteryGridExport alert.
  • max_power_change was never binding: the fastest setpoint change was about 190 W/s against the 400 W/s allowed.
  • pd_control_quality was oscillating for 0.35 h of 66 h, always with fast-changing loads.

Candidate changes, applied together on 2026-11-06 (kp 0.40 instead of the 0.45 candidate):

  1. pd_min_cycle_interval 1.0 -> 0.5 s. It was expected to shorten the feedforward confirm by up to about 1 s; per the correction above the confirm is not on the load-down path, and the interval instead sets how often a dropped update waits for the timer (about 50% of updates at 1.0 s, about 25% at 0.5 s). Risk: more Modbus traffic, so watch sensor.omnibattery_non_responsive_batteries.
  2. kp 0.35 -> 0.40, a cautious first step towards the 0.45 candidate. Do not go above 0.55, where oscillation risk rises, so aggressive/very_aggressive are not recommended.

Everything else stays at baseline.

Loop timing and the grid meter (measured 2026-11-07).

  • A cycle runs on every Shelly update plus the 2 s timer, and updates inside pd_min_cycle_interval are dropped. Because the timer resets the throttle clock, a dropped update waits up to about 2 s: about 50% of updates at 1.0 s, about 25% at 0.5 s. The EMA snaps on jumps over 200 W.
  • Without the guard (battery AC power unreadable) cutting 1.4 kW takes 5-6 cycles, about 10-12 s.
  • Grid meter: Shelly EM Gen1 (SHEM, firmware v1.14.0). Mean update interval 1.69 s (2.0 s in 57% of intervals). On load drops it sees the change 0.3-2.0 s after the heat pump's own sensor (median about 0.95 s). Transport: the 2026-11-07 investigation read it as CoIoT UDP push to HA core, but the cutover record in Design notes has the grid power entity on MQTT every 2 s (or sooner on a change), which fits the 1.69 s mean better, and CoIoT multicast reaching HA core is not recorded anywhere. Unverified; check before relying on either.
  • Dropouts of 12-35 s happened about 20 times between 2026-11-03 and 11-05, none since the HA restart at 17:18 UTC on 11-05. During a dropout Omnibattery holds its last command.

Evaluating a change:

  • Compare at least a week of real events against the baseline: seconds below 0 W, export Wh per event, settle time, 60 s steady std and oscillating time.
  • Or run an owner-triggered test: switch a 1-1.6 kW load off about 10 times per setting, ABAB.
  • Revert if any of these happens: oscillating for more than 2 min, an export episode over 5 s or 0.5 Wh, non_responsive_batteries not None, or import above 4700 W while charging.

Interim verdict on the 2026-11-06 change (2026-11-07): keep, no revert criterion hit. Window: 2026-11-06 09:30 UTC to 2026-11-07, against the baseline above.

  • Oscillation: 0 s after the change (6 episodes before, longest 120 s).
  • Export episodes: 4, longest 2.0 s, largest 0.20 Wh.
  • non_responsive_batteries None throughout.
  • Maximum import while charging 4563 W against the 4700 W limit. Only about 0.9 h of charging, so weak evidence.
  • Steady 60 s std, median/p90/p99: 10/16/30 W after against 12/29/54 W before.

The 7-day review is still due around 2026-11-13.

Measured load-down exports (3 evening hot-water stops of 1.9-2.3 kW):

When Export Before the change -251 W for 4.1 s (0.23 Wh); -289 W for 3.5 s (0.27 Wh) After the change -364 W for 2.0 s (0.20 Wh)

Expected export with load-following (optimizer 0.15.0, from 2026-11-07). With the discharge cap raised in planned discharge slots, the battery carries the real load, so a load-down step now leaves the battery discharging at the old load until the guard acts.

  • Peak export of step - 100 W, so 1.3-1.8 kW for about 2 s: 1-2 Wh per event, 2-10 Wh per evening, under 1 EUR/year.
  • Rare worst case: a load drop during a Shelly dropout, about 15 Wh.
  • This exceeds the 0.5 Wh per-episode revert criterion above and may trip BatteryGridExport (5 Wh/24 h). The owner chose to keep that alert at 5 Wh.
  • Optional owner lever: pd_min_cycle_interval 0 cuts about 15-20% of the export, at the cost of more Modbus traffic.
  • Open: the grid registration. If the installation is registered as self-consumption without surplus (zero export required; RD 244/2019, UNE 217001-IN), any export matters beyond the alert. Check with the installer; it belongs to TODO-0.6 in the app repository's docs/planning/home-battery-optimizer-implementation.md.

Change log:

Date Setting Old -> new Why Result 2026-11-06 all PD settings - Baseline recorded, no change See baseline 2026-11-06 09:30 UTC pd_min_cycle_interval; pd_controller_kp 1.0 -> 0.5 s; 0.35 -> 0.40 Shorten the feedforward confirm and the PD tail on load-down steps to cut export transients (the feedforward premise was corrected 2026-11-07, see above). Kp kept below the 0.45 candidate as a cautious first step. Both changed together (not one at a time), so the effects can't be separated Interim 2026-11-07: keep, no revert criterion hit (verdict above). Final: compare with the baseline after at least 7 days (about 2026-11-13)

docs.title: Open issue: planned discharge is not delivered
docs.text:
Status: monitoring. The planner bound planning.discharge_margin_bound: true has been live with optimizer 0.14.0 since 2026-11-05 14:14 UTC, at discharge_margin_w 100. Next review about 2026-11-11, after 7 live days.

The "Final plan energy not delivered" panel on battery-model-actuation shows a discharge shortfall. Diagnosis of 2026-11-04, kept as history: part of it is an artefact of the shadow counters that ran before live control started (2026-11-03 22:45 UTC) and leaves the 24 h window after the first live day. The live part, in the morning discharge window, comes from the no-export rule, the import margin (200 W at that time) and a load forecast that ran high; the device limits and the per-slot cap are not involved. First evening at 100 W (2026-11-05): 2 s and 30 s data show the battery delivering exactly its per-slot cap whenever the house load allowed, with no temperature or actuator derating; the remaining gap was the load forecast, which placed the evening peak about 1 h late and overestimated it. 15-min means mix load-limited and cap-limited minutes, so do not use them to infer an actuator shortfall. Diagnosis, candidate fix and decision criteria: the app repository's docs/known-issues.md, section "Planned discharge is not delivered".

docs.title: First run (2026-10-25)
docs.text:
Manual Job from the CronJob on an empty PVC: success in 5m46s including the full Prometheus bootstrap (1028 parts, 5.84 M rows), peak working set about 1.15 GiB (requests 768 Mi, limit 2 Gi), about 0.54 core peak, 41.5 MiB on the volume afterwards. Steady-state runs only re-pull 8 days of HA history and 3 days of Prometheus. The PVC is the store of record. A migration of the manual ~/data/energy-baseline store was checked on 2026-10-25 and is not needed: every HA row in it (39 distinct) is already in the PVC (54), Prometheus is re-extractable, and the OMIE backfill is public. The local store stays frozen as the record behind the offline evaluation runs.

Container logs carry one httpx INFO line per request (roughly 1000 for the bootstrap), so kubelet log rotation can drop the early step N/4 lines of a long run; Loki keeps the full stream.

docs.title: Operate
docs.text:
# State
kubectl --context=grigri -n battery-optimizer get cronjob,job,pvc,externalsecret
kubectl --context=grigri -n battery-optimizer logs job/<job-name> -c pipeline

# Run one pipeline outside the schedule (e.g. after fixing a failure)
kubectl --context=grigri -n battery-optimizer create job --from=cronjob/battery-optimizer-pipeline battery-optimizer-pipeline-manual-<n>

Local analysis copy (read-only on the cluster; streams the PVC out of the service pod, validates it, and syncs it into a separate directory — never into the frozen ~/data/energy-baseline):

cd ~/home-energy-optimizer && KUBE_CONTEXT=grigri just pull-store   # ~/data/battery-optimizer-cluster

Bumping the image is a Renovate PR changing tag in apps/battery-optimizer/values.yaml. A new code version changes every dataset id, so expect one extra dataset on the next build.

Growing the volume: raise spec.resources.requests.storage in templates/pvc.yaml (allowVolumeExpansion is on). Never delete the PVC; Prune=false and Retain protect it.

docs.title: App Repository Notes
docs.text:
• Code lives in pando85/home-energy-optimizer (moved history-preserving from scripts/energy-baseline on 2026-10-24/25). Releases are cut with just release; the auto-tag workflow uses the repo secrets PAT and GPG_PRIVATE_KEY (both set). Renovate (Mend app) automerges.
  • Local analysis env: a gitignored .envrc (direnv) sets UV, KUBE_CONTEXT=grigri and BATTERY_OPTIMIZER_DATA_DIR=~/data/battery-optimizer-cluster.
  • The load-forecaster and price-outlook improvement plans (app repo docs/planning/) are parked since 2026-10-25; resume triggers are in the load plan §6 (spring 2027 cooling season, battery commissioning, household or rule change). Evaluation results stay in the private data directory.
  • Owner decisions, do not re-raise: taxes in tariff.yaml (PVPC, not important); license, DCO and GHCR bootstrap are done or not needed.

docs.title: Cilium BGP Control Plane
docs.text: Cilium replaces MetalLB for creating K8s LBs based on BGP.

docs.title: API Version
docs.text: Cilium 1.19+ uses the v2 BGP API (cilium.io/v2). The v2alpha1 CiliumBGPPeeringPolicy was removed. See troubleshooting/cilium-1.19-bgp-migration.md for migration details.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: Ansible sets up the configuration and ArgoCD deploys Cilium.

docs.title: Router config
docs.text:
In order to use Cilium BGP control plane mode we must configure Pfsense as router to be able of share BGP route table and route all network to that load balancer IPs. We use this tutorial

  • install package ffr

  • configure Services->FRR->Global Settings:

[general options]
enable=x
default_router_id=192.168.192.1
  • Services->FRR->Global Settings->Route Maps:
- name: allow-all
  description: Match any route
  action: permit
  Sequence: 100
  • Services->FRR->BGP->BGP:
[bgp router options]
enable=x
local_as=64512

[graceful restart/shutdown]
enable_bgp_graceful_shutdown=true
  • in Services->FRR->BGP->Neighbors:
- name: 192.168.192.2
  descr: grigri
  remote_as: 64513
  next_hop_self: true
  route_map_filters:
    inbound_router_map_filter: allow-all
    outbound_router_map_filter: allow-all
  allow_as_inbound: enabled
- name: 192.168.192.3
  descr: prusik
  remote_as: 64513
  next_hop_self: true
  route_map_filters:
    inbound_router_map_filter: allow-all
    outbound_router_map_filter: allow-all
  allow_as_inbound: enabled

Important: to access Cilium IP pools network from kubernetes subnet you need to add your host to bgp Some issues could be experimented if not added as docker push not working correctly.

docs.title: Deploy a New Hermes Agent Instance
When to Create a New Instance
docs.text:
Each Hermes agent runs in its own namespace with isolated storage, auth, and lifecycle. Create a new instance when you need:

  • A separate agent for a different purpose (e.g., different messaging channels, different skills)
  • Isolated data and configuration (each instance has its own /opt/data PVC)
  • Independent scaling and resource allocation

docs.title: Naming Convention
docs.text:
Parameterize by instance name N (e.g., hermes, hermes-2, hermes-3):

Resource Pattern Directory apps/hermes-N/ Namespace hermes-N Controller/Pod hermes-N / hermes-N-0 PVC hermes-N-data Ingress hermes-N.internal.grigri.cloud Kanidm OAuth2 Client hermes-N Kanidm Group hermes-users (shared across all instances) ServiceAccount hermes-agent (in namespace hermes-N) Snapshot Schedule hermes-N-zfs-backups Backup label backup: hermes-N-zfs

docs.title: 1. Create the Chart Directory
docs.text: mkdir -p apps/hermes-N/templates

docs.title: 2. Create Chart.yaml
docs.text:
apiVersion: v2
name: hermes-N
version: 0.0.0
dependencies:
  - name: app-template
    version: 5.0.1
    repository: https://bjw-s-labs.github.io/helm-charts/

docs.title: 3. Create values.yaml
docs.text:
Copy from an existing instance and replace:

  • Controller name: hermes → hermes-N
  • Container name: hermes → hermes-N
  • HERMES_DASHBOARD_PUBLIC_URL: https://hermes-N.internal.grigri.cloud
  • HERMES_DASHBOARD_OIDC_ISSUER: https://idm.grigri.cloud/oauth2/openid/hermes-N
  • Secret name: hermes-kanidm-oauth2-credentials → hermes-N-kanidm-oauth2-credentials
  • Ingress host: hermes.internal.grigri.cloud → hermes-N.internal.grigri.cloud
  • TLS secret: hermes-dashboard-tls-certificate → hermes-N-dashboard-tls-certificate
  • PVC claim: hermes-data → hermes-N-data
  • advancedMounts keys: hermes → hermes-N

Important: Keep allowed_groups=hermes-users@idm.grigri.cloud in ingress annotations — all instances share the same Kanidm group.

docs.title: 4. Create templates/pvc.yaml
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: hermes-N
    app.kubernetes.io/name: hermes-N
    backup: hermes-N-zfs
    backup/retain: quaterly
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Prune=false
  name: hermes-N-data
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi

docs.title: 5. Create templates/snapshots.yaml
docs.text:
apiVersion: snapscheduler.backube/v1
kind: SnapshotSchedule
metadata:
  name: hermes-N-zfs-backups
spec:
  retention:
    maxCount: 5
  schedule: "0 1 * * *" # UTC
  claimSelector:
    matchLabels:
      backup: hermes-N-zfs

docs.title: 6. Create templates/kanidm-oauth2-client.yaml
docs.text:
---
apiVersion: kaniop.rs/v1beta1
kind: KanidmOAuth2Client
metadata:
  name: hermes-N
spec:
  kanidmRef:
    name: kanidm
    namespace: kanidm

  displayname: hermes-N

  origin: https://hermes-N.internal.grigri.cloud/

  redirectUrl:
    - https://hermes-N.internal.grigri.cloud/auth/callback

  scopeMap:
    - group: hermes-users
      scopes:
        - openid
        - profile
        - email

  preferShortUsername: true
  strictRedirectUrl: true

Note: No kanidm-group.yaml — all instances share the existing hermes-users group.

docs.title: 7. Create templates/rbac.yaml (Optional)
docs.text:
Only needed if the agent requires internal cluster access (e.g., exec into other pods).

If the agent only needs external access (Telegram, web dashboard), skip this file entirely.

If needed, copy from an existing instance and update:

  • Role names: hermes-agent-* → hermes-N-agent-* (must be unique per instance to avoid ArgoCD shared resource conflicts)
  • RoleBinding names: hermes-agent-* → hermes-N-agent-*
  • RoleBinding subjects namespace: namespace: hermes → namespace: hermes-N
  • RoleBinding roleRef names: update to reference the new Role names

docs.title: 8. Validate and Deploy
docs.text:
# Build dependencies
helm dependency build apps/hermes-N/

# Lint
helm lint apps/hermes-N/

# Template (verify resource names)
helm template --include-crds --namespace hermes-N hermes-N apps/hermes-N/

# Commit and push — ArgoCD auto-syncs
git add apps/hermes-N/
git commit -m "hermes-N: Add Hermes agent instance N"
git push

docs.title: Post-Deployment Configuration
docs.text: After ArgoCD syncs and the pod is running, configure the agent by copying files to the PVC.

docs.title: Configuration Files (on PVC)
docs.text:
All runtime configuration is stored on the PVC at /opt/data/:

File Purpose config.yaml Main config: model, skills, plugins, dashboard settings auth.json API credentials for inference providers .env Environment variables: Telegram bot token, allowed users

Important: These files are NOT managed by GitOps. Copy them from an existing instance or create new ones.

Standalone CLI tools and their runtime credentials must also be placed under /opt/data; files installed into the container root filesystem disappear when the pod is recreated. See Persistent CLI Tools in Hermes for the fj installation and authentication pattern.

docs.title: Copy Configuration from Existing Instance
docs.text:
# Copy config files from hermes to hermes-N
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes hermes-0 -- cat /opt/data/config.yaml > /tmp/config.yaml
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes hermes-0 -- cat /opt/data/auth.json > /tmp/auth.json
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes hermes-0 -- cat /opt/data/.env > /tmp/.env

# Update instance-specific values in config.yaml:
# - dashboard.public_url: https://hermes-N.internal.grigri.cloud
# - dashboard.oauth.self-hosted.issuer: https://idm.grigri.cloud/oauth2/openid/hermes-N

# Copy to new instance
kubectl --context=grigri cp /tmp/config.yaml hermes-N/hermes-N-0:/opt/data/config.yaml
kubectl --context=grigri cp /tmp/auth.json hermes-N/hermes-N-0:/opt/data/auth.json
kubectl --context=grigri cp /tmp/.env hermes-N/hermes-N-0:/opt/data/.env

docs.title: Configure Telegram
docs.text:
Edit /opt/data/.env on the PVC:

# Telegram Bot Token (from @BotFather)
TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=<bot-token-from-botfather>

# Comma-separated list of allowed user IDs
TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS=<user-id-1>,<user-id-2>

# Default chat for cron delivery
TELEGRAM_HOME_CHANNEL=<user-id-1>

Getting Telegram User IDs: Users must send a message to the bot first, then check updates:

curl -s "https://api.telegram.org/bot<TOKEN>/getUpdates" | jq '.result[].message.from'

docs.title: Restart Gateway
docs.text:
After configuration changes, restart the gateway:

kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- pkill -f "hermes gateway"
# s6-overlay will auto-restart the gateway

docs.title: Verify Configuration
docs.text:
# Check gateway status
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- /opt/hermes/.venv/bin/hermes gateway status

# Check config
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- /opt/hermes/.venv/bin/hermes config show

# Check logs
kubectl --context=grigri logs -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 --tail=50

docs.title: ArgoCD Shared Resource Conflicts
docs.text: If RBAC Roles have the same name across instances (e.g., hermes-agent-radarr in both hermes and hermes-2), ArgoCD reports SharedResourceWarning and the app stays OutOfSync. Solution: Use unique Role names per instance (hermes-N-agent-*).

docs.title: Dashboard Refuses to Bind (No Auth Provider)
docs.text: Dashboard logs Refusing to bind dashboard to 0.0.0.0 and ingress returns 502. Solution: Ensure HERMES_DASHBOARD_OIDC_ISSUER is set and the Kanidm OAuth2 client is registered with the correct origin and redirect URL.

docs.title: Kanidm Rejects Redirect URI
docs.text: Login redirects to Kanidm but shows an error. Solution: Set HERMES_DASHBOARD_PUBLIC_URL to the exact external URL (with https://). Kanidm requires an exact match.

docs.title: Telegram Bot Not Responding
docs.text: Gateway logs show No messaging platforms enabled. Solution: Ensure .env file has TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN set and the file is readable by the hermes user. Restart the gateway after changes.

docs.title: OIDC Issuer Must Be Unique
docs.text: Each instance needs its own Kanidm OAuth2 client with a unique issuer URL (openid/hermes-N). Sharing the same issuer across instances causes redirect conflicts.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Kanidm users are members of hermes-users group (shared across all instances)
  • DNS propagated for hermes-N.internal.grigri.cloud
  • TLS certificate issued (check cert-manager)
  • Dashboard accessible at https://hermes-N.internal.grigri.cloud
  • OIDC login works (Kanidm OAuth2 client registered)
  • Inference provider configured
  • Required skills/plugins enabled
  • Messaging channels connected (if needed)
  • Required standalone CLI tools and their configuration are stored under /opt/data

docs.title: Useful Commands
docs.text:
# Check pod status
kubectl --context=grigri get pod/hermes-N-0 -n hermes-N -o wide

# View logs
kubectl --context=grigri logs -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 --tail=50 -f

# Open interactive session
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N -it hermes-N-0 -- /opt/hermes/.venv/bin/hermes

# Health check
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- /opt/hermes/.venv/bin/hermes doctor

docs.text:
• Network
  • Pfsense

    • amd64 instances
