  python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(json.dumps(d['credential_pool']['custom:isidoro'], indent=2))"

# Check file permissions
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- ls -la /opt/data/auth.json

# Verify config.yaml has all required fields
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- cat /opt/data/config.yaml | grep -A 10 "^model:"

docs.title: Check for stale state
docs.text:
# Look for 401 errors in logs
kubectl --context=grigri logs -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 --tail=100 | grep -iE "(401|auth|error)"

# Check request dumps for actual API key being sent
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- ls -t /opt/data/sessions/request_dump_*.json | head -1 | \
  xargs kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- cat | \
  python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(d['request']['headers']['Authorization'])"

docs.title: Test the credential directly
docs.text:
# Test API key with curl from inside the pod
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- \
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <api-key>" https://isidoro.grigri.cloud/v1/models

docs.title: 1. Copy working config from another instance
docs.text:
When config.yaml is corrupted or missing fields, copy the entire working config from another instance:

# Export config from working instance
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-3 hermes-3-0 -- cat /opt/data/config.yaml > /tmp/config.yaml

# Import to broken instance
kubectl --context=grigri cp /tmp/config.yaml hermes-N/hermes-N-0:/opt/data/config.yaml

docs.title: 2. Ensure auth.json has base_url
docs.text:
The credential must have the base_url field populated:

kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- python3 -c "
import json
data = json.load(open('/opt/data/auth.json'))
data['credential_pool']['custom:isidoro'][0]['base_url'] = 'https://isidoro.grigri.cloud/v1'
json.dump(data, open('/opt/data/auth.json', 'w'), indent=2)
"

docs.title: 3. Clear stale state database
docs.text:
Delete state.db to force a clean credential load:

kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- \
  rm /opt/data/state.db /opt/data/state.db-wal /opt/data/state.db-shm

docs.title: 4. Fix file permissions
docs.text:
auth.json must be owned by hermes user with 600 permissions:

kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- \
  chown hermes:hermes /opt/data/auth.json && chmod 600 /opt/data/auth.json

docs.title: 5. Delete pod for clean restart
docs.text:
Don't use pkill - it doesn't fully reset state. Delete the pod instead:

kubectl --context=grigri delete pod hermes-N-0 -n hermes-N

This ensures: - In-memory credential cache is cleared - state.db is reloaded from disk - All services start fresh

docs.title: 6. Remove unused credentials
docs.text:
Having unused providers (like alibaba) in auth.json or .env creates confusion:

# Remove from auth.json
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- python3 -c "
import json
data = json.load(open('/opt/data/auth.json'))
data['credential_pool'].pop('alibaba-coding-plan', None)
json.dump(data, open('/opt/data/auth.json', 'w'), indent=2)
"

# Remove from .env
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- \
  sed -i '/ALIBABA_CODING_PLAN_API_KEY/d' /opt/data/.env

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
When deploying new Hermes instances:

  1. Copy entire config.yaml from a working instance instead of manual editing
  2. Verify auth.json structure - ensure base_url is populated for all credentials
  3. Set correct permissions - auth.json must be owned by hermes:hermes with 600 permissions
  4. Remove unused credentials - keep auth.json and .env clean
  5. Use pod deletion for restarts, not pkill
  6. Test immediately - send a test message to verify the model works before considering deployment complete

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Hermes Config Overwrite Recovery
  • Hermes Agent Deployment

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: When deploying a new Hermes instance, copying configuration files from an existing instance overwrote the target instance's original config, memories, and MCP configurations. The instance appeared to work but lost its unique identity and data.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
The deployment process involved copying /opt/data/config.yaml, /opt/data/auth.json, and /opt/data/.env from an existing instance to the new instance. This overwrote the target instance's configuration without checking if it already had its own config.

Key factors: - The config.yaml.bak-* files are CLI configs, not gateway configs - Hermes instances have unique memories, MCPs, and personalities that shouldn't be copied - ZFS snapshots provide daily backups that can be used for recovery

docs.title: How to Diagnose
docs.text:
Check if the instance already exists and has its own configuration:

# Check if instance exists
kubectl --context=grigri get pod -n hermes-N

# Check if config exists
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- ls -la /opt/data/config.yaml

# Check memories
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- ls -la /opt/data/memories/

# Check skills/MCPs
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n hermes-N hermes-N-0 -- ls /opt/data/skills/

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text: When deploying a new Hermes instance: 1. Check if instance already exists before deploying 2. Don't copy config files from other instances unless explicitly needed 3. Only copy auth.json for API credentials (if needed) 4. Create fresh config.yaml with instance-specific settings: - Update dashboard.public_url to the new instance URL - Update dashboard.oauth.self-hosted.issuer to the new OAuth client - Configure instance-specific MCPs and skills

docs.title: Recovery from ZFS Snapshot
docs.text:
If config was overwritten, recover from ZFS snapshot:

# 1. Scale down the instance
kubectl --context=grigri scale statefulset hermes-N -n hermes-N --replicas=0

# 2. Find the PVC
kubectl --context=grigri get pvc -n hermes-N

# 3. List ZFS snapshots (on the node where PVC is bound)
ssh <node> "zfs list -t snapshot | grep <pvc-uuid>"

# 4. Destroy newer snapshots if needed
ssh <node> "sudo zfs destroy <dataset>@<newer-snapshot>"

# 5. Rollback to the snapshot
ssh <node> "sudo zfs rollback <dataset>@<snapshot>"

# 6. Scale back up
kubectl --context=grigri scale statefulset hermes-N -n hermes-N --replicas=1

docs.title: What NOT to Copy
docs.text:
• /opt/data/config.yaml — Contains instance-specific settings, personalities, MCPs
  • /opt/data/memories/ — Instance memories and knowledge
  • /opt/data/skills/ — Instance-specific skills and MCP configurations
  • /opt/data/state.db — Instance state and session data

docs.title: What CAN be Copied
docs.text:
• /opt/data/auth.json — API credentials (if needed, but prefer creating fresh)
  • /opt/data/.env — Environment variables (Telegram token, allowed users)

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Hermes Agent Deployment
  • ZFS Rollback

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Tools copied to /usr/bin, /usr/local/bin, or another container-image directory disappear when a Hermes pod is recreated. Tool configuration under /root disappears for the same reason.

Hermes mounts its persistent volume at /opt/data. The image already includes /opt/data/.local/bin in PATH, so install standalone tools there and keep their configuration on the same volume.

This runbook uses the Forgejo CLI (fj) as the concrete example.

docs.title: Persistent Layout
docs.text:
Path Purpose /opt/data/.local/bin/fj.bin Official fj executable /opt/data/.local/bin/fj Wrapper that selects persistent XDG storage /opt/data/.local/share/forgejo-cli/keys.json fj authentication data

The wrapper is necessary because fj otherwise stores authentication under $HOME/.local/share/forgejo-cli. The container uses HOME=/root, which is not PVC-backed.

docs.title: Install fj
docs.text:
Set the target instance and pin the release. Do not use an unversioned or latest download URL.

namespace=hermes-N
pod=hermes-N-0
version=0.6.0
archive=forgejo-cli-x86_64-linux.tar.gz
url="https://codeberg.org/forgejo-contrib/forgejo-cli/releases/download/v${version}/${archive}"

curl --fail --location "$url" --output "/tmp/$archive"

# Upstream did not publish a checksum for this release. The archive verified during this install
# had SHA-256 ea559da5449b6dd7e0dd9f7ea51c906b575696f782edd606b52adcf773602742.
printf '%s  %s\n' \
  'ea559da5449b6dd7e0dd9f7ea51c906b575696f782edd606b52adcf773602742' \
  "/tmp/$archive" | sha256sum --check

mkdir -p /tmp/forgejo-cli
tar --extract --gzip --file "/tmp/$archive" --directory /tmp/forgejo-cli

kubectl --context=grigri exec -n "$namespace" "$pod" -- \
  mkdir -p /opt/data/.local/bin /opt/data/.local/share
kubectl --context=grigri cp /tmp/forgejo-cli/fj \
  "$namespace/$pod:/opt/data/.local/bin/fj.bin"

Create the persistent-data wrapper without placing a token in shell history:

kubectl --context=grigri exec -i -n "$namespace" "$pod" -- sh -c \
  'umask 022; cat > /opt/data/.local/bin/fj' <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
XDG_DATA_HOME=/opt/data/.local/share exec /opt/data/.local/bin/fj.bin "$@"
EOF

kubectl --context=grigri exec -n "$namespace" "$pod" -- sh -c \
  'chmod 0755 /opt/data/.local/bin/fj /opt/data/.local/bin/fj.bin && \
   chown hermes:hermes /opt/data/.local/bin/fj /opt/data/.local/bin/fj.bin && \
   fj version'

Use the official release archive rather than copying the local workstation package. A distribution package may depend on shared-library versions not present in the Hermes Debian image.

docs.title: Create and Configure a Forgejo Token
docs.text:
Create the token from an account whose access is limited to the intended organization. For Hermes 3, that organization is multivara. Forgejo tokens inherit the account's permissions, and the All repositories resource selection is account-wide rather than restricted to one organization. Do not use a broadly privileged personal or administrator account if strict organization isolation is required.

In git.grigri.cloud, open Settings > Applications > New access token and select:

  • Resource access: All repositories
  • write:organization
  • write:repository
  • write:issue (also covers pull requests)
  • read:user

Do not grant admin, package, notification, or ActivityPub access unless the agent has a specific requirement. A token cannot exceed the Forgejo account's existing organization and repository permissions.

Use write:user instead of read:user only when the agent must modify user data.

Enter the token through a hidden prompt and pipe it directly to the pod. Do not put it in a command argument, Git, a temporary file, or shell history.

read -rsp 'Forgejo token: ' forgejo_token
printf '\n'
printf '%s' "$forgejo_token" | kubectl --context=grigri exec -i \
  -n "$namespace" "$pod" -- fj auth add-token -H git.grigri.cloud
unset forgejo_token

kubectl --context=grigri exec -n "$namespace" "$pod" -- sh -c \
  'chown -R hermes:hermes /opt/data/.local/share/forgejo-cli && \
   chmod 0700 /opt/data/.local/share/forgejo-cli && \
   chmod 0600 /opt/data/.local/share/forgejo-cli/keys.json'

keys.json contains a bearer token in plaintext. It is protected by filesystem permissions and the Kata-isolated, PVC-backed instance boundary, but it is also present in PVC snapshots and backups. Use a dedicated, least-privilege token and rotate it if the instance or a backup is compromised.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n "$namespace" "$pod" -- fj auth list
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n "$namespace" "$pod" -- \
  fj -H git.grigri.cloud org view multivara
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n "$namespace" "$pod" -- \
  fj -H git.grigri.cloud org repo list multivara

# Confirm both the executable and authentication data are on the PVC.
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n "$namespace" "$pod" -- sh -c \
  'test -x /opt/data/.local/bin/fj.bin && \
   test -f /opt/data/.local/share/forgejo-cli/keys.json'

After the next normal pod recreation, rerun the verification commands. Do not manually restart a healthy agent solely to test persistence.

docs.title: Upgrade or Revoke
docs.text:
To upgrade, download and verify a new pinned release, then replace only /opt/data/.local/bin/fj.bin. Keep the wrapper and authentication directory unchanged.

To revoke access, delete the token in Forgejo first, then remove the local authentication entry:

kubectl --context=grigri exec -n "$namespace" "$pod" -- \
  fj auth logout git.grigri.cloud

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Home Assistant 2026.7.1 logs show repeated WebSocket errors:

TypeError: WebSocketResponse.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'decode_text'

The WebSocket API is broken, preventing frontend and mobile app connections.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
The home-operations/home-assistant:2026.7.1 image ships with incompatible dependency versions:

  • Home Assistant 2026.7.1 uses decode_text=False in websocket_api/http.py:98
  • aiohttp 3.14.1 (system package) removed the decode_text parameter
  • aiohttp 3.14.0 has the decode_text parameter
  • aiohttp 3.13.3 (venv package) also has it

The image's entrypoint creates a venv with --system-site-packages, but the running process uses system Python which loads aiohttp 3.14.1 from system site-packages, not the venv's 3.13.3.

This is a bug in the home-operations/home-assistant image packaging.

docs.title: How to Diagnose
docs.text:
# Check for the error in logs
kubectl --context=grigri logs home-assistant-hass-0 -n home-assistant | grep decode_text

# Check which aiohttp version is loaded
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n home-assistant home-assistant-hass-0 -- \
  python3 -c "import aiohttp; print(aiohttp.__version__); print(aiohttp.__file__)"

# Check venv aiohttp version
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n home-assistant home-assistant-hass-0 -- \
  /config/.venv/bin/python3 -c "import aiohttp; print(aiohttp.__version__)"

# Check if decode_text parameter exists
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n home-assistant home-assistant-hass-0 -- \
  /config/.venv/bin/python3 -c "from aiohttp import web; import inspect; print('decode_text' in inspect.signature(web.WebSocketResponse.__init__).parameters)"

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
Install aiohttp 3.14.0 in the venv (the version that has decode_text):

kubectl --context=grigri exec -n home-assistant home-assistant-hass-0 -- \
  /config/.venv/bin/uv pip install --target /config/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages 'aiohttp==3.14.0'

kubectl --context=grigri delete pod home-assistant-hass-0 -n home-assistant

The fix persists across pod restarts because /config is on a PVC.

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
This issue will recur when the image is updated to a new HA version. Check if the upstream image fixes the dependency mismatch. If not, repeat the fix after updating the image tag.

See Home Assistant Python Package Management for details on managing packages in the HA container.

docs.title: Home Assistant API Access and HACS Deploys for Agents
Overview
docs.text: Agents can drive Home Assistant headlessly (no browser/Playwright needed) through the REST and websocket APIs, using a short-lived token obtained with the normal login flow. This is also how to deploy a change to a HACS-installed custom integration without writing into the pod.

docs.title: Getting a Token
docs.text:
Credentials live in pass as web/hass.grigri.cloud (first line is the password, user agil; no MFA). Never print the password or token; write the token to a 0600 file in the scratchpad and delete it afterwards.

H=https://hass.grigri.cloud; CID=https://hass.grigri.cloud/
FID=$(curl -s -X POST $H/auth/login_flow -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"client_id\":\"$CID\",\"handler\":[\"homeassistant\",null],\"redirect_uri\":\"${CID}?auth_callback=1\"}" \
  | jq -r .flow_id)
CODE=$(pass show web/hass.grigri.cloud | head -1 \
  | jq -R --arg u agil --arg c "$CID" '{username:$u,password:.,client_id:$c}' \
  | curl -s -X POST $H/auth/login_flow/$FID -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @- \
  | jq -r '.result // empty')
umask 077
curl -s -X POST $H/auth/token -d grant_type=authorization_code -d code=$CODE -d client_id=$CID \
  | jq -r .access_token > "$TOKEN_FILE"

When finished, revoke the short-lived session's refresh token (the snippet above keeps only the access token, so use the UI): the session under the user's profile, Security tab, refresh tokens. Then check that a refresh with that token fails.

REST examples (Authorization: Bearer $(cat $TOKEN_FILE)):

  • GET /api/config — HA version
  • GET /api/states/<entity_id> — state and attributes (e.g. supported_color_modes)
  • POST /api/services/light/turn_on with {"entity_id": "...", "color_temp_kelvin": 4000}
  • POST /api/services/homeassistant/restart — restart; /api/ returns 503 for a few seconds
  • GET /api/history/period/<iso>?filter_entity_id=... — check whether an entity ever reached a state

docs.title: Deploying a HACS Custom Integration Change
docs.text:
HACS-installed integrations (e.g. pando85/localtuya) are plain copies under /config/custom_components/<name>/ on the home-assistant-config PVC — not git checkouts, and not managed by the chart. Repos without releases track the default branch commit. To deploy:

  1. Merge/push the change to the integration repo's default branch.
  2. Over the websocket API (wss://hass.grigri.cloud/api/websocket, send {"type":"auth","access_token":...} first), with the repo id from /config/.storage/hacs.repositories:
  3. {"type":"hacs/repository/refresh","repository":"<id>"}
  4. {"type":"hacs/repository/info","repository_id":"<id>"} — expect available_version = new commit, pending_upgrade: true
  5. {"type":"hacs/repository/download","repository":"<id>"} — omit version to take the default branch Command names were checked against HACS 2.0.5 (custom_components/hacs/websocket/repository.py); re-check there if a call fails after a HACS upgrade.
  6. Verify the files in the pod match the repo (read-only kubectl exec ... cat + diff).
  7. Restart HA (homeassistant.restart) and re-test.

hacs/repository/info is the source of truth for the installed version: after a websocket download, .storage/hacs.repositories keeps last_commit but may drop version_installed.

Do not copy files into the pod with kubectl exec/cp — HACS would not know about them and would overwrite them on the next update.

docs.title: Driving the UI with Playwright
docs.text:
The Playwright MCP is configured for opencode, not Claude Code. For UI checks (e.g. what payload a frontend control actually sends) use Python Playwright with the system browser, so no browser download is needed:

python -m venv "$SCRATCH/pw-venv" && "$SCRATCH/pw-venv/bin/pip" install playwright
# chromium.launch(executable_path="/usr/bin/chromium", headless=True)

Pass the password through an environment variable, never screenshot the login form, and capture page.on("websocket") → framesent to see the exact call_service payloads. Open a dialog directly with https://hass.grigri.cloud/?more-info-entity-id=<entity_id>.

docs.title: Home Assistant Dashboards: Live Editing and Pitfalls
Overview
docs.text:
Every Lovelace dashboard except one is UI-managed (mode: storage): the config lives in /config/.storage/lovelace.<id> on the home-assistant-config PVC, not in git. The dashboard list is /config/.storage/lovelace_dashboards. They were redesigned on 2026-10-30 into sections views; the build scripts used then were throwaway, so the live storage files are the source of truth.

Dashboard (url_path) Sidebar Content Overview (lovelace, default) yes Badges, a "Now" section of conditional cards (errors, washer/dishwasher running, vacuum out, irrigation running, rack > 40 °C), energy, one section per area. Room headings link to the detail pages below Climate (dashboard-climate) yes Rooms (thermostats + 24h history), heat pump, controls (advanced ones in an expander), AppDaemon smart scheduling with a PVPC "cheapest N hours" markdown card Schedules (dashboard-schedules) yes Every custom:scheduler-card (heat pump, thermostats, shutters, extractor) Battery (dashboard-battery) yes Operating the house battery (Omnibattery venus): a templated health card (optimizer live switch and heartbeat once deployed, Omnibattery mode, grid meter freshness, import headroom under the 5 kW trip, SOC, permissions, competing Omnibattery features, RS485 ownership), the two Allow switches as the stop control, live tiles with the PVPC price, 24 h price/power/SOC history and today's energy; the optimizer's plan (config/integrations/battery_optimizer_plan.yaml polls the service's /plan): planned vs actual battery power and SOC over 24 h and a next-hours table; manual override, limits and firmware in expanders. Created 2026-11-03 Office (dashboard-rack), Terrace, Tanque, Plants, Mobiles yes Detail pages; diagnostics and rarely used entities live in custom:expander-card sections Kitchen, Bedroom, Office T (dashboard-kitchen, dashboard-bedroom, office-t) hidden Detail pages reached from Overview room headings Areas, Map yes Auto-generated strategies Voice assistant (voice-assistant) yes YAML mode, in git (the only one): config/voice_assistant_dashboard.yaml, registered under lovelace: dashboards: in config/configuration.yaml, mounted at /config/gitops/. Built-in cards only: Kivi take button, a card per LG TV satellite (c3-a, c3-b), pipelines and Wyoming services, 24 h activity. Edit the file in git, not in the UI; a file change shows after a page refresh, a new or changed lovelace: entry needs a restart (the ConfigMap change rolls the pod through the reloader annotation). Created 2026-11-07

Installed custom cards (lovelace_resources): scheduler-card, expander-card, valetudo-map-card, flower-card. Anything else (apexcharts-card, card-mod) is not installed.

docs.title: Editing a Dashboard Live
docs.text:
Use the websocket API from inside the pod (kubectl exec -i home-assistant-hass-0 -- python3, HA's Python ships aiohttp), with an admin token passed on stdin, never printed. Get the token with the login flow in home-assistant-api-hacs-deploy.md; saving dashboards needs an admin user, so service tokens such as battery-optimizer's cannot do it.

Command Use lovelace/config (url_path, force: true) Read a config. The default dashboard is url_path: null, not "lovelace" lovelace/config/save (url_path, config) Replace a config; takes effect on page reload, no restart lovelace/dashboards/list / create / update / delete Dashboard list; update takes dashboard_id (e.g. show_in_sidebar: false); url_path must contain a hyphen get_states, render_template Check entities exist and test markdown templates before saving config/area_registry/update, config/entity_registry/update Area temperature/humidity sensors, entity area_id

Procedure that kept every change reversible:

  1. Back up before the first change: cp -p /config/.storage/lovelace* /config/.storage/core.area_registry /config/lovelace-backup-<date>/ in the pod, plus a local copy. (sha256sum * order differs between the pod and a desktop locale; compare per file.)
  2. Validate every entity the new config references with get_states; render markdown templates with render_template.
  3. Compare the live config with the backup (or with your last save) and refuse to save if it changed — someone may have edited it in the UI.
  4. Save, then read it back and compare with what you built.
  5. Rollback = lovelace/config/save with the backup's data.config. Restore show_in_sidebar, delete created dashboards, and reset area sensors the same way.

Dashboard edits are not GitOps; agree each change with the user before applying it.

Do not run heavy commands inside the HA container. It has a 1 GiB memory limit: a grep -o '.{0,1500}pattern.{0,1500}' over the minified frontend bundles in hass_frontend/ got the container OOM-killed (HA restarted, 2026-10-30). Copy the files out with kubectl exec ... cat and search locally; grep -l -F to find the file is fine.

docs.title: Entity references silently break
docs.text: A tile or entities row whose entity does not exist renders as "Entity not available" with no log line. The old Climate dashboard pointed at sensor.heishamon_power_consumed/_produced/_cop for months after the template sensors became sensor.aquarea_*. After renaming or removing an entity, grep the dashboards (/config/.storage/lovelace.*) as well as the repo.

docs.title: Card behaviour
docs.text:
• Markdown cards need a blank line between lines; a single newline is joined.
  • statistic cards (e.g. "today" with period: {calendar: {period: day}}, stat_type: change) need long-term statistics: the sensor must have a state_class. Template sensors without one (e.g. sensor.aquarea_power_consumed) only work in history-graph/tiles.
  • history-graph on climate.* entities plots current vs target temperature and shades periods by hvac_action, so it is only meaningful when hvac_action is real (see localtuya below).
  • Per-card visibility (state_not: [...], numeric_state) is how the "only when relevant" cards and hidden-when-unavailable tiles work; it also applies to badges.
  • A heading card's tap_action: navigate makes the section title a link to a detail page.

docs.title: Data behind the cards
docs.text:
• Shelly EM main channels: channel 1 (sensor.shellyem_main_channel_1_*) is the whole house; channel 2 is circuit 2 (aerotherm, dishwasher, washer, extractor), not just the heat pump. Circuit 1 (cooker, sockets, humid areas, thermostats, lighting) is sensor.circuit_1_power = ch1 − ch2 + battery AC power (config/integrations/energy_circuits.yaml): the house battery plugs into circuit 1, so ch1 − ch2 alone is net of the battery (see Energy dashboard). The source of this mapping is the row titles in apps/home-assistant/dashboards/iot-energy.json. The heat pump's own reading is sensor.aquarea_power_consumed.
  • Room temperatures come from the thermostats' current_temperature attribute via template sensors (config/integrations/room_temperatures.yaml), set as each area's temperature sensor so the Areas dashboard shows them. The terrace uses the Higrow 1 DHT sensor.
  • Aquarea Z1/Z2 water temperature is not fitted (HeishaMon reported -78 for a year); the sensors were removed from heishamon.yaml.
  • HeishaMon firmware: the heat pump's CZ-TAW1 runs the owner's pando85/GoHeishaMon fork. SetOperationMode accepts 0–10 and sends mode byte 0 for any other payload (HandleSetOperationMode in src/taw2mqtt.go), so the "Set heatmode" automation in heishamon.yaml maps every input_select.heishamon_heatmode option to 0–8, mirroring "Set heatmode selector".
  • Disabled sensor.shellyem_main_channel_*_power_2 entities look stale but are the rollback anchors of the MQTT handover — do not delete them. Orphan *_mqtt_probe rows in states_meta are harmless and cannot be removed. See home-assistant-entity-id-handover.md.

docs.title: Energy dashboard
docs.text:
The built-in Energy dashboard is configured in /config/.storage/energy (API: energy/get_prefs, energy/save_prefs, energy/validate). It is a hierarchy with included_in_stat, name and live power (stat_rate):

Grid: Shelly EM channel 1 (PVPC price)
Battery: Venus E V3 (from = sensor.venus_total_discharging_energy, to = ..._charging_energy,
         power sensor.venus_ac_power, SOC sensor.venus_battery_soc, 5.12 kWh)
├─ Circuit 1 (sensor.circuit_1_energy, gross of the battery): cooker, sockets, humid areas,
│   thermostats, lighting
│   ├─ Z800 (Shelly PM mini)
│   ├─ Snapmaker (smart plug)
│   └─ Servers (sensor.servers_energy = ∫ sensor.venus_ac_offgrid_power, battery backup port)
└─ Circuit 2 (Shelly EM channel 2): aerotherm, dishwasher, washer, extractor
    ├─ Heat pump (sensor.aquarea_energy_consumed)
    │   └─ Hot water / Heating / Cooling (sensor.aquarea_{dhw,heat,cool}_energy_consumed)
    └─ Washing machine (sensor.lavadora_energy_this_month)

HA shows each parent's remainder as <name> (untracked) in the device charts and as untracked consumption in the flows (dishwasher, extractor and standby on circuit 2).

  • Only devices drawing at least 0.1% of the total power are drawn in the "Now" power flow; an idle circuit 2 (~35 W) is a thin strip.
  • sensor.lavadora_energy_yesterday has negative statistics; use ..._this_month (monthly reset is handled as a meter reset). The Shelly 2PM shutter energy sensors are left out (~0.1 kWh/month).

docs.title: Battery and circuit 1
docs.text:
The battery's AC plug is on circuit 1 and the servers hang off its backup (EPS) port. HA counts home consumption as grid import + battery discharge − battery charge, so circuit 1 has to be gross of the battery for the devices to add up: Circuit 1 Power = ch1 − ch2 + sensor.venus_ac_power (+ discharging, − charging). venus_ac_power and the two counters are the inverter's whole AC side, backup-port feed included: on 2026-11-03 a ~300 W discharge with ~250 W of servers on the backup port lowered ch1 − ch2 by ~260 W (not ~550 W) and the discharge counter rose ~0.31 kWh/h. The battery's grid-port draw is therefore servers − venus_ac_power, and the cases are:

Battery state ch1 − ch2 (net) Gross circuit 1 Bypass / idle (AC power 0) other loads + servers (passed through) same; no battery flow Discharging P W other loads + servers − P (can be negative) other loads + servers Charging C W (AC power −C) other loads + servers + C other loads + servers Grid outage house meters dark servers fed by the battery; circuit 1 unavailable, so Servers can exceed Circuit 1 for that window
  • The net difference must not be clamped before adding the battery (it goes negative while the battery feeds circuit 2 too); only the gross is clamped at 0 for sampling skew.
  • An unavailable venus_ac_power counts as 0 W (idle), so an Omnibattery outage while the battery keeps discharging under-counts circuit 1 for that time.
  • Servers (sensor.servers_energy) is the backup-port output whether it comes from the grid (Bypass) or the battery, and is always inside gross circuit 1, so there is no double count.
  • The battery's own standby draw shows as Circuit 1 (untracked); its conversion losses are the charge − discharge difference on the battery flow, not consumption. The gross is integrated from power while HA's total uses the 0.01 kWh counters, so a small residual lands in untracked.
  • Before the gross formula was deployed, sensor.circuit_1_energy integrated the net difference: from battery commissioning (2026-11-03) to the HA restart it is low by discharge − charge (a few tenths of a kWh); not backfilled.

docs.title: Statistics backfill (2026-10-30)
docs.text:
Two energy series were repaired with the websocket API rather than re-deployed sensors:

  • sensor.aquarea_energy_consumed stopped counting on 2025-12-10 18:00 because its source sensor.aquarea_power_consumed had a wrong availability check (fixed in bdfdc5825); 1560.6 kWh were missing. The gap hours were rebuilt from the sum of the three per-mode sensors with recorder/import_statistics, continuing from the last good sum, and every later row was shifted with recorder/adjust_sum_statistics (it shifts hourly and 5-minute rows, so live counting continues). Monthly totals now equal the per-mode sum since 2024-04.
  • sensor.circuit_1_energy (created 2026-10-30) got history back to 2024-04 from channel 1 − channel 2 hourly deltas (negatives clamped), imported with sums anchored so the first live hour counts in full. Its old sums are negative by design; only differences are ever displayed.

Rules that made this safe: export the rows first (\copy ... TO STDOUT WITH CSV on statistics, statistics_short_term and statistics_meta); only import hours older than the sensor's first live row, or shift live rows with adjust_sum_statistics — never import over live rows, because new statistics are compiled from the last 5-minute row; wait for the hour's compile (HH:00:10) when the anchor hour is the current one; check monthly totals against the source series afterwards. The import is queued in the recorder, so re-check after a few seconds. Login-flow access tokens expire after 30 minutes.

docs.title: Grafana energy dashboard: counter functions (iot-energy.json)
docs.text:
apps/home-assistant/dashboards/iot-energy.json is a Grafana dashboard (provisioned from git, unlike the Lovelace dashboards above) that sums energy counters from hass_sensor_energy_kwh in prometheus-long-term.

Restart merge. Each Home Assistant pod restart changes the instance and pod labels and starts a new series, so summing increase() per series loses the energy accrued in the gap between the old and the new series (commits c0295b0ce and 64472d1a0). Every energy panel therefore first merges the series with max without(instance, pod) and takes the function over a 1 m subquery (the scrape interval), for example increase((max without(instance, pod) (hass_sensor_energy_kwh{entity="..."}))[$__interval:1m]).

Which function per counter. Checked against the history since 2023-11-07:

Counter Function Why Shelly EM channels 1 and 2, Z800 (sensor.shellypmmini_z800_energy), Venus charging and discharging totals increase Never dipped or reset Snapmaker plug increase The device really resets to 0 (44 times) Aquarea heat, hot water and cool, and sensor.servers_energy delta They dip after a restart restores a stale value (81 dips on Aquarea; on 2024-04-29 two dips of 5.5 and 11.7 kWh never recovered)

Rule. Never use increase on a counter that dips: increase takes a drop for a counter reset and adds the whole counter value (for example +2198 kWh instead of 8.2 for one Aquarea dip of 0.13 kWh). Never use delta on a counter that resets, because it subtracts the reset. When adding a panel for a new counter, look up its history for dips and resets first and pick the function from the table.

Rejected alternative. Summing clamped per-minute increases is safe for both cases, but it loses the energy that accrues in data gaps longer than 5 minutes (about 1.5 to 2%).

Rename. sensor.shellypmmini_servers_energy was renamed sensor.shellypmmini_z800_energy on 2026-11-03, when the servers moved to the battery's backup port and that Shelly PM mini began metering the Z800 workstation. The servers are now sensor.servers_energy, the integral of sensor.venus_ac_offgrid_power (see Battery and circuit 1). The old id no longer exists, so a panel or query that still uses it must be pointed at the new one.

docs.title: Where history lives
docs.text:
• The recorder keeps 10 days.
  • hass_* metrics (the /api/prometheus ServiceMonitor) are scraped by prometheus-long-term (https://prometheus-long-term.internal.grigri.cloud) only; prometheus.internal.grigri.cloud has none. Use it for anything older than 10 days, e.g. hass_climate_action{entity=~"climate.thermostat_.*"} == 1 together with hass_climate_mode, hass_climate_current_temperature_celsius and hass_climate_target_temperature_celsius.

docs.title: Thermostat heating state
docs.text: The thermostats' own hvac_action source (DP 36) follows the mode, not the demand; heuristic_action derives it from temperatures instead. See home-assistant-localtuya.md.

docs.title: Home Assistant: moving an entity ID to another platform without losing its history
docs.text: Status: used in production 2026-10-27 to move sensor.shellyem_main_channel_{1,2}_power from the native shelly integration to MQTT at a 2 s cadence. History, long-term statistics, Prometheus labels and every consumer survived unbroken. Automation: scripts/shelly-em-registry.py (via metal/playbooks/shelly-em.yaml --tags registry).

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
You want an existing canonical entity_id — one that already has recorder history, long-term statistics, dashboards, Prometheus series and external consumers pinned to it — to be fed by a different integration instead (here: Shelly REST/CoIoT polling → MQTT push), with the ID, the friendly_name and the metric labels unchanged.

The obvious approach is to rename the old entity out of the way and rename the new one onto the freed ID. That silently moves the history to the old entity's new name, so the canonical ID starts from zero rows: dashboards and the energy panel go blank before the cutover, the Parquet archive starts a new series, and nothing errors out loudly enough to notice.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
HA's recorder migrates metadata in place whenever an entity is renamed:

  • components/recorder/entity_registry.py filters registry events with event_data["action"] == "update" and "old_entity_id" in event_data, then calls both async_update_statistics_metadata(old, new_statistic_id=new) and async_update_states_metadata(old, new_entity_id=new).
  • table_managers/states_meta.py::update_metadata runs UPDATE states_meta SET entity_id = <new> WHERE entity_id = <old> — but returns False without updating when <new> already exists (collision guard).
  • table_managers/statistics_meta.py::update_statistic_id has the same guard and logs Cannot rename statistic_id <old> to <new> because the new statistic_id already exists at ERROR level.

Two consequences that the rename approach gets exactly backwards:

  1. Renaming the old entity away succeeds (the target ID is free), so the production history follows it to the new ID.
  2. A registry removal fires action="remove", which the recorder's rename filter ignores — so nothing migrates and the canonical states_meta / statistics_meta rows stay put.

docs.title: Fix / correct procedure: remove-then-promote
docs.text:
1. Deploy the new platform's entity under a temporary ID and verify it — state, unit, friendly_name and the actual update cadence, all before touching anything production.
  2. Remove the old entity with config/entity_registry/remove. History stays under the canonical ID; the entity platform also drops it from the state machine immediately (it listens for action="remove"), so there is no window where two entities write the same ID.
  3. Promote the new entity with config/entity_registry/update and new_entity_id: <canonical>. The recorder attempts a migration and the collision guard refuses it — which is the desired outcome: the canonical rows survive and new states append to the same metadata_id.
  4. Reload the old integration's config entry (homeassistant.reload_config_entry service — the websocket command config_entries/reload does not exist). It recreates its entity under a suffixed ID, then disable that entry (disabled_by: user) so it can never reclaim the canonical ID or pollute the state machine, recorder and Prometheus export. Find the recreated entry by unique_id, never by an assumed _2 suffix.

Order matters: promote before reloading, or the old integration reclaims the canonical ID.

docs.title: Expected log noise
docs.text: The two Cannot rename statistic_id ... because the new statistic_id already exists ERROR lines are the collision guard doing its job. Do not "fix" them — their absence would mean the guard did not fire and history was moved.

docs.title: How to verify (all read-only)
docs.text:
# 1. Canonical IDs must keep their original metadata_id / statistic id
kubectl --context=grigri -n home-assistant exec home-assistant-postgres-0 -c postgres -- \
  psql -U postgres -d home_assistant -At -c \
  "select metadata_id, entity_id from states_meta where entity_id like '<prefix>%' order by 1"

# 2. Rows must exist on BOTH sides of the cutover under the same metadata_id.
#    NB: statistics tables have a legacy NULL `start` column — use `start_ts` (epoch).
kubectl --context=grigri -n home-assistant exec home-assistant-postgres-0 -c postgres -- \
  psql -U postgres -d home_assistant -At -c \
  "select count(*) filter (where start_ts < <cutover_epoch>) before,
          count(*) filter (where start_ts >= <cutover_epoch>) after
     from statistics_short_term where metadata_id=<statistic_id>"

# 3. Prometheus label sets must be byte-identical (instance/pod_ip are volatile by design)
curl -sS -G <prometheus>/api/v1/query --data-urlencode 'query=<metric>{entity="<canonical>"}'

Also confirm the 5-minute statistics bucket after the cutover appears — it is compiled at HH:M5:10, so check a few minutes later, not immediately.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Revert the new platform's YAML and let HA restart so its entities are removed. Never rename them off the canonical ID — that drags the accumulated history with them. Then rename the disabled native entry back onto the canonical ID (the guard skips the migration again) and re-enable it. scripts/shelly-em-registry.py rollback enforces this ordering and refuses to run while an MQTT entity still owns a canonical ID.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• The disabled suffixed native entries are rollback anchors, not leftovers. For the Shelly EM they are sensor.shellyem_main_channel_{1,2}_power_2; a cleanup pass must not delete them, or scripts/shelly-em-registry.py rollback has nothing to rename back.
  • A disabled entity still reserves its entity_id. You cannot promote onto an ID held by a disabled entry — remove that entry instead.
  • friendly_name is part of the Prometheus label set (hass_sensor_power_w{friendly_name=...}). For a YAML MQTT sensor it comes from name:; for a native Shelly entity it is assembled from the device and channel names. They must match exactly — assert it in the promotion preflight, do not eyeball it.
  • default_entity_id only applies at first creation when unique_id is set, so a temporary ID in YAML does not fight a later registry rename across restarts.
  • Orphaned metadata is harmless: the temporary ID keeps its own states_meta row and its states age out with normal retention. There is no supported API to delete it, so leave it alone.
  • Registry update returns as soon as the registry is written, not when the recorder has processed the queued migration tasks. Verify from the database afterwards rather than trusting the API response.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• shelly-gen1-coiot-disabled-breaks-ha-setup.md — the CoIoT dependency that makes any HA restart on a Gen1 device risky
  • ../../planning/shelly-em-mqtt-implementation.md — the 2 s MQTT cutover this technique was built for, with its measurements and rollback

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Tuya devices are controlled locally by the localtuya custom integration, installed through HACS from pando85/localtuya master (no releases, HACS tracks commits). Local checkout: ~/localtuya. Deploy procedure and API access: home-assistant-api-hacs-deploy.md.

The fork is deliberately narrowed to what is used. On 2026-10-10 the unused cover, vacuum, select and binary_sensor platforms were removed (PR #9). This matters beyond tidiness: config_flow.py builds its YAML schema from every platform in PLATFORMS, so every platform module is imported at load time — an HA API removal in an unused platform would take down the whole integration. Adding a new device type means restoring its platform from git history.

docs.title: Devices in Use
docs.text:
One config entry, 5 devices, 22 entities (HA 2026.9.4):

Device Protocol Entities and DPs Thermostat bedroom / hall-kitchen / office A / office T 3.3 climate DP 1 (hvac mode DP 2, target temp 16, current temp 24, action 36 open/close — follows the mode, not demand, so heuristic_action: true see below, heat/cool flag 104 bool True=heat, False=cool), switch Frost DP 10, switch Child lock DP 40, number Backlight DP 105 (0–100), sensor Control mode DP 101 Fan and light office A 3.2 fan DP 1 (speed DP 3 int 1–6, direction DP 8); light DP 15 (brightness 16 0–100, color temp 17 0–100 → 3000–6000 K)

Device config lives in /config/.storage/core.config_entries (contains local_key secrets — never print or copy it out of the scratchpad).

docs.title: Light Color Temperature Ignored / Light Never Turns On (fixed)
docs.text:
Symptom: color temperature changes did nothing; history showed the light never reached on; log:

HomeAssistantError: light.ceiling_light_office_a (...LocaltuyaLight) set to unsupported color mode
brightness, expected one of {<ColorMode.HS: 'hs'>, <ColorMode.COLOR_TEMP: 'color_temp'>}
Entity light.ceiling_light_office_a is requesting unknown DPS index -1

Root causes, fixed in d72f3f7 and 68ae9e6 (PR #8):

  1. Mired API removed in HA 2026.x. LightEntity only passes color_temp_kelvin and only reads color_temp_kelvin / min_color_temp_kelvin / max_color_temp_kelvin. The old color_temp / min_mireds code was silently ignored (no deprecation warning remains) and the entity showed HA's default 2000–6535 K. An earlier attempt (0f48723, reverted) skipped turn_on and ignored the min-Kelvin offset and reverse option.
  2. HA 2026.x raises on an unsupported color_mode (it used to warn). The light's color_mode was configured as DP 2, which is the fan's mode DP — not a DP this device reports.
  3. has_config() only treated the string "-1" as unset, but the config stores the int -1 and False, so the light advertised hs and the effect feature.

Verified live: supported_color_modes: ["color_temp"], 3000–6000 K. Readback is quantised (~30 K per DP step): 4000 K reads back as 3960 K.

docs.title: Audit Findings (2026-10-10)
docs.text:
A read-only audit of the deployed entities found five more code bugs, all reproduced in a venv with the live config. Fixed in PR #10 (one commit per bug, 927ac80..e239364), deployed and verified live on 2026-10-10:

  1. Thermostat heat/cool switch fails while in auto (climate.py set_hvac_mode): the write of manual to DP 2 lacks await (log: RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'TuyaDevice.set_dp' was never awaited), and auto has no branch when a cooling DP is configured. It only worked on 2026-10-08 because the thermostats were already manual.
  2. Cool mode always reports hvac_action: heating: DP 104 (bool) is compared to the string "cool".
  3. Fan speed one step off for integer percentages: math.ceil on 16.67% steps maps 17 → speed 2, 34 → 3, 51 → 4, 67 → 5, 84 → 6. The HA UI is not affected (verified with Playwright): the more-info slider (6 speeds → ha-control-slider with step = percentage_step) sends floats like 16.666…, and HA core's vol.Coerce(int) truncates them to 16/33/50/66/83/100, which ceil maps correctly. Only integer callers hit it: automations/scripts (percentage: 17), Assist ("set the fan to 67%"), or API clients that round instead of truncate. The dialog label shows "17%"/"67%" — display rounding only.
  4. Number entities write floats (57.0) to integer DPs.
  5. All entities registered on the last device's interface (common.py tuyainterface.add_entities outside the per-device loop) — latent, only matters with restore-on-reconnect.

Plus unconfigured DPs (-1, the white-only light's mode DP 2) are still included in status requests; PR #10 drops them (fan+light now requests [1, 15, 16, 17, 3, 8]).

Behaviour changes PR #10 brings to the thermostats (DP 104 True = heat, False = cool, confirmed from history; the PR keeps that mapping):

  • heat/cool from auto now really writes manual to DP 2 (then waits MODE_WAIT, then DP 104).
  • Selecting auto now writes auto to DP 2 (previously a no-op).
  • A missing DP 104 displays heat instead of cool; cool mode with an open valve shows cooling. (Later found misleading: DP 36 is open for the whole cool season regardless of demand — see below.)
  • Configs without a cooling DP behave exactly as before.

docs.title: Live verification (2026-10-10, e239364)
docs.text:
All 22 entities came back unchanged and each entity is now registered on its own device. Tests, each restored afterwards:

Test Result fan.set_percentage 17 / 67 / 50 16% (speed 1) / 66% (speed 4) / 50% (speed 3) Office T backlight 64 → 65 raw_state 65 (integer) Office T auto → heat (previously broken path) auto applied the device schedule (target 19 °C); heat restored manual 22.5 °C; no never awaited Light 4000 K color_temp, 3960 K

Not tested live: cool mode (and the new cooling action), and whether the fan+light device stopped requesting DPs -1/2 (needs DEBUG logging to observe). Test cool only with the user, when cooling is wanted.

docs.title: hvac_action: DP 36 Follows the Mode, Not the Demand
Problem
docs.text: All four thermostats showed hvac_action: idle permanently in heat mode — including Bedroom and Hall/Kitchen sitting 1–5 °C below target for days — so dashboards could not show which rooms were heating, and climate history graphs had no heating shading.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Not a localtuya bug: the devices report DP 36 = "close" and localtuya maps it correctly. Over 60 days of prometheus-long-term history, DP 36 tracked DP 104 (the heat/cool flag), never the temperatures: open (→ heating/cooling) for the whole cool season 2026-08-31 → 10-08 — including 85–233 h per room when the room was already below target — and close for the whole heat season since, including 166–257 h below target. A direct one-off, read-only local status query to each device confirmed "close" on all four while two rooms were below target. DPs 102 (floor temperature limit, 50) and 103 (floor sensor, 0 = none) carry nothing either. These units match tuya-local's "Essentials Smart Home Wall thermostat" profile, which maps DP 36 the same way — the firmware simply does not report relay demand.

Office A sitting up to ~6 °C above target is expected: it is heated by the servers and its occupant.

docs.title: How to Diagnose
docs.text:
P=https://prometheus-long-term.internal.grigri.cloud
curl -s -G $P/api/v1/query_range --data-urlencode 'query=hass_climate_action{entity=~"climate.thermostat_.*"} == 1' \
  --data-urlencode start=$(date -d '-60 days' +%s) --data-urlencode end=$(date +%s) --data-urlencode step=1800
# join with hass_climate_mode, hass_climate_current_temperature_celsius and
# hass_climate_target_temperature_celsius: action only ever changes when the mode changes

The HA recorder keeps only 10 days, so use prometheus-long-term for season-long checks.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
heuristic_action was reworked in 876b229 (deployed 2026-10-30) and enabled on the four thermostat climate entities:

  • Computed in status_updated (the old code mutated state inside the hvac_action property).
  • Heating starts when the room is more than half a temperature_step (0.25 °C) below target, stops at the target, and keeps the previous action in between, so sensor noise does not toggle it.
  • Mirrored for cool mode, and for auto when DP 104 selects cooling; off when the thermostat is off.
  • DP 36 is still configured but its value is overridden whenever heuristic_action is on.

The result is room demand, not proof that water is flowing: whether the heat pump is actually heating the floors is on the Climate dashboard (sensor.aquarea_3_way_valve, compressor frequency), and AppDaemon may hold it off until cheap hours.

Enabling it: localtuya options flow → edit device → re-submit every entity with its stored values plus heuristic_action: true. Each completed flow reloads the whole config entry (all five devices drop for a few seconds and log "Disconnected - waiting for discovery broadcast"); the entity registry is preserved.

docs.title: Pending Options-UI Cleanup
docs.text:
• Light: clear color_mode (DP 2) and color (-1).
  • Fan and light device: remove scan_interval: 10 (sends empty UPDATEDPS every 10 s, none of its DPs are in the update allow-list), enable_debug, and manual DP 300.
  • "Thermostat office A" device: the localtuya friendly_name has a stray trailing ". Masked on 2026-10-10 with a device-registry name_by_user override (entity names never included it); the config entry value is unchanged and is harmless to leave.

docs.title: Operational Notes
docs.text:
• The HA pod is not on the host network, so Tuya UDP discovery broadcasts never arrive; devices reconnect via the 60 s reconnect timer. Short (15–95 s) unavailable blips are device/Wi-Fi side — the bedroom thermostat drops most (10× in 7 days).
  • enable_debug: true on a device produced no DEBUG lines in the HA log; DP values cannot be read from logs without also raising the logger level.
  • A whole-HA outage (all entities unavailable, including sun.sun) is not a localtuya problem — e.g. 2026-10-03 08:27 → 10-05 03:15 UTC.

docs.title: Home Assistant: Omnibattery and the house battery
docs.text: The house battery (Marstek Venus E V3, venus in Home Assistant) is driven by the Omnibattery integration (HACS, v1.5.1b1 beta since 2026-11-04, Modbus TCP). battery-optimizer controls it through Omnibattery's entities in live mode; deployment, rollout and rollback are in docs/deployment/battery-optimizer.md.

docs.title: Version and upgrade
docs.text:
Installed: v1.5.1b1 (beta) since 2026-11-04, the owner's choice, from https://github.com/ffunes/omnibattery. It was installed for upstream issue #598: v1.5.0 capped the PD grid target at 2500 W (the device maximum), so charging was at most 2500 W minus the house load. The beta bounds the target by the contracted power (max 5000 W).

The upstream fix for the backup threshold (#723, for #660) is not in the beta, so the 500 W workaround stays. Before upgrading, check that both still hold: the target bound by the contracted power, and the #723 fix.

docs.title: Modbus access
docs.text:
The Venus accepts one Modbus TCP client, Omnibattery. Other clients are refused, so do not run read-only Modbus probes while Omnibattery is connected.

When Modbus fails, Omnibattery keeps the last SOC and AC values; the only visible change is sensor.omnibattery_non_responsive_batteries going from None to venus.

docs.title: integration_status stuck in backup_mode after the grid returns
Problem
docs.text:
With the backup function on and a load on the battery's backup (EPS) port, Omnibattery can keep sensor.omnibattery_integration_status at backup_mode after AC is back and the inverter is in Bypass. While it does, Omnibattery excludes the battery from PD control, and battery-optimizer's guard holds safe idle (integration_unhealthy), so the battery does nothing.

Seen in the commissioning test on 2026-11-03: a 57-85 W load on the backup port kept the status at backup_mode until the threshold below was raised.

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text: Upstream bug ffunes/Omnibattery#660, fixed by ffunes/Omnibattery#723. In Bypass the grid feeds the backup port, so Omnibattery should treat the port as idle, but only when the inverter state and ac_offgrid_power come from the same poll. The coordinator stamps the reading times in the middle of a poll and publishes the data later, so the same-poll check fails and the Bypass zeroing is skipped. The backup-port load then counts as off-grid load; above number.venus_backup_offgrid_threshold (default 50 W) it re-arms the 5-minute post-backup cooldown on every poll, and the cooldown never runs out.

docs.title: How to diagnose
docs.text:
• sensor.omnibattery_integration_status is backup_mode while the inverter reports Bypass (AC present) for more than 5 minutes.
  • sensor.venus_ac_offgrid_power is above number.venus_backup_offgrid_threshold.
  • battery-optimizer: battery_optimizer_actuator_guard_reason{reason="integration_unhealthy"} == 1, and BatteryOptimizerActuatorSafeIdle after 30 minutes.

docs.title: Workaround (active since 2026-11-03)
docs.text:
number.venus_backup_offgrid_threshold = 500 W (set by the owner in Home Assistant; 200 W during the test). A backup-port load below the threshold never re-arms the cooldown, so the status returns to balanced within 5 minutes of AC coming back.

Side effects of the high threshold, until it is set back to 50 W:

  • A real outage with a small backup load is not detected as backup. With a backup-port load of 500 W or less, Omnibattery does not exclude the battery from PD control during a grid outage and the status does not change to backup_mode, so neither Omnibattery's exclusion nor the optimizer's integration_unhealthy guard reacts. (The optimizer's other guards still apply; in a real outage the grid meter and usually Home Assistant are down too.)
  • No post-backup cooldown below 500 W. After an outage, or after the AC failsafe plug turns AC back on, Omnibattery resumes PD writes at once instead of waiting 5 minutes.
  • Shutdown standby is not skipped. On an Omnibattery unload or Home Assistant stop, the battery is sent to standby and RS485 control is released unless the backup-port load is above the threshold; with 500 W that happens even while the battery is feeding a small backup load.
  • The workaround only covers loads up to 500 W. A larger backup-port load in Bypass still hits the latch. Keep the backup-port load (servers, once moved there) under 500 W or remove the workaround first.

docs.title: Removing the workaround
docs.text:
Once an Omnibattery release that contains #723 is installed (check the release notes, then update through HACS and restart Home Assistant):

  1. Set number.venus_backup_offgrid_threshold back to 50 W.
  2. Verify with a load on the backup port while the inverter is in Bypass: either the existing backup load, or briefly cut AC (the battery's AC plug off, then on) with a test load connected.
  3. sensor.omnibattery_integration_status must return to balanced within 5 minutes of AC being back and stay there. If it stays at backup_mode, set the threshold to 500 W again and reopen the upstream issue.
  4. Update this page and the battery-optimizer deployment doc.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The home-operations/home-assistant image uses a virtual environment at /config/.venv for user-installed packages, while system packages live in /usr/local/lib/python3.14/site-packages/.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
/usr/local/lib/python3.14/site-packages/  # System packages (read-only, from image)
/config/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/  # Venv packages (writable, persistent)

The entrypoint script: 1. Creates the venv with uv venv --system-site-packages 2. Activates it via source /config/.venv/bin/activate 3. Runs python3 -m homeassistant

docs.title: Package Resolution
docs.text:
Python loads packages in this order: 1. Venv site-packages (/config/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/) 2. System site-packages (/usr/local/lib/python3.14/site-packages/)

When using /config/.venv/bin/python3, the venv takes precedence. When using system python3, only system packages are loaded.

docs.title: Install a package
docs.text:
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n home-assistant home-assistant-hass-0 -- \
  /config/.venv/bin/uv pip install <package>==<version>

docs.title: Check installed version
docs.text:
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n home-assistant home-assistant-hass-0 -- \
  /config/.venv/bin/python3 -c "import <package>; print(<package>.__version__)"

docs.title: List installed packages
docs.text:
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n home-assistant home-assistant-hass-0 -- \
  /config/.venv/bin/uv pip list

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• The venv persists across pod restarts (stored on PVC at /config)
  • System packages cannot be modified (read-only image layers)
  • Use --target /config/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages if uv pip install fails with permission errors on system directories
  • Restart the pod after installing packages: kubectl delete pod home-assistant-hass-0 -n home-assistant

docs.title: Home Assistant Shelly CoIoT push updates (Gen1 devices)
docs.text:
Status: diagnosed 2026-10-26. The repair is still not fixed, and it is now only a hygiene item: the frequency problem it was the fallback for is solved. Since 2026-10-27 07:34Z the two power sensors are fed by MQTT at a measured 2.01 s (was 33 s polling), with entity IDs, friendly names, Prometheus labels and recorder history preserved. See planning/shelly-em-mqtt-implementation.md.

The reboot loop that made MQTT look dead on 2026-10-26 was root-caused, not fixed around: it needs MQTT and CoIoT disabled and an HA setup_retry storm hammering the /cit/d endpoint that hangs. With CoIoT enabled — which is mandatory anyway — MQTT is stable (11 h 14 m soak, then the cutover).

Unicast CoIoT is capped at 15 s (coiot_update_period is documented as 15..65535 s, and without push HA polls at 2.2 × 15 s = 33 s), so it is now slower than the production path. The procedure below remains worth doing for exactly one reason: it clears the standing push_update_* repair, so a genuine future push failure becomes signal again. It costs a pfSense UDP rule (human step) and a Service, and it no longer buys any telemetry improvement.

⚠️ Do not "clean up" by disabling CoIoT on a Gen1 device that HA owns. With coiot.enabled: false the firmware stops serving /cit/* entirely: HTTP GET /cit/d hangs instead of 404-ing and CoAP goes silent. HA's BlockDevice.initialize() needs /cit/d, so the next HA restart drops every entity of that config entry into setup_retry with Device communication error occurred for <name> — while the device itself keeps answering /settings and /status normally. shellyem-main drifted into exactly that state and cost ~48 min of grid telemetry (18:02:35Z → 18:50:34Z on 2026-10-26) before it was found. It is now restored to {"enabled": true, "update_period": 15, "peer": ""}. Diagnosis, the correct re-enable endpoint and the pitfalls: shelly-gen1-coiot-disabled-breaks-ha-setup.md.

Generation-1 Shelly devices (shellyem-main, a Shelly EM) talk to Home Assistant over CoIoT (CoAP on UDP 5683). CoIoT is enabled on the device, but its peer is empty, so the device only sends multicast status announcements — and multicast does not reach the HA pod. HA therefore falls back to polling, which works but at 2.2× the device's own update period and leaves a standing error-level repair issue.

This page records the evidence, the root cause, the diagnosis commands, and the step-by-step configuration for unicast CoIoT push in this cluster.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Symptoms, all observed on 2026-10-26:

  • Home Assistant shows an active, non-ignored, error-severity repair for the device: push_update_244CAB417668 ("Shelly device shellyem-main push update failure"), created 2026-10-25T01:03:58Z. It is re-created about 3 minutes after every HA restart (is_persistent: false, and it takes MAX_PUSH_UPDATE_FAILURES = 5 poll replies to trip).
  • sensor.shellyem_main_channel_1_power changed state every 33 s — not every 15 s, the device's configured coiot.update_period. (Historical: as of 2026-10-27 this entity comes from MQTT at 2 s, so the CoIoT polling path no longer sets its cadence. The repair itself is unchanged.)
  • The device's own CoIoT multicast announcements are visible on the wire but never arrive at HA.

Data is not missing: both emeter channels report sane values. This is a resolution/latency and hygiene problem, not an outage.

docs.title: What is configured today
docs.text: Item Value Source Device shellyem-main, Shelly EM (SHEM), Gen1, fw 1.14.0-gcb84623 HA device registry, /shelly MAC / IP 24:4c:ab:41:76:68 / 192.168.86.130 (DHCP with a pfSense static mapping) HA registry, pfSense ARP/DHCP Network IoT VLAN 501 (igb1.501, pfSense opt6, 192.168.86.254/24) pfSense config coiot {"enabled": true, "update_period": 15, "peer": ""} — empty peer = multicast HA diagnostics + device /settings Cloud / MQTT Cloud disabled; MQTT enabled since 2026-10-27 (mosquitto.internal.grigri.cloud:1883, update_period: 2) and now feeds both power sensors. Everything else still arrives over CoIoT + HTTP polling device /settings Device clock skew 0 s vs. UTC, uptime ~3.8 d, RSSI −56 dBm, both emeters is_valid: true device /status HA 2026.10.4, aioshelly==13.34.1, pod home-assistant-hass-0 = 10.0.4.218 on prusik /api/config, manifest, kubectl HA internal_url / external_url both null /api/config HA CoAP socket UDP 0.0.0.0:5683 bound in the pod, joined IGMP group 224.0.1.187 on eth0 /proc/net/udp, /proc/net/igmp HA service home-assistant-hass exposes TCP 8123 only — nothing exposes UDP 5683 kubectl get svc Other Shelly devices shellypmmini-z800, shellyplus2pm-{office-a,office-t,bedroom} are Gen2+ (RPC/WebSocket) and are unaffected HA device registry

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
Three independent gaps, all of which must be closed for push to work:

  1. CoIoT is in multicast mode. With peer: "" the device publishes status to 224.0.1.187:5683 instead of unicasting to HA. Captured on igb1.501: 
    16:07:04.922328 IP (ttl 128) 192.168.86.130.5683 > 224.0.1.187.5683: UDP, length 239
16:07:19.924779 IP (ttl 128) 192.168.86.130.5683 > 224.0.1.187.5683: UDP, length 239
    ~15 s apart, matching update_period. TTL 128 means the packets are routable in principle — the problem is forwarding, not TTL.
  2. Nothing forwards that multicast. pfSense has no IGMP proxy and no multicast routing (igmp absent from /conf/config.xml, no IGMP joins observed on igb1.501/igb1.101), and HA's pod CIDR (10.0.0.0/8, Cilium native routing) is not routable from pfSense at all — only the node addresses (192.168.192.0/24) and the Cilium LoadBalancer VIPs (192.168.193.0/24, BGP-learned /32s) are. HA has joined the group on eth0; the packets simply never get there.
  3. No unicast path exists either. The HA Service exposes only TCP 8123, so there is no stable address the device could push to. In addition, the IoT VLAN's catch-all pass rule carries flags S/SA without an explicit proto, which pf treats as TCP-only (pf.conf(5): "when flags is specified without proto, the rule is treated as if proto tcp was specified"). Device-initiated UDP from the IoT VLAN to anywhere outside it is blocked today — confirmed by the state table: 4 TCP states from IoT to 192.168.193.9 (mosquitto), 0 UDP states from IoT to any cluster VIP. Any unicast design needs an explicit UDP pass rule.

docs.title: Why it still works: the polling fallback
docs.text:
What actually reaches HA is HA's own CoAP request, answered by the device:

16:07:24.022560 IP (ttl 62)  192.168.192.3.45104 > 192.168.86.130.5683: UDP, length 12   # request
16:07:24.061033 IP (ttl 128) 192.168.86.130.5683 > 192.168.192.3.45104: UDP, length 239  # reply

192.168.192.3 is prusik (the pod's traffic is SNAT'd by the node), 45104 is an ephemeral source port — not a configuration value. The cadence comes from HA:

  • ShellyBlockCoordinator sets update_interval = UPDATE_PERIOD_MULTIPLIER × coiot.update_period = 2.2 × 15 s = 33 s (homeassistant/components/shelly/coordinator.py, const.py: UPDATE_PERIOD_MULTIPLIER = 2.2).
  • Each interval calls device.update() → _coap_request("s") (aioshelly/block_device/device.py), i.e. a CoAP GET of /cit/s. The reply is classified CoapType.REPLY (CoAP code 69 = 2.05) and increments _push_update_failures; a genuine push would be CoapType.PERIODIC (code 30 = 0.30) and would reset the counter and delete the repair.

Rule of thumb: if a Gen1 Shelly's entities update at exactly 2.2 × the device's update_period, you are on the polling fallback, not on push.

Energy cross-check (device /status vs. HA): device total is in Wh — 17257856.8 Wh = 17257.8568 kWh, matching sensor.shellyem_main_channel_1_energy = 17257.5508 kWh.

docs.title: How to diagnose (read-only)
docs.text:
# 1. HA side: is the repair there, and what does the device report?
#    (token flow: docs/troubleshooting/home-assistant-api-hacs-deploy.md)
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://hass.grigri.cloud/api/diagnostics/config_entry/<shelly-entry-id> \
  | jq '.data.device_settings, .data.device_info, .data.last_error'
#    -> {"coiot":{"enabled":true,"update_period":15,"peer":""}, ...}

# 2. HA side: is the CoAP socket up, and did it join the multicast group?
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n home-assistant home-assistant-hass-0 -c hass -- cat /proc/net/udp
#    00000000:1633  == 0.0.0.0:5683 (0x1633 = 5683)
kubectl --context=grigri exec -n home-assistant home-assistant-hass-0 -c hass -- cat /proc/net/igmp
#    BB0100E0 on eth0 == 224.0.1.187

# 3. HA side: measure the real update cadence
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://hass.grigri.cloud/api/history/period/<iso-start>?filter_entity_id=sensor.shellyem_main_channel_1_power&minimal_response"

# 4. Device side (read-only GETs; credentials in `pass iot/shellyem-main`,
#    username is the `login:` line, password the first line — basic auth works):
curl -sS -u "$USER:$PASS" http://shellyem-main.iot.grigri/shelly   # no auth needed: type/mac/auth/fw
curl -sS -u "$USER:$PASS" http://shellyem-main.iot.grigri/settings | jq .coiot,.cloud,.mqtt
curl -sS -u "$USER:$PASS" http://shellyem-main.iot.grigri/status   | jq .time,.unixtime,.uptime,.emeters

# 5. Wire (pfSense, root read-only): distinguish push from poll-reply.
#    A push has NO preceding request from HA; a poll reply does.
tcpdump -p -n -i igb1.501 'udp port 5683 and host 192.168.86.130'
pfctl -ss | grep 5683          # active CoAP states
pfctl -sr | grep -n igb1.501   # IoT rule order (watch for `flags S/SA` on the catch-all)

docs.title: Fix: unicast CoIoT to a LoadBalancer VIP
docs.text:
Target path — the device pushes unsolicited CoAP to a stable VIP, Cilium delivers it to the pod:

ShellyEM 192.168.86.130 --UDP/5683--> 192.168.193.12 (Cilium LB VIP, BGP-learned by pfSense)
                                              --> home-assistant-hass-0 10.0.4.218:5683

HA needs no configuration change: the CoAP socket is already bound to 0.0.0.0:5683, and aioshelly dispatches incoming datagrams by the CoAP device-ID option 3332 (last 6 of the MAC), not by source IP (block_device/coap.py:208-225, device.py:98-103). So SNAT through the LoadBalancer is harmless.

docs.title: Step 1 — GitOps: expose UDP 5683 (agent may prepare, ArgoCD applies)
docs.text:
Add a second Service to apps/home-assistant/values.yaml (service: block, next to hass:):

  service:
    hass:
      controller: hass
      ports:
        http:
          port: 8123
    # CoIoT (Gen1 Shelly push). UDP; consumed by the Shelly devices, not by browsers.
    hass-coiot:
      type: LoadBalancer
      controller: hass
      annotations:
        lbipam.cilium.io/ips: "192.168.193.12"
      ports:
        coap:
          port: 5683
          protocol: UDP

Notes:

  • VIP choice: the pool is CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool/default = 192.168.193.0/24. In use by Services: .1 .2 .3 .4 .5 .7 .8 .9 .10; reserved by pfSense aliases but not currently advertised: .6 (k8s_deluge), .11 (k8s_pt). Use .12 and re-verify both sides at implementation time (kubectl get svc -A -o json | jq '[.items[].status.loadBalancer.ingress[]?.ip]' plus the pfSense k8s_* aliases).
  • No externalTrafficPolicy: Local here (unlike mosquitto/unifi). The HA pod is pinned to prusik by its node-local PVC, the BGP peering config selects all Linux nodes, and some VIPs are learned ECMP via both nodes — with Local, pushes landing on the node without the pod are dropped. The default Cluster policy SNATs, which is fine because dispatch is by device ID. If you do choose Local, first confirm with vtysh -c 'show ip bgp 192.168.193.12/32' on pfSense that the VIP is advertised only by prusik.
  • Validate before committing, per repo convention: 
    helm dependency build apps/home-assistant/
helm template --include-crds --namespace home-assistant home-assistant apps/home-assistant/ \
  | grep -B4 -A14 'name: home-assistant-hass-coiot'
pre-commit run --all-files
    Then commit and let ArgoCD sync (selfHeal will revert any kubectl apply).

docs.title: Step 2 — pfSense: alias + UDP pass rule (human action)
docs.text:
Routing needs nothing: pfSense's FRR (AS 64512) learns the new /32 automatically from Cilium (AS 64513) once the Service exists. The firewall does need a change, because IoT-initiated UDP is blocked (root cause #3). Agents must not mutate pfSense — do this in the UI:

  1. Firewall → Aliases → Add: name k8s_ha_coiot, type Host(s), address 192.168.193.12, description "K8s Home Assistant CoIoT (UDP 5683) LB VIP".
  2. Firewall → Rules → IoT (opt6) → Add, placed above the two reject rules (i.e. next to the existing mDNS pass, position 3-4):
  3. Action Pass, Protocol UDP
  4. Source: IoT net (or narrower: single host 192.168.86.130)
  5. Destination: k8s_ha_coiot, port 5683
  6. Description: ShellyEM CoIoT push to Home Assistant (UDP 5683)
  7. Apply, then confirm the rule is loaded and not TCP-only: 
    pfctl -sr -v | grep -i 5683

Prefer the narrow single-host source if only shellyem-main needs it; widen it only when another Gen1 device is onboarded.

docs.title: Step 3 — Shelly device: set the CoIoT peer (human action)
docs.text:
WebUI (http://shellyem-main.iot.grigri, log in with the pass iot/shellyem-main credentials): Internet & Security → ADVANCED - DEVELOPER SETTINGS → keep Enable CoIoT checked → set CoIoT peer to 192.168.193.12:5683 → SAVE → then reboot the device (the peer change only takes effect after a restart; HA's own docs require it).

Equivalent REST call (Gen1 /settings/advanced, the same endpoint aioshelly's configure_coiot_protocol() uses):

PASS=$(pass show iot/shellyem-main | head -1)
USER=$(pass show iot/shellyem-main | sed -n 's/^login: //p')
curl -sS -u "$USER:$PASS" -X POST \
  "http://shellyem-main.iot.grigri/settings/advanced?coiot_enable=true&coiot_peer=192.168.193.12:5683"
curl -sS -u "$USER:$PASS" http://shellyem-main.iot.grigri/settings | jq .coiot
unset PASS USER   # never echo or commit these

Expect {"enabled": true, "update_period": 15, "peer": "192.168.193.12:5683"}. The reboot can be triggered from HA (button.shellyem_main_reboot) or the device UI. Keep update_period at 15.

docs.title: Step 4 — Verify
docs.text:
# a) Push packets with NO preceding HA request (compare against the poll pattern above):
ssh root@pfsense.grigri "tcpdump -p -n -i igb1.501 'udp port 5683 and dst 192.168.193.12'"
#    expect 192.168.86.130.5683 > 192.168.193.12.5683, length 239, every ~15 s
ssh root@pfsense.grigri "pfctl -ss | grep 193.12"

# b) HA update cadence drops from ~33 s to ~15 s:
#    websocket subscribe_events/state_changed on sensor.shellyem_main_channel_1_power,
#    or the /api/history/period call from the diagnosis section.

# c) Device settings persisted:
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://hass.grigri.cloud/api/diagnostics/config_entry/<shelly-entry-id> \
  | jq '.data.device_settings.coiot'

# d) Repair gone (auto-deleted on the first CoAP PERIODIC message):
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://hass.grigri.cloud/api/repairs/list_issues \
  | jq '[.issues[] | select(.domain=="shelly")]'

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
• Device only: set the peer back to multicast — coiot_peer=mcast (or clear the field in the UI) and reboot. HA resumes 33 s polling; the repair returns after ~3 min.
  • Cluster only: delete the hass-coiot Service block from values.yaml; Cilium releases the VIP and pfSense drops the BGP route. Leave the pfSense alias/rule in place (harmless) or remove them in the same change window.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Option Verdict IGMP proxy + multicast routing on pfSense Rejected. Needs igmpproxy (IoT upstream → DMZ downstream), IGMP firewall rules, and a multicast route into 10.0.0.0/8, which Cilium does not route to pods. Much larger blast radius on the router for one device, and still not guaranteed to reach the pod netns. hostNetwork: true on the HA pod Rejected. Binds 5683 on the node, conflicts with anything else using it, bypasses the Service/Ingress model, and complicates node moves. NodePort + node IP (192.168.192.3:<nodePort>) as the peer Works, and needs the same pfSense UDP rule, but ties the device config to a node address and a random port. The LB VIP matches cluster convention (mosquitto, unifi, transcoder …) and survives node changes. HA's own "Configure CoIoT" repair button Do not use — see pitfalls. Do nothing Legitimate. Polling delivers correct data at 33 s; the cost is a permanent error-level repair and coarser grid-power resolution. If this is the decision, ignore the repair deliberately rather than "fixing" it from HA.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• The push_update_* repair survives both "disable CoIoT" and "switch to MQTT". check_coiot_config() returns True when the device reports coiot.enabled: false (components/shelly/utils.py:1070), which makes async_manage_coiot_issues_task() take the push-update-failure branch and raise the error-severity issue rather than the coiot_unconfigured warning. And ShellyBlockCoordinator._handle_update() increments _push_update_failures on every COAP_REPLY unconditionally (coordinator.py:456-462), regardless of the device's CoIoT setting. HA keeps polling over CoAP whether or not the device has CoIoT or MQTT enabled, so the only ways to clear it are a genuine CoAP PERIODIC push (unicast CoIoT, Step 1-3 below), removing the shelly config entry, or ignoring the issue in the UI. Ignoring is persisted (helpers/issue_registry.py, storage key repairs.issue_registry) even though the issue itself is is_persistent: false, so it survives restarts.
  • Never click "Configure CoIoT" in HA repairs. CoiotConfigureFlow (homeassistant/components/shelly/repairs.py:262-288) writes get_coiot_address(hass):get_coiot_port(hass) straight onto the device via configure_coiot_protocol(). get_coiot_address() derives the address from HA's own URL (get_url(prefer_external=False) → source IP toward that host). Today internal_url and external_url are both null, so it returns None and the flow aborts with cannot_configure (harmless). If an internal URL is ever configured, HA would overwrite the peer with an address it can see — the pod IP 10.0.4.218, which is unreachable from the IoT VLAN — silently breaking push. Fixing it then requires re-setting the peer on the device by hand.
  • Leave internal_url unset, or accept a coiot_unconfigured warning repair: once a peer is configured, check_coiot_config() compares it against get_coiot_address():port and flags a mismatch. An empty peer is treated as correctly configured (the check is falsy-guarded), which is why today's issue is push_update_failure (not fixable) rather than coiot_unconfigured.
  • 45104 (or any similar port) in a capture is HA's ephemeral polling source port, not something to configure. The CoIoT peer port is always 5683 unless you override it with shelly: coap_port: in configuration.yaml (not used here).
  • Don't point the peer at hass.grigri.cloud. The external ingress LB exposes TCP 80/443 only; there is no UDP 5683 path behind it.
  • IoT VLAN blocks device-initiated UDP. Adding the Service and setting the peer without the pfSense rule produces no visible error — HA just keeps polling and the repair stays. Verify with tcpdump, not with "the sensors still update".
  • externalTrafficPolicy: Local + ECMP advertisement = ~50 % push loss. See Step 1.
  • The peer change needs a device reboot; until then the device keeps multicasting and nothing appears to have changed.
  • Gen2+ devices don't use this path. shellypmmini-z800 and the shellyplus2pm-* devices use RPC/outbound WebSocket (and are on 192.168.86.0/24 too); they need no CoIoT peer and are not affected by the IoT UDP rule.
  • Shelly relies on SNTP for metering. This device reports 0 s clock skew, so nothing to do — but if power/energy ever looks wrong, check /status unixtime before blaming CoIoT.

docs.title: Relevance to battery-optimizer
docs.text:
apps/battery-optimizer/files/service.yaml maps the shadow service's grid signals to this device: grid_power: sensor.shellyem_main_channel_1_power, grid_energy: sensor.shellyem_main_channel_1_energy, observed: [sensor.shellyem_main_channel_2_power].

This is not a blocker for Phase C. With freshness_s.grid_power: 300 and home_assistant.poll_interval_s: 60, a 2 s source is ~150× inside budget, and the slot-energy accounting uses the grid_energy counter deltas, which polling captures fine.

Since the 2026-10-27 cutover, grid_power and observed arrive over MQTT at 2.01 s — measured as battery_optimizer_input_age_seconds{role="grid_power"} = 2.3 s, down from 31.9 s. The remaining entity, grid_energy, is still a native Shelly counter at 33 s, which is correct for it: it is a monotonic total consumed as 900 s deltas, so a faster transport would add recorder rows without adding information.
