  1. Move CI off prusik — planning/ci-runner-amd64-1.md. Blocked on k8s-amd64-1 going 16 → 32 GiB RAM (planning/k8s-amd64-1-node-addition.md TODO-9.2): ci-runner-0 peaks at 17.4 GiB / 7.68 cores and the node has only 16 GiB, so it cannot host the runner today.
  2. Bound the calypso gVisor runners — different repo (multivara/gitops). Their 0.29Gi-request / 16Gi-limit shape is the actual overcommit: the scheduler places them believing 0.29 GiB and they take gigabytes. They drove the second failure of 2026-10-13. The existing ResourceQuota is CI-only; calypso is outside this repo's scope, so the second failure mode remains unresolved until the other repo is updated.
  3. Validate MemoryLow effectiveness under load — the 6G MemoryLow on k3s.service and the matching 6G on system.slice (via drop-in) are now applied and verified on prusik (6442450944 in both cgroups), so the ancestor budget exists and the child's protection is not capped to 0. The cgroup chain is -.slice → system.slice → k3s.service; init.scope is a sibling of system.slice under the root slice, not an ancestor. What is still unvalidated is behaviour: whether this actually prevents the etcd freeze under CI pressure — monitor during the next pressure window. Calypso gVisor runners remain uncovered (see Deferred §2).
  4. Attribution dashboard on top of the gVisor-aware recording rule — the rule itself is done (2026-10-13): node_namespace_pod:container_memory_working_set_bytes_incl_gvisor in system/monitoring/resources/gvisor-memory-recording-rules.yaml, so CI memory is no longer invisible to per-pod queries. What remains is a dashboard that consumes it, replacing panels built on image!="" / container!="".
  5. Raise zfs_arc_max above 5 GiB (planning/k8s-amd64-1-node-addition.md TODO-6.6) — only after CI leaves. Raising the cap while MemAvailable bottoms out at ~3 GiB trades one stall for a worse one. See docs/conventions/prusik-fast-storage-tier.md.
  6. Dedicated etcd device, separate from the OS filesystem and swap, so reclaim I/O cannot queue ahead of a WAL fsync.
  7. 3-member etcd HA — an availability project, explicitly not a fix for this. A second member gives no quorum tolerance, and overcommit breaks any member whose host is starved.

docs.title: Rejected approaches
docs.text:
Do not re-propose these; each was considered and rejected on the evidence.

  • Disabling or reducing etcd snapshots — they are not the observed trigger (0.3–0.7s), and they are the recovery path.
  • Raising etcd timeouts / heartbeat intervals — masks the stall, makes the API slower for everyone, and leaves the memory collapse in place.
  • Removing swap before freeing RAM — with 204.6 GiB of limits on 50.7 GiB allocatable, removing the overflow valve converts thrash into OOM kills of whatever the kernel picks, including the control plane.
  • Tuning vm.swappiness alone — changes the balance between reclaim paths, not the total pressure on the shared device.
  • ionice/nice on k3s — one process contains the API server, scheduler, controllers, and etcd; lowering its I/O priority starves exactly what you are protecting.

docs.title: If this recurs — how to keep investigating
docs.text:
Everything below is read-only. SSH commands on prusik are for inspection only (AGENTS.md: no ad-hoc mutation on a remote host); if a command needs root, it is marked [root] and it only reads. All kubectl commands use --context=grigri (the kustomize local context can include other contexts). Do not escalate to local privileged commands; do not execute mutating kubectl commands. The one mutating command this doc names — a scoped, committed, config-only ANSIBLE_EXTRA_ARGS="-t k3s --limit <node>" make cluster — is agent-allowed per AGENTS.md, and only in that form: an unscoped or all-node make cluster, -t k3s without --limit, and any k3s_version bump remain prohibited. It restarts k3s on the targeted node (brief API downtime on the sole control plane), so it is a maintenance action, not part of this read-only investigation path.

Resolve the root device first — see the device-instability section. Use DEVICE below for "whatever node_disk_info/lsblk says the SanDisk Extreme 500GB is today".

docs.title: 1. Confirm it is the same mechanism (60 seconds)
docs.text:
Five discriminating signals. An outage is this mechanism when all of them move together; a healthy baseline is flat on all five.

Signal Query Healthy This incident Alert MemAvailable node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes{instance="prusik"} ≥ 8 GiB (flat) < ~4 GiB (~3 GiB) PrusikMemoryAvailableLow / Critical Memory PSI "full" rate(node_pressure_memory_stalled_seconds_total{instance="prusik"}[1m]) 0 0.24–0.63 PrusikMemoryPSIHigh (>0.1) Swap rate rate(node_vmstat_pswpout{instance="prusik"}[1m]) pages/s ~0.5 pages/s > 1000 pages/s (storm ~25k) PrusikSwapThrashing Root-NVMe queue rate(node_disk_io_time_weighted_seconds_total{instance="prusik",device="DEVICE"}[1m]) single digits > 32 (218 measured, 400+ in a later storm) PrusikRootDiskQueueHigh etcd WAL fsync p99 see Prometheus ~1–3ms > 0.25s, peaked 1.92s EtcdWALFsyncSlow / Critical etcd backend commit p99 see Prometheus ~1–3ms > 0.25s, peaked 3.71s EtcdBackendCommitSlow / Critical

Memory-thrash vs a pure disk problem — the decision rule:

  • Memory signals (PSI full > 0.1, swap, MemAvailable < 4 GiB) all zero but root-disk queue and etcd latency are high → it is the device: check SMART, write-cache flush behaviour, thermal throttling, and who else is writing to that NVMe. Do not reach for the CI playbook.
  • Memory signals non-zero → this mechanism. Go straight to attribution (§4).
  • High I/O-PSI with no memory PSI is normal on this host during a scrub — 0.5–0.78 was measured with healthy control-plane latency. Never treat node_pressure_io_* as the trigger.
  • If etcd latency is high and etcd_server_has_leader is still 1 with etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total unchanged, that is consistent with this mechanism: the killer is the Kubernetes Lease, not raft.

docs.title: 2. On the node (SSH, read-only)
docs.text:
# The outage signature. Also confirms snapshot duration and the startup defrag. [root]
# Use --utc because the host timezone is CEST; explicit --since/--until in UTC avoids ambiguity.
sudo journalctl -u k3s --utc --since "2026-10-13 02:00:00 UTC" --until "2026-10-13 04:00:00 UTC" \
  | grep -iE "apply request took too long|ReadIndex|leaderelection lost|Saving etcd snapshot|fetched snapshot|Defragmenting|DeadlineExceeded"

# Did k3s actually die, and how many times? NRestarts is the outage counter. [root]
systemctl show k3s -p MemoryLow,MemorySwapMax,MemoryCurrent,MemoryPeak,NRestarts
sudo systemctl status k3s --no-pager

# etcd's own view: latency, DB size, leadership (metrics are served in-process on :2381, so
# target-down here means k3s is down or restarting)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:2381/metrics \
  | grep -E "db_total_size|has_leader|leader_changes|wal_fsync|backend_commit"
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:2381/metrics | grep -E "^process_start_time_seconds"

# Snapshot timing — confirms snapshots are 0.3-0.7s, not the freeze
sudo k3s etcd-snapshot ls

# Is the swapfile really on the root device, and is it fragmented across it? [root]
swapon --show --bytes; findmnt -T /swapfile; sudo filefrag -v /swapfile | head

# Resolve current NVMe naming BEFORE using any device name in a query. [root]
lsblk -o NAME,MODEL,SERIAL,MOUNTPOINT
sudo ls -l /dev/disk/by-id/

# Pressure per resource, live. memory:full > 0 is the tell; io:full alone is not. [root]
cat /proc/pressure/{io,memory,cpu}

# Device-level view: %util, aqu-sz (queue depth), await on the root NVMe
iostat -xz 5 2

# How much of k3s is actually swapped out right now? Large VmSwap = the control plane is paying
# reclaim latency directly. [root]
pgrep -af "k3s server"; sudo grep VmSwap /proc/<k3spid>/status

docs.title: 3. Prometheus (audited query set)
docs.text:
# --- Host: is the node out of RAM? ---
node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes{instance="prusik"}
node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes{instance="prusik"}
  / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes{instance="prusik"}          # < 0.08 warning, < 0.05 critical

# --- Host: is anything blocked in reclaim? (the "full" line = *_stalled series) ---
rate(node_pressure_memory_stalled_seconds_total{instance="prusik"}[1m])
rate(node_pressure_memory_waiting_seconds_total{instance="prusik"}[1m])

# --- Host: swap traffic, converted to MiB/s (counters are PAGES, not bytes) ---
rate(node_vmstat_pswpin{instance="prusik"}[1m]) * 4096 / 1048576
rate(node_vmstat_pswpout{instance="prusik"}[1m]) * 4096 / 1048576

# --- Device: resolve DEVICE by model BEFORE using it in queries ---
# The SanDisk Extreme 500GB root disk kernel name flips across reboots. Resolve it now:
node_disk_info{instance="prusik"}
# Look for model="Extreme_500GB" (or similar) and note the current device name.

# --- Device: queue depth (weighted time = avg in-flight), mean write await, utilisation ---
# DEVICE = resolved from node_disk_info above, NOT a remembered nvmeXnY
rate(node_disk_io_time_weighted_seconds_total{instance="prusik",device="DEVICE"}[1m])

# Mean write await in milliseconds (not tail, not weighted time / total IO).
# weighted time is useful for queue depth, NOT the standard await numerator; use write_time.
# clamp_min prevents division by zero when writes are idle.
1000 * rate(node_disk_write_time_seconds_total{instance="prusik",device="DEVICE"}[1m])
  / clamp_min(rate(node_disk_writes_completed_total{instance="prusik",device="DEVICE"}[1m]), 0.001)

# Read await analogous (optional, one query enough):
1000 * rate(node_disk_read_time_seconds_total{instance="prusik",device="DEVICE"}[1m])
  / clamp_min(rate(node_disk_reads_completed_total{instance="prusik",device="DEVICE"}[1m]), 0.001)

rate(node_disk_io_time_seconds_total{instance="prusik",device="DEVICE"}[1m])   # %util

# --- etcd: the symptom that pages. Use [1m] around restarts to avoid mixed populations. ---
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (job, instance, le) (
  rate(etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds_bucket{job="etcd"}[1m])
))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (job, instance, le) (
  rate(etcd_disk_backend_commit_duration_seconds_bucket{job="etcd"}[1m])
))

# --- etcd: snapshots and DB bloat ---
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (job, instance, le) (
  rate(etcd_disk_backend_snapshot_duration_seconds_bucket{job="etcd"}[1m])
))
rate(etcd_debugging_snap_save_total_duration_seconds_sum{job="etcd"}[1m])
  / rate(etcd_debugging_snap_save_total_duration_seconds_count{job="etcd"}[1m])
etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_bytes{job="etcd"}
  / etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_use_in_bytes{job="etcd"}    # ~2.7x = dead pages, not a freeze

# --- etcd: leadership (expect has_leader=1, leader_changes flat at 1) ---
etcd_server_has_leader{job="etcd"}
etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total{job="etcd"}

# --- ZFS ARC: is reclaim eating the cache? (cap is pinned at 5 GiB) ---
node_zfs_arc_c_max{instance="prusik"}                     # 5 GiB, metal/inventory/host_vars/prusik.yml

Metrics that do not exist on this node — do not write queries or alerts against them, they will silently return nothing (empty panels look identical to a healthy system):

  • node_vmstat_pgscan_direct, node_vmstat_pgscan_kswapd — absent from prusik's node-exporter. Use PSI (node_pressure_memory_stalled_seconds_total) and node_vmstat_pswpin/pswpout instead.
  • node_memory_page_size_bytes — absent, which is why PrusikSwapThrashing thresholds in pages/s (4 KiB pages) rather than bytes.

docs.title: 4. Attribute the memory to a workload
docs.text:
Query at a point in time at the peak, not max_over_time across a window. A windowed max summarises every short-lived pod at its own moment and reports a total that never existed on the node simultaneously — which is exactly how a gVisor burst gets blamed on a runner that already exited, or missed entirely.

# Prometheus HTTP API: instant query evaluated AT the peak timestamp
curl -sG http://prometheus.internal.grigri.cloud/api/v1/query \
  --data-urlencode 'query=max by(namespace,pod)(container_memory_working_set_bytes{node="prusik",pod!="",container="",id!~".*cri-containerd.*"})' \
  --data-urlencode "time=2026-10-13T03:07:30Z"

# Verified pod-aggregate form — USE THIS ON PRUSIK.
# Excludes the root empty Pod series (container="") and excludes named container paths by matching
# id!~".*cri-containerd.*". max by (namespace,pod) picks the aggregate sandbox series if present,
# but this is not a generic guarantee — verify the metadata id filter against your node-exporter
# version. Use point-in-time instant queries, not summing max_over_time.
max by(namespace,pod)(container_memory_working_set_bytes{node="prusik",pod!="",container="",id!~".*cri-containerd.*"})

# Node-total sanity check against the same instant
sum(container_memory_working_set_bytes{node="prusik",pod!="",container="",id!~".*cri-containerd.*"})

# Was anything actually OOM-killed? (In these incidents: no. Answer the question, then move on.)
increase(container_oom_events_total{node="prusik"}[15m])
node_vmstat_oom_kill{instance="prusik"}

Expect: non-CI baseline flat at 30–35 GiB; anything below that is CI. Check ci-runner-0 first, then calypso-runners, then any pod that started between the two.

docs.title: 5. The restart + startup-defrag amplifier
docs.text:
The downtime per cycle is stall + unconditional defrag, so quantify both.

# Restart count as an outage counter (also exposed as process_start_time_seconds on job="etcd")
systemctl show k3s -p NRestarts

# Each restart: Defragmenting ... before the API comes up (0.5-4.06s measured)
sudo journalctl -u k3s --utc --since "2 hours ago UTC" | grep -iE "Defragmenting|Starting k3s|Main process exited|Failed with result"

# Every change in process start time = one k3s restart. > 0 is the outage, not a rate.
changes(process_start_time_seconds{job="etcd"}[1h])
up{job="etcd"} == 0

If the defrag grows steadily across cycles, the DB is accumulating dead pages (etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_bytes vs _in_use_...): compact and defrag during a quiet window, not during a stall — defrag on a saturated device is the worst possible time.

docs.title: 6. Then check the collateral
docs.text:
Every k3s exit mid-backup leaves state behind. Verify it, do not assume a clean recovery:

kubectl --context=grigri get backups -n velero | grep -E "InProgress|Queued|PartiallyFailed|Failed"
kubectl --context=grigri get zb -n zfs-localpv | grep -v Done

Recovery procedure: docs/troubleshooting/velero-2026-09-25-oom-etcd-outage.md and docs/troubleshooting/velero-backup-failures.md.

docs.title: Prevention and success criteria
docs.text:
Fixes are working when, across a CI burst and a backup window:

  1. No k3s lease-loss exits — changes(process_start_time_seconds{job="etcd"}[1h]) == 0 and NRestarts flat; no leaderelection lost in the journal.
  2. etcd latency stays sub-100ms at p99 for WAL fsync and backend commit during CI/backup windows (incident peak: 1.92s / 3.71s).
  3. CI dies at its own boundary — the runner container is OOM-killed or evicted (with low-priority it is first in line) instead of the node thrashing. container_oom_events_total rising on ci-runners while the control plane stays healthy is success, not an incident.
  4. memory-PSI "full" ≈ 0 and swap rate ≈ 0 at the peaks; MemAvailable never under the eviction-soft 4 GiB for more than the 1m grace period.
  5. Alerts fire early — PrusikMemoryAvailableLow, PrusikMemoryPSIHigh and PrusikSwapThrashing precede EtcdWALFsyncSlow, which precedes K3sEtcdRestarted. If the restart alert is the first thing you see, the host-side thresholds are too slow: tune them down, do not add more etcd rules.

Baseline caveat — read before comparing "before/after". The pre-incident baseline is metrics-only, and the metrics were added while a scrub was running: the scrub started 2026-10-11 00:24 and the node-exporter/etcd series went live 2026-10-11 ~19:11Z. There is therefore no clean pre-scrub window in Prometheus. Treat "healthy" as healthy under I/O-PSI 0.5–0.78 with memory-PSI at zero — which is precisely the comparison that ruled out the scrub. Do not conclude "I/O-PSI is high, so we are still broken" from the scrub overlap, and re-measure the memory/swap floors after the Tier 0/1 changes land rather than reusing these numbers as a target.

docs.title: prusik L2ARC is misconfigured, not useless
docs.text:
Measured 2026-09-30 over 7d and 30d windows. Prometheus: instance="prusik".

Correction: an earlier version of this doc concluded the L2ARC was net-negative and should be removed. That was wrong. It reasoned from the low hit ratio (34-39%) and the small share of total reads served (1.4%) without checking what the L2ARC was caching. The average hit size proves it is serving the most latency-sensitive traffic on the node. Do not remove the L2ARC.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
The 2TB FIKWOT FN960 NVMe (nvme0n1, M.2_1) is the L2ARC cache vdev for the datasets RAIDZ1 pool. Symptoms that looked like L2ARC failure:

  • Hit ratio only 34-39%
  • l2_abort_lowmem firing ~0.6-1.0/sec (365K-589K events per 7d)
  • l2_hdr_size 1.68 GiB against a 5 GiB ARC cap — ~34% of the ARC spent on L2ARC metadata
  • HDD read latency still 14-17ms average, 54ms peak, with Forgejo git-upload-pack at 200-310ms

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text: The L2ARC is genuinely valuable and simultaneously badly starved. Three distinct issues.

docs.title: 1. Why the low hit ratio is misleading
docs.text:
The ratio is computed over the population that already missed the ARC — 3.7% of all reads. It is not a measure of usefulness.

sum(increase(node_zfs_arc_hits{instance="prusik"}[7d]))       # 4.94B  (96.3% of all reads)
sum(increase(node_zfs_arc_l2_hits{instance="prusik"}[7d]))    #  71.3M
sum(increase(node_zfs_arc_l2_misses{instance="prusik"}[7d]))  # 118.8M

71.3M reads per week rescued from 14-54ms HDD latency down to 0.29ms. That is 1.4% of total volume and close to 100% of the painful reads.

docs.title: 2. What it is actually caching — the load-bearing number
docs.text:
increase(node_zfs_arc_l2_read_bytes{instance="prusik"}[7d])
  / increase(node_zfs_arc_l2_hits{instance="prusik"}[7d])

≈17-28KB per hit. Video streaming reads 128KB-1MB blocks. Small hits mean metadata, thumbnails, SQLite pages, git objects, and Postgres blocks — exactly the latency-critical population.

Corroborated by config-jellyfin reading 1.42TB in 7d, more than either media dataset. That PVC holds no video: media is mounted HostPath read-only from datasets/peliculas and datasets/series, and transcodes/ is an emptyDir that never touches ZFS. The 1.42TB is entirely UI traffic:

Path Contents metadata/library/ 1,511 entries — posters, backdrops, logos metadata/People/ 521 dirs — actor images and metadata data/jellyfin.db 218MB SQLite + WAL/SHM data/subtitles/ 196 cached subtitle dirs cache/images/ 73MB

Demand-read hit ratios are healthy — demand data 93.7% (2.31B hits / 154M misses), demand metadata 98.1% (18.44B / 356M). The L2ARC feeds application reads, not speculation.

docs.title: 3. The real defect: l2arc_noprefetch=0
docs.text:
metal/roles/setup/templates/zfs.conf.j2 sets l2arc_noprefetch=0, caching one-shot sequential prefetch. Jellyfin video playback reads each block exactly once, so this occupies the device with data that will never be hit again, evicting the small random blocks that matter.

Bucket Size Share Prefetch 462GB 41% — one-shot video, near-zero reuse MRU 444GB 39% — demand MFU 243GB 21% — demand Useful (MRU+MFU) 687GB of 1.13TB 59%

Prefetch hit ratio is 20.7% (11.3M hits / 54.4M), consistent with read-once streaming.

docs.title: 4. The upstream cause: the ARC is too small
docs.text:
Every block cached on the L2ARC device needs an index header (l2arc_buf_hdr_t, ~175 bytes) that lives in ARC RAM, not on the NVMe. That is what node_zfs_arc_l2_hdr_size measures — the RAM cost of describing the cache, as opposed to node_zfs_arc_l2_size, which is the data on the device. On prusik the ratio is ~0.14%: 1.68 GiB of headers indexing 1227 GiB of cached data.

That sounds negligible until you compare it against the right denominator. The headers are charged to a 5 GiB ARC cap, so they consume ~34% of it. l2_abort_lowmem at ~1/sec is the same pressure showing up differently: ZFS drops L2ARC writes when the ARC cannot afford them, so the device cannot retain what it caches. Both are symptoms of an ARC capped at 5 GiB on a node whose container limits sum to ~85GB against 64GB of RAM.

The header tax is proportional to the ARC cap, not to the L2ARC — at a 20 GiB ARC the same 1.68 GiB is 8% instead of 34%. This is the main reason growing the ARC also fixes the L2ARC.

Grafana caveat: the L2 ARC size panel (id 365) in system/zfs-exporter/dashboards/zfs.json plots actual (l2_size) and hdr (l2_hdr_size) as two series on the same bytes axis. At 1227 GiB versus 1.68 GiB that is a 730:1 ratio, so hdr renders as a flat line at zero and the problem is invisible on the dashboard. The two series also measure different resources with very different scarcity — device space (60% of 2TB, harmless) versus ARC RAM (34% of 5 GiB, severe). Always evaluate headers as a fraction of arc_c_max, never against l2_size:

node_zfs_arc_l2_hdr_size / node_zfs_arc_c_max * 100   # prusik ~34%, grigri ~4%

Fixing the ARC is what makes the L2ARC work. See docs/conventions/prusik-fast-storage-tier.md.

docs.title: How to Diagnose
docs.text:
# Average cached-read size — small (<64KB) means metadata/random, large means streaming
increase(node_zfs_arc_l2_read_bytes{instance="prusik"}[7d])
  / increase(node_zfs_arc_l2_hits{instance="prusik"}[7d])

# How much of the device is wasted on one-shot prefetch?
node_zfs_arc_l2_prefetch_asize{instance="prusik"} / node_zfs_arc_l2_asize{instance="prusik"}

# Is the ARC too small to sustain the L2ARC?
rate(node_zfs_arc_l2_abort_lowmem{instance="prusik"}[1h])
node_zfs_arc_l2_hdr_size{instance="prusik"} / node_zfs_arc_c_max{instance="prusik"}

# Is the app's own read path being served? (the ratio that matters)
node_zfs_arc_demand_data_hits
  / (node_zfs_arc_demand_data_hits + node_zfs_arc_demand_data_misses)

Device health was clean: l2_cksum_bad 0, l2_io_error 0, l2_evict_reading 0, l2_evict_lock_retry 0. The NVMe is not the problem.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
Step 1 — l2arc_noprefetch=1 (the ZFS default) in metal/roles/setup/templates/zfs.conf.j2. One-line, reversible.

Expected: 462GB released from one-shot video, letting demand data grow from 687GB toward the full ~1.05TB (+53% useful cache). Jellyfin library browsing, search, and poster loading should get snappier; Forgejo git reads and Postgres also benefit. Video playback is unaffected — a 4K remux is ~12MB/s against ~400-500MB/s of RAIDZ1 sequential throughput, and transcodes already bypass ZFS.

Verify by watching l2_prefetch_asize fall toward zero while l2_hits holds steady or rises.

Baseline captured 2026-09-30 (prusik, 7d), for comparison:

Metric Before Target after l2_prefetch_asize / l2_asize 462GB / 1.13TB = 41% < 5% l2_mru_asize + l2_mfu_asize 444 + 243 = 687GB ≥ 900GB l2_hits per day ~10.2M ≥ baseline (must not fall) Avg L2ARC hit size 17-28KB ~unchanged l2_abort_lowmem ~0.6-1.0/sec unchanged — needs ARC growth, not this

L2ARC is a circular log: the 462GB already resident is overwritten gradually, not evicted immediately. At l2arc_write_max=300MB/s a full 1.05TB cycle is ~1h in theory, but real write rate tracks actual miss volume. Allow 24-48h before judging, and compare 7d windows.

The change also affects grigri, which has its own L2ARC (l2arc_write_max_mb: 120) and an 8GB ARC cap on 32GB RAM. Roll out to prusik first, measure, then extend.

Revert per host with l2arc_noprefetch: 0 in metal/inventory/host_vars/<host>.yml and re-running the zfs-config tag — no template edit needed.

Step 2 — grow the ARC (the real fix). Requires freeing RAM on prusik first; moving the CI runner off the node reclaims ~19GB and supports zfs_arc_max of 20-24GB. This largely stops l2_abort_lowmem, shrinks the header tax to ~8%, and puts the whole 12-14GB hot set in RAM.

Do not remove the cache vdev. Without it every poster, thumbnail, and SQLite page read falls to 14-54ms HDD latency.

Do not raise zfs_arc_max before freeing RAM. Available memory hit a 2.15-3.5GB minimum during CI builds, and that pressure already caused a control-plane outage — see docs/troubleshooting/velero-2026-09-25-oom-etcd-outage.md. Raising the cap without relieving container pressure risks repeating it on the sole control-plane node.

docs.title: PVPC Updated: ESIOS API Returns ZIP Instead of JSON
Problem
docs.text:
The pvpc_updated custom integration (HACS, from oscarrgarciia/HA-PVPC-Updated) silently fails to load PVPC electricity prices. Symptoms:

  • HASS logs: WARNING [pvpc_updated] Client error in '...' -> 200, message='Attempt to decode JSON with unexpected mimetype: json'
  • AppDaemon climate_control / dhw_control stuck in retry loop: Less than 15 hours of data available: []. Retrying in 10 minutes
  • sensor.esios_pvpc shows unavailable or stale data

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
The ESIOS API (api.esios.ree.es) changed its response behavior for the public PVPC endpoint (/archives/70/download_json):

  1. Content-Type changed from application/json to text/html
  2. Response body changed from plain JSON to a ZIP archive containing JSON files

aiohttp's resp.json() validates Content-Type by default, raising ContentTypeError on the mismatch. Even with content_type=None, the ZIP body cannot be parsed as JSON.

Per the ESIOS API docs, the endpoint should return application/json; charset=utf-8. This is an API bug on ESIOS's side (reported to consultasios@ree.es on 2026-07-08).

docs.title: How to Diagnose
docs.text:
# Check response headers
curl -sI "https://api.esios.ree.es/archives/70/download_json?locale=es&date=$(date +%F)"

# Check if response is ZIP (magic bytes PK\x03\x04)
curl -s "https://api.esios.ree.es/archives/70/download_json?locale=es&date=$(date +%F)" | file -

# Check HASS logs for the warning
kubectl --context=grigri -n home-assistant logs home-assistant-hass-0 --tail=100 | grep pvpc

# Check AppDaemon for the retry loop
kubectl --context=grigri -n home-assistant logs -l app=appdaemon --tail=50 | grep "Less than"

docs.title: Fix / Workaround
docs.text:
A fix has been submitted upstream: PR #5. It reads raw bytes, detects ZIP by magic bytes, extracts JSON from the archive, and falls back to plain JSON parsing.

If the upstream fix is merged and installed via HACS, no manual action is needed.

To apply the fix manually on the running pod (temporary, lost on restart):

# Copy the patched file from the local fork
kubectl --context=grigri -n home-assistant cp \
  HA-PVPC-Updated/custom_components/pvpc_updated/aiopvpc/pvpc_data.py \
  home-assistant-hass-0:/config/custom_components/pvpc_updated/aiopvpc/pvpc_data.py

# Restart the pod to pick up changes
kubectl --context=grigri -n home-assistant delete pod home-assistant-hass-0

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Forgejo (git.grigri.cloud) shows intermittent latency spikes — git operations take 1-2 seconds, runner UpdateTask calls spike to 100-300ms, and pre-receive hooks exceed 1.5s.

HDD disks on prusik show queue depth 8-11 (saturated at ~240 IOPS each), with only moderate throughput (~8 MB/s per disk).

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
qBittorrent uses HostPath volumes mounted directly to HDD datasets (/datasets/{series,peliculas,musica}/download). Seeding torrents read small pieces (256KB-4MB) from random locations across the disk. This random I/O pattern saturates HDDs at their ~240 IOPS ceiling.

L2ARC does not help with writes — it's a read cache only. For reads, L2ARC has a 40% hit ratio which helps but doesn't fully solve the problem when many torrents are actively seeding with random access patterns.

The combined random I/O from qBittorrent + other workloads (ci-runner, cross-backups minio, jellyfin) exceeds the HDD IOPS ceiling, causing queue depth to spike and affecting all workloads on prusik.

docs.title: How to Diagnose
docs.text:
1. Check HDD queue depth (values > 1 indicate I/O queuing):
# Via Grafana/Prometheus
kubectl --context=grigri query_prometheus --expr 'rate(node_disk_io_time_weighted_seconds_total{instance="prusik", device=~"sd[abcd]"}[5m])'
  1. Check per-container I/O on HDDs:
# Top consumers of HDD reads
kubectl --context=grigri query_prometheus --expr 'topk(10, rate(container_fs_reads_bytes_total{node="prusik", device=~"/dev/sd.*"}[5m]))'
  1. Check qBittorrent I/O priority:
kubectl --context=grigri exec qbittorrent-0 -n qbittorrent -c qbittorrent -- ionice -p 1
  1. Check qBittorrent config values:
kubectl --context=grigri exec qbittorrent-0 -n qbittorrent -c qbittorrent -- cat /config/qBittorrent/qBittorrent.conf | grep MaxActive

docs.title: Fix
docs.text: Two changes applied together:

docs.title: 1. ionice idle priority (the key fix)
docs.text:
Run qBittorrent with I/O class 3 (idle) — only does I/O when no other process needs disk:

# values.yaml — qbittorrent container
command:
  - /bin/sh
  - -c
  - |
    exec ionice -c 3 /entrypoint.sh

securityContext:
  capabilities:
    add:
      - SYS_NICE  # Required for ionice

docs.title: 2. Increase startup probe timeout
docs.text:
With idle I/O priority, qBittorrent startup is slow (loading 4400+ torrents from BT_backup). Increase the startup probe to 10 minutes:

startup:
  failureThreshold: 60  # was 30
  periodSeconds: 10

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Metric Before After HDD queue depth 8-11 1.5-5.5 HDD IOPS ~240 (ceiling) ~145-190 Forgejo git ops 1511ms 5-7ms Forgejo runner updates 112-295ms 5-78ms

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• ionice -c 3 (idle) is the lowest possible I/O priority. There is no class 10.
  • MaxActiveUploads was kept at 2800 to avoid hit-and-run penalties on private trackers. The ionice setting handles I/O prioritization, not the upload limit.
  • L2ARC (1.28 TB on prusik) only caches reads, not writes. It has a ~40% hit ratio which helps but doesn't eliminate the problem for random seeding reads.
  • If further I/O reduction is needed, consider moving qBittorrent downloads to NVMe storage.

docs.title: Understanding the Settings
docs.text: qBittorrent has two types of limits that are often confused:

docs.title: Queue Limits (which torrents can seek peers)
docs.text:
• max_active_uploads: How many seeding torrents can be "active" (allowed to find/connect peers)
  • max_active_downloads: How many downloading torrents can be "active"
  • max_active_torrents: Total active torrents (uploads + downloads)

Critical: If max_active_uploads is too low, torrents get stuck in queuedUP state and cannot even attempt to connect to peers. This is the #1 cause of slow speeds with many seeding torrents.

docs.title: Bandwidth/Slot Limits (how many can transfer data)
docs.text:
• max_uploads: How many torrents can upload data simultaneously
  • max_uploads_per_torrent: Upload slots per torrent
  • max_connec: Total peer connections across all torrents
  • max_connec_per_torrent: Peer connections per torrent

docs.title: Memory Limits
docs.text:
• Container memory limit: Too low causes OOMKilled restarts, disrupting all connections
  • Each torrent + peers consumes memory; 2000+ torrents need 6-8 GiB

docs.title: Symptom: Many torrents "Stalled Uploading" or "queuedUP"
docs.text:
Root cause: max_active_uploads too low

Torrents in queuedUP state cannot connect to peers at all. They're waiting in a queue for an "active" slot.

Example: With 2000 seeding torrents and max_active_uploads=100: - Only 100 torrents can seek peers - 1900 torrents stuck in queue, never connecting - Total peers: ~100-300 (very low)

Fix: Increase max_active_uploads to cover 40-50% of seeding count (see Lessons Learned)

docs.title: Symptom: Slow downloads despite many seeds
docs.text:
Root causes: 1. max_active_downloads too low (torrents queued, not connecting) 2. Upload blocked → BitTorrent tit-for-tat penalizes you 3. Container restarting (OOMKilled) disrupts connections

BitTorrent protocol: Peers prioritize uploaders. If you're not uploading, you get slower download slots.

docs.title: Symptom: Container restarting frequently
docs.text:
Root cause: Memory limit too low

Check with: 

kubectl describe pod qbittorrent-0 -n qbittorrent | grep -A5 "Last State"

If "OOMKilled", increase memory limit in values.yaml.

docs.title: Symptom: High SYN_SENT:CLOSED on router (>500)
docs.text:
Root cause: max_connec too low

Peers try to connect but qbittorrent can't accept them (connection slots full). Connections stay stuck at SYN_SENT then timeout.

Fix: Increase max_connec based on router capacity (see below).

docs.title: Router Capacity Analysis
docs.text: pfSense state table stores each network connection. Each torrent peer creates ~19 state entries over its lifecycle (SYN → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT → TIME_WAIT).

docs.title: Check Capacity
docs.text:
ssh pfsense.grigri "pfctl -s info | grep -E 'current entries'"
ssh pfsense.grigri "pfctl -s memory"  # shows limit

docs.title: Calculate Safe Limits
docs.text:
Router State Limit Safe Ceiling (50%) Max Connections 402,000 (default) 201,000 states ~10,500 connections 200,000 100,000 states ~5,250 connections

Formula: max_connec = (safe_ceiling_states - baseline_states) ÷ 19

Where baseline_states = states from other services (~2-5k)

docs.title: Example Calculation
docs.text:
Router limit: 402,000
Safe ceiling: 201,000 (50%)
Current non-torrent states: 5,000
Available for torrents: 196,000
Max connections safe: 196,000 ÷ 19 = ~10,000
Recommended: 8,000 (leaving buffer)

docs.title: Check Queue State
docs.text:
curl -s http://qbittorrent.internal.grigri.cloud/api/v2/sync/maindata | jq '
  .torrents | to_entries |
  group_by(.value.state) |
  map({state: .[0].value.state, count: length})
'

Key states to watch: - queuedUP: Stuck waiting for active slot (BAD) - stalledUP: Active but no peers connected (OK if low) - uploading: Actively transferring (GOOD)

docs.title: Check Container Health
docs.text:
kubectl --context=grigri describe pod qbittorrent-0 -n qbittorrent | grep -A3 "Last State"
kubectl --context=grigri top pod qbittorrent-0 -n qbittorrent --containers

docs.title: Check Router State
docs.text:
ssh pfsense.grigri "pfctl -s states | grep 50413 | grep -c ESTABLISHED"
ssh pfsense.grigri "pfctl -s states | grep -c 'SYN_SENT:CLOSED'"

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text: Metric Healthy Warning Critical queuedUP torrents < 5% 5-20% > 20% stalledUP torrents < 20% 20-40% > 40% Total peer connections 500+ < 200 < 50 SYN_SENT:CLOSED < 100 100-500 > 500 Router state % < 25% 25-50% > 80% Container restarts/day 0 1-3 > 5

docs.title: For High-Seeding Scenarios (2000+ torrents)
docs.text: Setting Recommended Purpose max_active_uploads 600-1000 Queue slots - allows torrents to seek peers max_active_downloads 10-20 Queue slots for downloads max_active_torrents 800-1200 Total queue limit max_uploads 60-100 Bandwidth slots - actual upload transfers max_uploads_per_torrent 4-6 Per-torrent upload slots max_connec 5000-8000 Total peer connections (router dependent) max_connec_per_torrent 20-25 Per-torrent peers Memory limit 10 GiB Prevent OOMKilled

docs.title: Relationship Summary
docs.text:
seeding_torrents ≈ 2000
max_active_uploads ≈ 40-50% of seeding = 800-1000
max_uploads ≈ bandwidth_based (9 MB/s ÷ 90 KB/s/slot = 100)
max_connec ≈ router_safe (8000 with 400k limit)

docs.title: Tuning Workflow
docs.text:
1. Diagnose the bottleneck:
  2. High queuedUP → increase max_active_uploads
  3. High SYN_SENT:CLOSED → increase max_connec
  4. OOMKilled → increase memory limit

  5. Slow downloads → check upload is working

  6. Adjust via API: 

    curl -X POST http://qbittorrent.internal.grigri.cloud/api/v2/app/setPreferences \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "json={'max_active_uploads':600,'max_connec':8000}"

  7. Verify router capacity: 

    ssh pfsense.grigri "pfctl -s info | grep 'current entries'"

  8. Monitor 10-30 minutes:

  9. queuedUP should drop to < 5%
  10. Peer connections should increase
  11. Upload/download speeds should improve

docs.title: Memory does NOT scale with active upload slots
docs.text:
Finding (May 2026): Increasing max_active_uploads from 600 → 1000 had negligible memory impact. Memory settled at ~6 Gi regardless of the active upload count.

Reason: Memory is driven by the total torrent count (session metadata, piece maps), not by how many torrents are in the active upload set. Moving a torrent from queuedUP to stalledUP (active but 0 peers) adds almost no memory since no peer state is allocated.

Implication: It is safe to increase max_active_uploads aggressively as long as the container memory limit has headroom for the total torrent count. The memory floor is ~2.5-3 Gi per 1000 torrents regardless of queue settings.

docs.title: stalledUP is the dominant state with DHT/PeX/LSD disabled
docs.text:
Finding: With anonymous mode enabled and DHT/PeX/LSD disabled, peer discovery relies solely on tracker HTTP announces. This causes ~50% of active torrents to be stalledUP (active in the seeding pool but 0 connected peers) even with ample queue slots.

Implication: Increasing max_active_uploads moves torrents from queuedUP → stalledUP, which still improves seeding because stalled torrents can respond to incoming connections. But to significantly increase uploading counts, peer discovery must improve (enable DHT/PeX or add more trackers).

docs.title: Incremental tuning workflow works well
docs.text:
Validated approach (May 2026, 2396 torrents):

  1. Start with conservative increase (e.g. +50% of current max_active_uploads)
  2. Monitor at 10-minute intervals: queuedUP, stalledUP, uploading, peers, memory
  3. Expect: queuedUP drops, stalledUP absorbs, uploading ramps over 20-30 min
  4. Memory stabilizes in ~60 min post-restart; compare against pre-change baseline
  5. If queuedUP plateaus above 5%, another round of increases is safe (memory permitting)

Results from 600 → 1000 increase:

Metric Before After (30 min) Change queuedUP 1,586 (66%) 1,187 (50%) -25% uploading 26 37 +42% Peer connections 135 304 +125% Memory 6.2 Gi 6.1 Gi Negligible Restarts 0 0 Stable

docs.title: Queue plateaus at MaxActiveUploads limit
docs.text: When queuedUP stops decreasing after a config change, it means the active upload pool (stalledUP + uploading + forcedUP) has saturated max_active_uploads. The remaining queuedUP count equals total_torrents - max_active_uploads - forcedUP. To eliminate the queue, max_active_uploads must exceed the total torrent count.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text: Pitfall Result Fix max_active_uploads = 100 with 2000 seeding 1900 torrents queued Increase to 500+ max_connec = 500 with 2000 seeding SYN_SENT overflow Increase to 5000+ Memory = 3.5 GiB with 2000 torrents OOMKilled restarts Increase to 10 GiB max_uploads_per_torrent = 1 Single torrent hogs bandwidth Use 4-6

docs.title: All torrents stuck in queue
docs.text:
# Increase active slots
curl -X POST http://qbittorrent.internal.grigri.cloud/api/v2/app/setPreferences \
  -d "json={'max_active_uploads':600,'max_active_torrents':800}"

docs.title: Slow downloads
docs.text:
# Ensure uploads work (tit-for-tat)
curl -s http://qbittorrent.internal.grigri.cloud/api/v2/transfer/info | jq '.up_info_speed'
# If 0 or very low, check max_uploads_per_torrent isn't too low

docs.title: Router SYN_SENT high
docs.text:
# Increase connection limit
curl -X POST http://qbittorrent.internal.grigri.cloud/api/v2/app/setPreferences \
  -d "json={'max_connec':8000}"

docs.title: Container restarting
docs.text:
# Check OOMKilled
kubectl describe pod qbittorrent-0 -n qbittorrent | grep OOMKilled
# If present, increase memory limit in values.yaml and redeploy

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Radarr web UI was slow or failed to load. Logs showed recurring SQLiteException: database is locked errors (15+ occurrences in 6 hours). The SQLite database had grown to 104 MB on ZFS storage, and frequent RSS syncs (900+ releases every 30 min) caused severe lock contention under SQLite's single-writer model.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
SQLite uses a single-writer lock. When Radarr processes RSS syncs, download monitoring, import lists, and web UI requests concurrently, writers block each other. On ZFS (copy-on-write), the I/O latency compounds the problem, causing longer lock hold times and more failures.

PostgreSQL handles concurrent readers and writers without locking, eliminating the bottleneck.

docs.title: Migration Procedure
docs.text: Based on the community migration guide, adapted for our Zalando Postgres operator and GitOps workflow.

docs.title: Step 1: Create Postgres cluster
docs.text: Add a postgresql.yaml template to the app's Helm chart (see existing apps like immich or home-assistant for patterns). Important: the Zalando operator rejects database names containing hyphens — see pitfall below. Create databases manually instead.

docs.title: Step 2: Let Radarr create the schema
docs.text:
Add RADARR__POSTGRES__HOST, PORT, USER, PASSWORD, MAINDB, LOGDB env vars to the values file. Deploy and let Radarr start — it creates all tables automatically. Verify via:

kubectl exec -n radarr radarr-postgres-0 -- psql -U radarr -d radarr-main -c "\dt"

docs.title: Step 3: Dump schema, drop/recreate databases with clean tables
docs.text:
Radarr inserts initial data (config entries, migration history) when creating the schema. These rows conflict with the SQLite data import. Clean slate is required:

# Dump schema
kubectl exec -n radarr radarr-postgres-0 -- pg_dump -U radarr -d radarr-main -s > radarr-main-schema.sql
kubectl exec -n radarr radarr-postgres-0 -- pg_dump -U radarr -d radarr-log -s > radarr-log-schema.sql

# Terminate connections before dropping
kubectl exec -n radarr radarr-postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres -c \
  "SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname IN ('radarr-main','radarr-log') AND pid <> pg_backend_pid();"

# Drop and recreate
kubectl exec -n radarr radarr-postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres -c 'DROP DATABASE "radarr-main";'
kubectl exec -n radarr radarr-postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres -c 'CREATE DATABASE "radarr-main" OWNER radarr;'
# Repeat for radarr-log

# Reimport clean schema
cat radarr-main-schema.sql | kubectl exec -n radarr -i radarr-postgres-0 -- psql -U radarr -d radarr-main
cat radarr-log-schema.sql | kubectl exec -n radarr -i radarr-postgres-0 -- psql -U radarr -d radarr-log

docs.title: Step 4: Migrate data with pgloader
docs.text:
Run pgloader as a Kubernetes Job inside the cluster (avoids port-forward SSL issues):

cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: pgloader-radarr-main
  namespace: radarr
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      initContainers:
      - name: copy-db
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "cp /config/radarr.db /work/radarr.db && chmod 644 /work/radarr.db"]
        securityContext:
          runAsUser: 995
          runAsGroup: 501
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /config
          readOnly: true
        - name: work
          mountPath: /work
      containers:
      - name: pgloader
        image: ghcr.io/roxedus/pgloader:latest
        command:
          - pgloader
          - --with
          - "quote identifiers"
          - --with
          - "data only"
          - /work/radarr.db
          - "postgresql://USER:PASS@radarr-postgres.radarr.svc:5432/radarr-main"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: work
          mountPath: /work
      volumes:
      - name: config
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: config-radarr
          readOnly: true
      - name: work
        emptyDir: {}
EOF

Run a separate job for the logs database (logs.db → radarr-log).

docs.title: Step 5: Start Radarr and verify
docs.text:
Remove replicas: 0 from values, push, wait for ArgoCD sync. Verify:

# Check no "database is locked" errors
kubectl logs -n radarr radarr-0 --tail=50 | grep -i "locked"
# Confirm movie count
kubectl exec -n radarr radarr-postgres-0 -- psql -U radarr -d radarr-main -c 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "Movies";'

docs.title: Zalando operator rejects hyphenated database names
docs.text: The databases field in the postgresql manifest rejects names with hyphens (radarr-main): database "radarr-main" has invalid name. Create databases manually with kubectl exec psql instead.

docs.title: pgloader can't connect via SSL to Zalando Postgres
docs.text:
Zalando's Spilo uses self-signed certs. pgloader's --no-ssl-cert-verification flag does not work (at least in ghcr.io/roxedus/pgloader:latest). Two workarounds:

  1. Preferred: Run pgloader as an in-cluster Job — the pod network uses hostnossl ... reject in pg_hba.conf, so temporarily add an allow rule: 

    kubectl exec -n radarr radarr-postgres-0 -- sed -i \
  '/hostnossl all.*all.*all.*reject/i host    all    all    10.0.0.0/8    md5' \
  /home/postgres/pgdata/pgroot/data/pg_hba.conf
kubectl exec -n radarr radarr-postgres-0 -- psql -U postgres -c "SELECT pg_reload_conf();"
# After migration, remove the line (or let the operator reconcile it)

  2. Alternative: Use port-forward with sslmode=require and accept the cert error won't apply (doesn't work reliably — port-forward dies, Docker --network=host can't reach it).

docs.title: SQLite needs write access to its directory
docs.text: pgloader cannot read SQLite from a read-only PVC mount — SQLite creates temp files (WAL, journal) in the same directory. Use an init container to copy the .db file to an emptyDir volume first.

docs.title: ArgoCD reverts manual scale changes
docs.text: kubectl scale statefulset radarr --replicas=0 gets reverted by ArgoCD auto-sync. Always set replicas: 0 in values.yaml and push to git instead.

docs.title: Check job status early, don't blind-wait
docs.text: When running Kubernetes Jobs, check pod status after a few seconds before committing to a long kubectl wait --timeout=600s. Failed jobs fail fast — a 30s delay then get pods reveals errors immediately instead of blocking for 10 minutes.

docs.title: Readest Android OAuth (Deep-Link Login)
docs.text:
Getting the official Readest Android APK to log in against the self-hosted stack. The web flow already worked (see docs/deployment/readest.md); the mobile app adds two hard constraints:

  1. The APK bundles its own minified JS — the init-container patching only affects the web image. The APK always sends provider=discord.
  2. The app's WebView is cross-origin with the API (Tauri apps load from tauri.localhost, not from readest.grigri.cloud), so every supabase-js call is subject to CORS preflight.

docs.title: Symptom Progression
docs.text: Phase Symptom Cause 1 App opens browser, login completes, app stays in browser redirect_to=readest://auth-callback dropped by the nginx provider rewrite 2 Same as 1 GoTrue rejected readest://auth-callback (not in GOTRUE_URI_ALLOW_LIST) 3 App returns from browser but shows "go to login" CORS preflight blocked setSession → /auth/v1/user call (missing apikey header)

docs.title: The Full OAuth Flow (Android)
docs.text:
1. App (WebView):   GET /auth/v1/authorize?provider=discord&redirect_to=readest://auth-callback
2. nginx:           302 → /auth/v1/authorize?provider=custom:kanidm&redirect_to=readest://auth-callback
3. GoTrue:          302 → Kanidm (redirect_uri=https://readest.grigri.cloud/callback,
                            passes redirect_to through)
4. Kanidm:          user authenticates → 302 → /callback?code=...
5. nginx:           301 /callback → /auth/v1/callback
6. GoTrue:          exchanges code, 302 → readest://auth-callback#access_token=...&refresh_token=...
7. Android:         intent → NativeBridgePlugin resolves pending authWithCustomTab invoke
8. App (WebView):   supabase.auth.setSession(...) → GET /auth/v1/user  ← CORS preflight here
9. App:             session persisted, navigate to library

Steps 1–7 worked after the nginx/GoTrue config fixes. Step 8 was the silent killer: the preflight failed, so no request ever reached GoTrue, and the app concluded there was no session.

docs.title: 1. Nginx provider rewrite dropped redirect_to
docs.text:
The original configuration-snippet replaced the whole query string with provider=custom:kanidm, discarding the app's redirect_to=readest://auth-callback. GoTrue then fell back to GOTRUE_SITE_URL and redirected the browser to the web UI after login.

Pitfalls hit while fixing this (nginx "if is evil"):

  • map is only valid in http context — cannot be used in ingress snippets.
  • Nested if blocks are not allowed; combine conditions via flag variables and a "gate" string.
  • rewrite ... last on the authorize URI re-enters the same location → rewrite loop (500). Use return 302 instead.
  • Variables set inside an if that doesn't match are empty — default them first (set $readest_redirect_to "..." before the if).

Working snippet (on both internal and external API ingresses):

set $readest_redirect_to "https://readest.grigri.cloud/auth/callback";
if ($arg_redirect_to != "") {
  set $readest_redirect_to $arg_redirect_to;
}
set $readest_authorize "no";
if ($uri ~* "^/auth/v1/authorize$") {
  set $readest_authorize "yes";
}
set $readest_rewrite "no";
if ($args ~* "provider=(google|apple|github|discord)") {
  set $readest_rewrite "yes";
}
if ($args = "") {
  set $readest_rewrite "yes";
}
set $readest_gate "$readest_authorize:$readest_rewrite";
if ($readest_gate = "yes:yes") {
  return 302 $uri?provider=custom:kanidm&redirect_to=$readest_redirect_to;
}

docs.title: 2. GOTRUE_URI_ALLOW_LIST must include the custom scheme
docs.text:
GoTrue silently ignores redirect_to values that don't match GOTRUE_URI_ALLOW_LIST and falls back to GOTRUE_SITE_URL. Add the deep-link target:

GOTRUE_URI_ALLOW_LIST: https://readest.grigri.cloud/**,https://readest.internal.grigri.cloud/**,readest://auth-callback

docs.title: 3. GoTrue CORS does not allow the apikey header (the hard one)
docs.text:
supabase-js sends apikey: <anon-key> on every request. GoTrue's built-in CORS middleware (rs/cors, internal/api/api.go) only allows:

Accept, Authorization, Content-Type, X-Client-IP, X-Client-Info, X-JWT-AUD, x-use-cookie, X-Supabase-Api-Version

A preflight that includes apikey gets a 204 with no Access-Control-Allow-* headers → the browser blocks the actual request. On Supabase Cloud Kong sits in front and handles this; when you expose GoTrue directly through ingress-nginx, cross-origin clients break.

Why the web app worked: it is served from the same origin as the API → no preflight. The Tauri WebView (origin tauri.localhost / https://tauri.localhost) is cross-origin, so after the deep link delivered the tokens, supabase.auth.setSession() → GET /auth/v1/user died at preflight. setSession always makes a network call (_getUser when the token is valid, refresh grant when expired) — the absence of that request in GoTrue logs is the diagnostic tell.

Fix (merged with the defaults via AllAllowedHeaders in gotrue conf):

GOTRUE_CORS_ALLOWED_HEADERS: apikey

docs.title: How to Diagnose
docs.text:
Verify the redirect chain end-to-end with curl (no real login needed until the last hop):

# Step 2: nginx rewrite preserves redirect_to
curl -sI "https://readest.grigri.cloud/auth/v1/authorize?provider=discord&redirect_to=readest://auth-callback" | grep -i location

# Step 3: GoTrue → Kanidm passes redirect_to
curl -s -D - -o /dev/null "https://readest.grigri.cloud/auth/v1/authorize?provider=custom:kanidm&redirect_to=readest://auth-callback" | grep -i location

# Step 5: /callback routes to GoTrue
curl -sI "https://readest.grigri.cloud/callback?code=x&state=y" | grep -i location

# Step 8: CORS preflight as the WebView would send it
curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -X OPTIONS "https://readest.grigri.cloud/auth/v1/user" \
  -H "Origin: https://tauri.localhost" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: GET" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: apikey,authorization,x-client-info" | grep -i access-control
# FAIL: 204 with no access-control-* headers  /  OK: allow-headers includes apikey

Android side (adb logcat, tag NativeBridgePlugin):

  • Launching OAuth URL: ... — what the app sends (shows hardcoded provider=discord).
  • Received intent: ... data=readest://auth-callback#access_token=... — deep link arrived with tokens in the fragment. If this line exists but the session still fails, the problem is in the WebView JS (CORS, storage) — not in intent delivery.

Server side:

  • GoTrue logs every request with remote_addr. List the paths a device IP called: kubectl logs deploy/readest-auth | grep <ip> | grep -oE '"path":"[^"]*"' | sort | uniq -c. The device calling only /authorize + /callback and never /token or /user after login means the client-side session call is being blocked (CORS) or never issued.
  • A token from an intercepted deep link can be replayed to prove the server side accepts it: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <access_token>" https://readest.grigri.cloud/auth/v1/user.

docs.title: Known Limitations / Follow-ups
docs.text:
• JWT claims nesting: our GoTrue puts plan, storage_quota, translation_quota inside user_metadata (inherited from Kanidm claims), not as top-level JWT claims. The app's getUserProfilePlan() reads the top-level plan claim, so mobile users resolve as "free" (redirected to /user after login; premium-gated UI may be limited). Server-side quotas are still enforced via STORAGE_FIXED_QUOTA/TRANSLATION_FIXED_QUOTA. A GoTrue custom access-token hook (or upstream change) would fix it.
  • provider_refresh_token leakage: GoTrue passes Kanidm's refresh token through the URL fragment to the app. Harmless here (self-hosted, HTTPS, single user) but worth knowing.
  • Custom OAuth provider row: the custom:kanidm provider in auth.custom_oauth_providers is auto-inserted by the db-migrate init container (was manual; now GitOps-managed).

docs.title: When It Breaks Again (Regression Checklist)
docs.text:
Mobile login only depends on server config + the APK's expectations, so regressions come from gotrue upgrades, ingress config drift, or new APK versions. Check in this order:

  1. Replay the redirect chain (each location must match): 
    curl -sI "https://readest.grigri.cloud/auth/v1/authorize?provider=discord&redirect_to=readest://auth-callback"
# expect: /auth/v1/authorize?provider=custom:kanidm&redirect_to=readest://auth-callback
curl -s -D - -o /dev/null "https://readest.grigri.cloud/auth/v1/authorize?provider=custom:kanidm&redirect_to=readest://auth-callback"
# expect: idm.grigri.cloud/ui/oauth2?...&redirect_to=readest%3A%2F%2Fauth-callback&redirect_uri=...
curl -sI "https://readest.grigri.cloud/callback?code=x&state=y"
# expect: /auth/v1/callback?code=x&state=y
  2. CORS preflight (deep link works but app says "go to login"): 
    curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -X OPTIONS "https://readest.grigri.cloud/auth/v1/user" \
  -H "Origin: https://tauri.localhost" -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: GET" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: apikey,authorization,x-client-info" | grep -i access-control
# allow-headers MUST include apikey; a bare 204 = preflight fails
  3. GoTrue env: GOTRUE_URI_ALLOW_LIST includes readest://auth-callback, GOTRUE_CORS_ALLOWED_HEADERS includes apikey.
  4. Device-side: adb logcat -s NativeBridgePlugin — compare Launching OAuth URL: and Received intent: against the expected shapes above. Token in intent but no session ⇒ step 2/3. No Received intent ⇒ intent filter/deep-link scheme changed in the APK.
  5. Server-side: device IP should hit /authorize, /callback, then /user (or /token). Missing /user ⇒ client blocked (CORS); /authorize shows provider=discord ⇒ nginx rewrite broken (see docs/deployment/readest.md failure runbook).

For non-mobile failures (init-container patch, /callback 404, lost provider row after DB recreate), see the "Failure Modes and Recovery" runbook in docs/deployment/readest.md.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Readest's frontend has hardcoded OAuth provider buttons (Google, Apple, GitHub, Discord) in the authentication UI. The OAuthProvider type in ProviderLogin.tsx is restricted to these specific values:

export type OAuthProvider = 'google' | 'apple' | 'azure' | 'github' | 'discord';

The UI doesn't support custom OAuth providers, and there's no runtime configuration to add them.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text: Readest is designed as a SaaS product with specific OAuth providers. The self-hosted version doesn't include configuration for custom providers because the upstream project doesn't anticipate self-hosters using different OAuth providers.

docs.title: Custom Docker Image
docs.text: Rejected - Building a custom Docker image for Readest would require: - Maintaining a fork of the Readest repository - Rebuilding the image on every Readest update - Tracking upstream changes to the auth UI - Significant maintenance burden

docs.title: Runtime Configuration
docs.text: Readest doesn't support runtime configuration for OAuth providers. The OAUTH_PROVIDERS environment variable suggested in some discussions doesn't exist in the codebase.

docs.title: CSS/JavaScript Injection via Nginx
docs.text:
Tried injecting CSS/JavaScript via nginx sub_filter to hide unwanted buttons:

sub_filter '</body>' '<script>setInterval(function(){document.querySelectorAll("button").forEach(function(b){if(b.textContent.includes("Sign in with Google")||b.textContent.includes("Sign in with Apple")||b.textContent.includes("Sign in with GitHub"))b.style.display="none"})},100);</script></body>';

Failed - Next.js SPA doesn't reliably execute injected scripts, and the buttons are rendered client-side after the initial HTML load.

docs.title: GoTrue Environment Variables
docs.text:
Tried disabling providers via GoTrue environment variables:

GOTRUE_EXTERNAL_GOOGLE_ENABLED: "false"
GOTRUE_EXTERNAL_APPLE_ENABLED: "false"
GOTRUE_EXTERNAL_GITHUB_ENABLED: "false"

Partial success - This disables the backend OAuth providers, but the UI still shows the buttons. Clicking them results in an error from GoTrue.

docs.title: Workaround
docs.text:
Use an init container to patch the compiled JavaScript bundles at pod startup:

initContainers:
  patch-oauth:
    image:
      repository: ghcr.io/readest/readest
      tag: 0.12.6
    command:
      - /bin/sh
      - -c
      - |
        set -e
        STATIC_DIR="/app/apps/readest-app/.next/static"
        PATCHED_DIR="/patched-static"

        echo "Copying static assets..."
        cp -r "${STATIC_DIR}/." "${PATCHED_DIR}/"

        echo "Patching OAuth provider..."
        PATCHED=0
        for f in $(find "${PATCHED_DIR}" -name "*.js" -type f); do
          if grep -q 'provider:"discord"' "$f" 2>/dev/null || grep -q '"Discord"' "$f" 2>/dev/null; then
            echo "Patching $f"
            sed -i 's/provider:"discord"/provider:"custom:kanidm"/g' "$f"
            sed -i 's/"Discord"/"Kanidm"/g' "$f"
            sed -i 's/(0,i\.jsx)(R,{provider:"google",handleSignIn:n,Icon:U,label:r("Sign in with {{provider}}",{provider:"Google"})}),//g' "$f"
            sed -i 's/(0,i\.jsx)(R,{provider:"apple",handleSignIn:n,Icon:O\.FaApple,label:r("Sign in with {{provider}}",{provider:"Apple"})}),//g' "$f"
            sed -i 's/(0,i\.jsx)(R,{provider:"github",handleSignIn:n,Icon:O\.FaGithub,label:r("Sign in with {{provider}}",{provider:"GitHub"})}),//g' "$f"
            PATCHED=$((PATCHED + 1))
          fi
        done

        if [ "$PATCHED" -eq 0 ]; then
          echo "ERROR: Could not find OAuth provider to patch"
          exit 1
        fi

        echo "Patched $PATCHED file(s)"
    volumeMounts:
      - name: patched-static
        mountPath: /patched-static

volumes:
  - name: patched-static
    emptyDir:
      sizeLimit: 500Mi

The patched static files are then mounted into the main container:

containers:
  client:
    volumeMounts:
      - name: patched-static
        mountPath: /app/apps/readest-app/.next/static

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. The init container copies the compiled JavaScript bundles from the Readest image
  2. It searches for files containing provider:"discord" or "Discord"
  3. It uses sed to:
  4. Replace provider:"discord" with provider:"custom:kanidm"
  5. Replace "Discord" with "Kanidm" (button label)
  6. Remove the Google, Apple, and GitHub button JSX
  7. The patched files are stored in an emptyDir volume
  8. The main container mounts the patched files, overriding the originals

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
• Maintenance burden: The patch must be updated if Readest changes its UI structure or JavaScript compilation output
  • Fragile: The sed patterns are specific to the current Readest version and may break on updates
  • Automatic: The init container runs on every pod start, so changes are applied automatically
  • No custom image: We don't need to maintain a fork of Readest

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Check that the patch was applied:

kubectl exec -n readest deployment/readest-client -c client -- \
  grep -r 'provider:"custom:kanidm"' /app/apps/readest-app/.next/static/

Check the logs:

kubectl logs -n readest deployment/readest-client -c patch-oauth

Expected output:

Copying static assets...
Patching OAuth provider...
Patching /patched-static/chunks/abc123.js
Patched 1 file(s)

docs.title: Future Improvements
docs.text:
If Readest adds support for custom OAuth providers via runtime configuration: - Remove the init container - Remove the nginx rewrite - Use standard OAuth provider configuration

If Readest makes the OAuth provider list configurable: - Update the init container to use the new configuration method - Remove the sed patching logic

docs.title: Gen1 Shelly: disabling CoIoT breaks Home Assistant setup on the next restart
docs.text:
Status: diagnosed and fixed 2026-10-26 on shellyem-main. Device restored, HA entry loaded. Extended the same day: the same root cause also explains a device reboot loop that had been mis-attributed to MQTT — see Second consequence.

⚠️ The stakes went up on 2026-10-27. MQTT is now permanently enabled on shellyem-main — it feeds both power sensors at 2 s. That means the reboot loop's co-factor is always present, so disabling CoIoT and restarting HA now produces both failures reliably rather than by chance. The blast radius also shifted: the two power entities come from MQTT and would survive a setup_retry storm, but the energy counters, voltage, power factor and the relay switch would not — and grid_energy is what the battery-optimizer dataset is built from. CoIoT is not optional on this device.

Disabling CoIoT on a Gen1 Shelly looks harmless — HA keeps polling and data keeps flowing. It is not harmless: it removes the one endpoint HA needs to initialize the device, so the next HA restart silently drops every entity of that config entry. The failure can surface hours or days later, triggered by something unrelated (a ConfigMap change and the Reloader restart it causes, an image bump, a node drain), which makes it very hard to attribute.

It has a second face: while HA retries, the requests it makes to the dead endpoint hang inside the device, consuming its heap and HTTP connection slots. That alone is survivable, but combined with an MQTT client it faults the firmware into a reboot loop.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text:
• Every entity of one Gen1 Shelly config entry is unavailable, all with the same last_reported timestamp (the moment HA gave up).
  • Settings → Devices & services shows the entry in setup_retry with reason Device communication error occurred for <name>.
  • The device itself is perfectly healthy: curl http://<device>/shelly, /settings and /status all return 200 from the HA pod and from a workstation, with correct live values.
  • Other Shelly devices in the same HA are fine — but note they are usually Gen2+ (RPC/HTTP), which does not use /cit/* at all. Only Gen1 is affected.
  • Nothing in the HA log: the failure is raised as ConfigEntryNotReady and only surfaces as the entry's reason string.
  • If MQTT is also enabled: the device spontaneously reboots every ~1–5 min (uptime resets with no request from you), and ram_free sits ~8 KB lower than normal. This reads like an MQTT fault and is not one.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Item Value Device shellyem-main, Shelly EM (SHEM), Gen1, fw 20230913-114150/v1.14.0-gcb84623, MAC 244CAB417668 Address 192.168.86.130 = shellyem-main.iot.grigri, IoT VLAN 501 HA 2026.10.4, home-assistant-hass-0, aioshelly 13.34.1 Trigger in this incident Reloader restarted HA at 18:01:16Z after an unrelated ConfigMap change; all 14 entities went unavailable at 18:02:35Z

docs.title: Root cause
docs.text:
With coiot.enabled: false, the Gen1 firmware does not serve the /cit/* family at all:

  • HTTP GET /cit/d hangs — no response, no 404, the client just times out.
  • CoAP on UDP 5683 is not answered either (/cit/d, /cit/s → NetworkError).

HA needs /cit/d on every setup:

BlockDevice.initialize()                      # aioshelly/block_device.py
  ├─ get_info()          -> GET /shelly       # works
  ├─ update_settings()   -> GET /settings     # works
  ├─ update_status()     -> GET /status       # works
  └─ if firmware_supported:
       _update_cit_d()                        # <- fails here

_update_cit_d() uses HTTP GET /cit/d for firmware ≥ 1.10 (GEN1_HTTP_CIT_D_MIN_FIRMWARE_DATE), falling back to a CoAP /cit/d request on older builds — so on this device the failure is an HTTP hang, and both transports are dead anyway.

The hang becomes TimeoutError → DeviceConnectionTimeoutError (a subclass of DeviceConnectionError), which HA catches in components/shelly/__init__.py:238-244:

except (DeviceConnectionError, MacAddressMismatchError) as err:
    await device.shutdown()
    raise ConfigEntryNotReady(
        translation_domain=DOMAIN,
        translation_key="device_communication_error",   # "Device communication error occurred for {device}"
        translation_placeholders={"device": entry.title},
    ) from err

ConfigEntryNotReady → the entry retries with a growing backoff and all its entities stay unavailable until a setup attempt succeeds.

An already-initialized HA is unaffected: ShellyBlockCoordinator polls /status over REST every 2.2 × coiot_update_period (33 s here), which does not touch /cit/*. That is exactly why the breakage stays invisible until the next restart.

docs.title: Second consequence: the retry storm can fault the device itself
docs.text:
The hanging /cit/d is not only a HA-side problem. Each stuck request pins a mongoose HTTP connection slot and its buffers on the device for as long as HA keeps retrying, and HA retries with a backoff that grows to SETUP_RETRY_MAX_WAIT = 600 s — so the consumption is standing, not transient.

Measured on shellyem-main (fw 1.14.0, ram_total 51 064 B):

CoIoT off + HA retrying CoIoT on ram_free 27 224 B 35 368 B GET /status while 6 /cit/d are hanging no response (2 of 3 rounds) answers normally device log heap floor New heap free LWM: 25960 → 25888 31408

On its own the device survives this — ~20 min stable with MQTT off while HA hammered it. But with an MQTT client also running, the remaining heap margin disappears and the firmware faults: spontaneous reboots every 71–280 s, which look exactly like "MQTT reboot-loops this device" and are very easy to mis-diagnose that way. The per-request leak is tiny (18 hanging requests cost ~280 B of unrecovered heap), which is why replaying hanging /cit/d calls by hand does not reproduce the fault — it takes HA's full initialize() sequence under retry backoff.

Isolation matrix, ruled-out hypotheses and the inferred mechanism (measurements are direct; the step from "heap and slots consumed" to "firmware resets" was never proven — no exception dump, and synthetic replay does not crash it): planning/shelly-em-mqtt-implementation.md.

Practical consequence: re-enabling CoIoT fixes both failures at once — HA's setup and the reboot loop. If a Gen1 Shelly is spontaneously rebooting, check coiot.enabled before suspecting MQTT.

docs.title: Diagnosis (read-only)
docs.text:
SUSER=$(pass show iot/shellyem-main | sed -n 's/^login: //p'); SPASS=$(pass show iot/shellyem-main | head -1)
D=http://shellyem-main.iot.grigri

# 1. The device is healthy and authenticated access works:
curl -sS -m 8 -u "$SUSER:$SPASS" "$D/shelly"   | jq -c '{type,auth,fw}'

# 2. The tell-tale: /cit/d hangs while /settings answers instantly
curl -sS -m 12 -u "$SUSER:$SPASS" -o /dev/null -w 'cit/d http=%{http_code}\n' "$D/cit/d"   # -> http=000 (timeout)
curl -sS -m 8  -u "$SUSER:$SPASS" "$D/settings" | jq -c '.coiot'                            # -> {"enabled":false,...}

# 3. Confirm HA's view of the entry (state + reason)
python3 ha_ws.py '{"type":"config_entries/get","domain":"shelly"}' \
  | jq -c '.result[] | {title,state,reason:(.reason//null)}'
# -> {"title":"shellyem-main","state":"setup_retry","reason":"Device communication error occurred for shellyem-main"}
unset SUSER SPASS

CoAP can be probed from inside the HA pod, which has aiocoap installed:

kubectl --context=grigri -n home-assistant exec home-assistant-hass-0 -c hass -- python3 -c "
import asyncio, aiocoap
async def main():
    ctx = await aiocoap.Context.create_client_context()
    req = aiocoap.Message(code=aiocoap.GET, uri='coap://192.168.86.130/cit/d')
    try:
        res = await asyncio.wait_for(ctx.request(req).response, 6)
        print('/cit/d ->', res.code, len(res.payload), 'bytes')
    except Exception as e:
        print('/cit/d -> ERR', type(e).__name__, e)
asyncio.run(main())"

To reproduce HA's exact setup path (including the real exception) inside the pod, pipe the credential in over stdin — never as an argv element — and use ConnectionOptions:

from aioshelly.block_device import COAP, BlockDevice
from aioshelly.common import ConnectionOptions

coap = COAP()                                  # HA does the same: components/shelly/utils.py:236-238
await coap.initialize()                        # coroutine, (socket_port=5683, socket_ips=None)
opts = ConnectionOptions(ip_address="192.168.86.130", username=USER, password=PW)
dev = await BlockDevice.create(session, coap, opts)   # create(aiohttp_session, coap_context, ip_or_options)
await dev.initialize()                         # raises DeviceConnectionTimeoutError when /cit/d hangs

In aioshelly 13.x, COAP lives in aioshelly.block_device (there is no aioshelly.coap module) and has no async_create classmethod; BlockDevice.create() does not call initialize(). Introspect the installed signatures before writing such a probe.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
Re-enable CoIoT and reboot. The endpoint matters:

SUSER=$(pass show iot/shellyem-main | sed -n 's/^login: //p'); SPASS=$(pass show iot/shellyem-main | head -1)
D=http://shellyem-main.iot.grigri
curl -sS -m 25 -u "$SUSER:$SPASS" -X POST -G "$D/settings/advanced" \
  --data-urlencode coiot_enable=true --data-urlencode coiot_update_period=15 --data-urlencode coiot_peer= \
  -o /dev/null          # the device applies it but does NOT answer: curl times out, that is normal
curl -sS -m 10 -u "$SUSER:$SPASS" "$D/reboot"     # required, /cit/d keeps hanging until then
sleep 50
curl -sS -m 12 -u "$SUSER:$SPASS" -o /dev/null -w 'cit/d http=%{http_code} size=%{size_download}\n' "$D/cit/d"
unset SUSER SPASS
# -> cit/d http=200 size=922

Then make HA retry immediately instead of waiting out the backoff:

curl -sS -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  https://hass.grigri.cloud/api/services/homeassistant/reload_config_entry \
  -d '{"entry_id":"<shelly entry id>"}'

Verified result: entry state: loaded, all 14 entities back within ~35 s, CoAP answering too (/cit/d → 2.05 Content 922 bytes, /cit/s → 2.05 Content 198 bytes).

coiot_peer="" (multicast) is enough — HA only needs /cit/d to initialize, it does not need to receive push. Push still never arrives and the 33 s REST polling plus the standing push_update_* repair remain; that part is home-assistant-shelly-coiot-push.md.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• POST /settings/coiot with enabled=true is silently ignored on fw 1.14.0. It answers 200 with the full settings document and coiot.enabled still false; enabled=1 behaves the same. The working call is POST /settings/advanced with coiot_enable / coiot_update_period / coiot_peer — exactly what aioshelly's own BlockDevice.configure_coiot_protocol() uses. When a Gen1 setting will not stick, read the aioshelly source for the real endpoint instead of trusting the API docs' URL shape.
  • A reboot is required for CoIoT (and MQTT) changes to activate. Without it the value is stored and GET /settings may even show it, but the service does not start.
  • Settings POSTs do not answer. curl reports (28) Operation timed out ... with 0 bytes received and http=000 even when the change was applied. Always verify with a follow-up GET.
  • Do not conclude "HA cannot reach the device". TCP to the device works fine; only /cit/* is gone. Symptom-level tests (/shelly, /settings) will mislead you — test /cit/d specifically.
  • setup_retry + device_communication_error has many causes (unreachable host, wrong credentials, MAC mismatch, unsupported firmware). /cit/d hanging while /settings works points at CoIoT being disabled.
  • The websocket command config_entries/reload does not exist in HA 2026.10.4 — it returns unknown_command. Use the homeassistant.reload_config_entry service over REST (or /api/services/... with entry_id).
  • Expired HA tokens are noisy and risky. A monitoring loop with a stale token produced ten homeassistant.components.http.ban warnings in the HA log ("Login attempt or request with invalid authentication"). Refresh the token before a long loop; if ip_bans_enabled were on, that host would have been banned.
  • Never disable CoIoT on a Gen1 device that HA owns — not even "to clean up", and not even temporarily. It arms a time bomb whose trigger is the next unrelated HA restart.
  • A spontaneous reboot loop is also a symptom of this, not only of MQTT. The stuck /cit/d handlers eat ~8 KB of heap and every HTTP slot; add an MQTT client and the device faults. Check coiot.enabled before blaming MQTT — and note the loop stops as soon as CoIoT is re-enabled.
  • /debug/log cannot catch the crash on fw 1.14.0. debug_enable=true is accepted by POST /settings and reads back false, so the endpoint keeps serving a frozen tail from an older boot. Don't build a diagnosis on it looking "live".
  • broker_clients_connected will not show you these reboots. The device reconnects with the same client id, mosquitto replaces the stale session, and the count stays flat (it held at 7 straight through two confirmed reboots). It also flaps from your own mosquitto_sub sessions. Subscribe to shellies/<id>/online instead — it fires on every MQTT connect.
