docs.title: Heat pump water temperature
docs.text:
How the Panasonic Aquarea outlet (heating water) temperature is controlled from Home Assistant and HeishaMon, which modes exist, what is exposed today and what is only reachable over MQTT.

This page was written from a read-only audit on 2026-10-30. Nothing was published to MQTT, no Home Assistant service was called and no setting was changed. Statements are either verified (read in code or observed live on that date) or believed (taken from the upstream HeishaMon docs or inferred, not tested on the unit). The ones that matter for a write experiment are marked believed.

Menu paths, ranges and the heater facts were later confirmed from the Panasonic service manual and are cited as "service manual p.N".

docs.title: Data path
docs.text:
Aquarea unit <-serial-> CZ-TAW1 running GoHeishaMon <-MQTT-> mosquitto <-MQTT-> Home Assistant
                                                                   (apps/mosquitto)
  • The CZ-TAW1 runs the owner's fork pando85/GoHeishaMon (audited at commit 561bcc8, main code src/taw2mqtt.go), not upstream HeishaMon. It speaks to the unit over serial and to the broker over MQTT. The broker is authenticated (mosquitto-user Secret from Vault /mosquitto/user, apps/mosquitto/templates/external-secret.yaml).
  • Base topics: state panasonic_heat_pump/main/<Topic>, commands panasonic_heat_pump/commands/<SetTopic>.
  • Home Assistant side: apps/home-assistant/config/integrations/heishamon.yaml (MQTT sensors, switches, helpers and the automations that publish the commands).

docs.title: Control modes
docs.text:
The unit decides how it derives the heating water target for a zone from the setting "Heating_Mode" (state topic main/Heating_Mode, also Cooling_Mode for cooling).

Heating_Mode Mode Z1_Heat_Request_Temp means Water target 0 Compensation curve A shift in K, -5 to +5 Read from the curve at the outside temperature, plus the shift 1 Direct The absolute water temperature, 20 to 55 degC (60 degC above -10 degC outdoor; service manual p.26, 131) The request itself

The curve is four points per zone and mode, published as state topics:

Topic (Z1 heating) Meaning Z1_Heat_Curve_Outside_Low_Temp Coldest outside temperature of the curve Z1_Heat_Curve_Target_Low_Temp Water target at the coldest point, so the highest water temperature ("low" follows the outside temperature, not the water) Z1_Heat_Curve_Outside_High_Temp Warmest outside temperature of the curve Z1_Heat_Curve_Target_High_Temp Water target at the warmest point (the lowest water temperature)

The unit keeps reporting the curve points while in direct mode; they are simply not used. Z1_Water_Target_Temp and Main_Target_Temp show the water target that is actually in force, in both modes.

Caveat (believed, from the upstream docs): when the zone sensor is a room thermostat or a thermistor instead of the water temperature, the "direct" temperature is stored in the high curve target and SetZ1HeatRequestTemperature does not set it. The fork does not publish Z1_Sensor_Settings, so this cannot be checked over MQTT. On 2026-10-30 Z1_Temp equals Main_Outlet_Temp (28), which suggests the zone sensor is the water temperature.

docs.title: Exposed in Home Assistant
docs.text:
Purpose HA entity MQTT topic Notes Set Z1 heating water request input_number.heishamon_heatshift_z1 commands/SetZ1HeatRequestTemperature Integer, helper range -5 to 40, step 1. Absolute in direct mode, shift in curve mode. heishamon.yaml:233-253, helper at :404-408 Read Z1 request sensor.aquarea_z1_heat_request_temperature main/Z1_Heat_Request_Temp Also mirrored into the helper by the "Set Z1 Heat selector" automation (:221-230) Read Z1 water target sensor.aquarea_z1_water_target_temperature main/Z1_Water_Target_Temp The effective target (:750) Read outlet target / actual sensor.aquarea_outlet_target_temperature, sensor.aquarea_outlet_temperature main/Main_Target_Temp, main/Main_Outlet_Temp Main target also follows the tank target in DHW Read Z1 curve points sensor.aquarea_z1_heat_curve_{target_high,target_low,outside_high,outside_low}_temperature main/Z1_Heat_Curve_* Read only (:679-700) Z2 equivalents input_number.heishamon_heatshift_z2, sensor.aquarea_z2_* commands/SetZ2HeatRequestTemperature Zone 2 is not active (Zones_State = 0) Cooling request input_number.heishamon_coolshift_z{1,2} commands/SetZ{1,2}CoolRequestTemperature Same range Operating mode input_select.heishamon_heatmode, sensor.aquarea_mode, sensor.aquarea_mode_code commands/SetOperationMode, main/Operating_Mode_State Driven by AppDaemon climate control (Heat+DHW / DHW) Quiet mode input_select.heishamon_quietmode, sensor.aquarea_quiet_mode commands/SetQuietMode, main/Quiet_Mode_Level Off, 1, 2, 3 Powerful mode input_select.heishamon_powermode, sensor.aquarea_powerful_mode commands/SetPowerfulMode, main/Powerful_Mode_Time Off, 30, 60, 90 min Holiday mode switch.aquarea_holiday_mode commands/SetHolidayMode, main/Holiday_Mode_State Heat pump power switch.aquarea_main_power commands/SetHeatpump, main/Heatpump_State Force DHW switch.aquarea_force_dhw_mode commands/SetForceDHW, main/Force_DHW_State Used by AppDaemon dhw_control Tank target input_number.heishamon_tank_temp commands/SetDHWTemp 40 to 75 Heating mode (read) sensor.aquarea_heating_mode main/Heating_Mode 0 curve, 1 direct. Read only; any water-temperature write must check it first Sterilization (read) binary_sensor.aquarea_sterilization_state, sensor.aquarea_sterilization_temperature, sensor.aquarea_sterilization_max_time main/Sterilization_State, main/Sterilization_Temp, main/Sterilization_Max_Time State 0/1, target in degC, maximum time in min Heater (read) binary_sensor.aquarea_force_heater_state, sensor.aquarea_tank_heater_enabled, sensor.aquarea_room_heater_enabled, sensor.aquarea_internal_heater_state, sensor.aquarea_external_heater_state main/Force_Heater_State, main/DHW_Heater_State, main/Room_Heater_State, main/Internal_Heater_State, main/External_Heater_State The four heater state sensor.* ones are Off/On strings, which the Prometheus exporter drops; each has a binary_sensor copy with the same object id (binary_sensor.aquarea_tank_heater_enabled, _room_heater_enabled, _internal_heater_state, _external_heater_state) that is exported Heater hours and limit (read) sensor.aquarea_room_heater_operating_hours, sensor.aquarea_dhw_heater_operating_hours, sensor.aquarea_heater_on_outdoor_temperature main/Room_Heater_Operations_Hours, main/DHW_Heater_Operations_Hours, main/Heater_On_Outdoor_Temp Hours are total_increasing; the outdoor limit is in degC Pump speed (read) sensor.aquarea_pump_speed, sensor.aquarea_pump_flow main/Pump_Speed, main/Pump_Flow

The helpers are not on the dashboards in apps/home-assistant/dashboards/; they are only reachable from the HA UI (entities, scripts, dev tools).

docs.title: Only at the MQTT level
docs.text: Topic Kind What it is main/Cooling_Mode state 0 curve, 1 direct for cooling. Not in HA (Heating_Mode now is, as sensor.aquarea_heating_mode) main/Zones_State state 0 zone 1, 1 zone 2, 2 both main/Heat_Delta, main/Cool_Delta state Floor heating / cooling delta (K) main/Heating_Off_Outdoor_Temp state Heating cut-off outdoor limit (Heater_On_Outdoor_Temp is in HA now) main/Pump_Duty state Pump duty (the fork has no max pump duty setting) main/Z1_Temp, main/Z2_Temp, main/Room_Thermostat_Temp state Zone actual temperatures. Z1_Water_Temp and Z2_Water_Temp read -78 (not fitted), Z2_Temp reads -128 main/Z1_Cool_Curve_*, main/Z2_*_Curve_* state Cooling curve and zone 2 curves commands/SetForceDefrost, commands/SetForceSterilization command 0/1 commands/SendRawValue command A raw hex frame, see below commands/OSCommand command Runs a shell command on the CZ-TAW1 (EnableCommand is true in the sample config). Treat as root access to the gateway

docs.title: Commands supported by the fork
docs.text:
All handlers are in src/taw2mqtt.go (subscriptions at :503-556). Every command is a 110-byte frame that starts f1 6c 01 10 with all other bytes zero (zero means "no change"), then the checksum is added on send. Byte offsets are 0-based.

Command Payload Byte Value written Line SetHeatpump 0 off, 1 on 4 1 (off) or 2 (on); any non-1 payload turns it off :839 SetForceDHW 0, 1 4 64 / 128; any non-1 payload clears it :736 SetHolidayMode 0, 1 5 16 / 32 :676 SetOperationMode 0-10 6 18, 19, 24, 33, 34, 35, 40, 24, 40, 24, 40 for payload 0 to 10 (7 and 8, Auto(Cool), are written as Auto); other payloads write 0 (no change) :602 SetPowerfulMode 0-3 7 (n+1) & 7 :658 SetQuietMode 0-3 7 (n+1) * 8 :821 SetForceDefrost 0, 1 8 0 / 2 :716 SetForceSterilization 0, 1 8 0 / 4 :696 SetZ1HeatRequestTemperature integer 38 n + 128 :756 SetZ1CoolRequestTemperature integer 39 n + 128 :773 SetZ2HeatRequestTemperature integer 40 n + 128 :789 SetZ2CoolRequestTemperature integer 41 n + 128 :805 SetDHWTemp integer 42 n + 128 :640 SendRawValue hex of a full frame any as given :591

Behaviour that matters for safety (verified in the code):

  • There is no range check in any handler. The value is parsed with Atoi, falling back to ParseFloat, and a payload that does not parse (including an empty one) becomes 0, which is written as byte 128, that is 0 degC, not "no change". The byte is truncated to 8 bits, so out of range values wrap.
  • Commands are queued FIFO (max 256) and sent one per loop with SleepAfterCommand (1 s) between them. A queued command expires after 2 minutes (commandTTL, :38-48), so a stale command is never replayed hours later.
  • There is no acknowledgement frame. The fork does not report whether the unit accepted a value.

Not in the fork (upstream has them): SetCurves, SetZones, SetMaxPumpDuty, SetPump, SetFloorHeatDelta/SetFloorCoolDelta, SetHeatingOffOutdoorTemp, zone sensor settings, heater and bivalent settings, SetReset and the rest of upstream SET15 to SET50. There is also no command (upstream or fork) that switches between curve and direct mode.

State topics published by the fork: TOP0 to TOP94 (ParseTopicList3, from :1178). Upstream publishes up to TOP143 plus the extra/ and optional/ groups; the fork has none of those. Heating_Mode is TOP76 (:1771, byte 28, low two bits minus one), Cooling_Mode is TOP81.

docs.title: Switching between curve and direct mode
docs.text:
There is no MQTT or HA command for this. It is an installer setting of the heat pump, made on the unit's own controller (CZ-TAW1 remote or the indoor unit panel). Per the service manual (p.99, 105): Menu > Installer setup > Operation setup > Heat > "Water temp. for heating ON", with the choices "Compensation curve" (default) or "Direct". After the change, main/Heating_Mode flips to the new value.

Manual-confirmed ranges (service manual p.26, 105, 131, 149):

  • Curve: four points, with a user shift of +/-5 degC.
  • Direct: 20 to 55 degC (60 degC above -10 degC outdoor).
  • Powerful mode does not apply in direct mode.

The manual covers the indoor unit WH-ADC0309J3E5 with the outdoor unit WH-UD09JE5. The owner's units are WH-ADC0309JE5C and WH-UD09JE5-1, assumed equivalent.

docs.title: Changing the curve
docs.text:
• From the controller: the same installer menu, per zone: the water target at two outside temperatures (the four points above; service manual p.105, 131). This is the supported way with this fork.
  • From HA/MQTT with the fork: not supported. SetCurves does not exist in the fork.
  • Upstream HeishaMon: commands/SetCurves takes a JSON document with zone1/zone2, heat/cool, target/outside, high/low. For Z1 heating it writes bytes 75 to 78 as value + 128 (upstream commands.cpp, set_curves).
  • Raw workaround (believed, untested): SendRawValue with a hand-built frame that sets bytes 75 to 78 to value + 128 would write the same bytes. It bypasses every check and a wrong frame goes straight to the unit; do not use it on the live system without a test plan.

docs.title: Current configuration (2026-10-30)
docs.text:
Read-only snapshot from the broker (full refresh at the fork's 300 s ForceRefreshTime) and the Home Assistant Prometheus metrics.

Item Value Heating mode (Heating_Mode) 1, direct; Cooling_Mode also 1 (direct) Operating mode (Operating_Mode_State) 3, DHW only (AppDaemon climate control currently has space heating off) Z1 heat request (Z1_Heat_Request_Temp) 26 degC (absolute, direct mode) Z1 water target (Z1_Water_Target_Temp) / Main_Target_Temp 26 / 26 degC Z1 heat curve (stored, not in use) -5 degC outside -> 35 degC, 15 degC outside -> 26 degC Z1 cool request / cool curve 15 degC; 20 degC outside -> 15, 30 degC outside -> 10 Z2 heat request / water target 28 / 28 degC (zone 2 inactive: Zones_State 0) Quiet / powerful / holiday / force DHW off / off / off / off Heat pump power on, no error Pump Pump_Duty 0, Pump_Speed 0, Pump_Flow 0.13 L/min (not heating) Tank target 49 degC, actual 49 degC (DHW_Heat_Delta -4, sterilization 65 degC / 10 min) Outlet / inlet 28 / 38 degC; outside 18 degC Deltas and limits Heat_Delta 5 K, Heating_Off_Outdoor_Temp 35 degC, Heater_On_Outdoor_Temp 0 degC Heat_Pump_Model -1 (the fork does not decode it)

History from the Prometheus metrics (90 days): the Z1 request stayed at 26 and the four Z1 curve points never changed. The Z1 and Z2 requests equal their curve "high" target (26 and 28); whether the two are linked in the unit is not known (see the experiment note below).

docs.title: Electric heater and power limits
docs.text: From the Panasonic service manual for this unit family (cited as "service manual p.N"). The manual covers WH-ADC0309J3E5 with WH-UD09JE5; the owner's WH-ADC0309JE5C with WH-UD09JE5-1 is assumed equivalent. The manual states no other heater steps for this model.

docs.title: The heater
docs.text:
• One 3.00 kW electric heater (13.0 A) on a separate supply (Power Supply 2, its own 16 A breaker); p.25-26. It is both the space-heating backup and, when the tank heater is set to Internal, the hot-water booster; p.138, 146.
  • The heat pump alone draws at most 3.47 kW / 15.9 A (about 2.0 kW rated at A7W35); p.25. Heat pump plus heater is about 6.5 kW, which exceeds the 5.0 kW contracted limit on its own.
  • The 5.0 kW limit is enforced by a smart meter that cuts the supply. The owner confirmed that cuts have happened. A trip is a safety and availability failure, so the heater must be treated as a load that can trip the house, not as a cost.

docs.title: What starts the heater automatically
docs.text:
Trigger Condition Page Space heating Outdoor temperature below "O/D temp for heater ON" (default 0 degC; the live Heater_On_Outdoor_Temp reads 0 degC), plus outlet and delay conditions 144 Defrost Only if the backup heater is enabled: outlet below 10 degC, outdoor below -10 degC or inlet below 27 degC 145 Hot water Tank target above what the heat pump reaches alone 138, 146 Sterilization Default 65 degC for 10 min, weekly; uses the heater 150 Anti-freeze Water below 6 degC 152 Heat pump error Only if "Force Heater" = Auto (default Manual) 144, 147-148

Consequences for control:

  • Hot water above about 51 degC starts the 3 kW heater. The heat pump alone practically reaches 51 to 55 degC (control reference 51 degC; "above 55 degC only possible with backup heater"; p.26, 107, 137). The tank range is 40 to 65 degC with the internal heater. The tank target of 49 degC in the current configuration is within the heat pump range.
  • A sterilization cycle starts the heater (65 degC target), a scheduled 3 kW load every week.
  • With the heater on, the heat pump plus the heater can exceed 5.0 kW before any other house load is counted.
  • SMART DHW (default 20:00 to 05:00) can suppress hot-water reheat; p.152.

docs.title: Inputs that limit power
docs.text:
All of these need the optional PCB CZ-NS4P, except CN-THERMO; p.92-93, 98, 103, 159-163.

Input Effect Note Demand control, 0-10 V Outdoor-unit current limited to 10-100% The manual does not say it limits the heater External compressor switch A DIP pin selects "heaters only off" or everything off SG-ready Grid-signal operating states CN-THERMO external switch Whole system off No PCB needed

Whether any of them is fitted is not known. They are the candidates for an import-limit interlock; the demand control input alone cannot be relied on to keep the heater off.

docs.title: Acknowledgement and latency
docs.text:
• Command path: HA mqtt.publish (QoS 0, retain false) -> fork queue -> serial frame at the next loop (about 1 to 3 s).
  • Confirmation: the unit answers every poll with a full data frame. The fork publishes a state topic only when its value changed (:1148), so the state topic itself is the acknowledgement: main/Z1_Heat_Request_Temp for the request and main/Z1_Water_Target_Temp / main/Main_Target_Temp for the effect. Expect the request to change within a few seconds (believed; not measured, nothing was written). The outlet itself follows the new target over minutes (compressor ramp), not seconds.
  • No change after about 10 s means the command was rejected or lost: there is no error topic.
  • A fresh subscriber only sees changed topics until the next full refresh (up to 300 s), so wait for the refresh to read a static value such as Heating_Mode.
  • HA mirrors the confirmed value back into the helper and mutes the command automation for 5 s (delay in heishamon.yaml:246-253).

docs.title: What happens if the request is written in the other mode
docs.text:
Not tested (writing is out of scope for the audit). Believed from the upstream ranges ("-5 to 5 or 20 to max"):

  • Direct mode, shift-sized value (for example 3): below the 20 degC minimum; the unit is expected to ignore or clamp it, but a clamp to 20 degC would still heat the floor with a target far below the desired one.
  • Curve mode, absolute value (for example 26): far above the -5 to 5 shift range; the unit is expected to ignore or clamp it. If it were accepted as a +26 K shift the water target would hit the unit's maximum.

Neither the fork nor the HA helper (range -5 to 40) prevents either case. Before any write, read main/Heating_Mode first.

docs.title: Safety notes
docs.text:
• Strictly shadow phase for the battery optimizer: nothing here authorises writing. Any experiment is a separate, owner-approved step.
  • The HA helper accepts -5 to 40 for every zone. It cannot reach direct temperatures above 40 degC and it accepts shift-sized values in direct mode. A dedicated helper or script with a narrower range (for example 20 to a chosen maximum in direct mode) and a check on Heating_Mode should sit in front of the command.
  • The firmware clamp is unknown. The fork clamps nothing; upstream set_z1_heat_request_temperature clamps nothing either. The unit's own limits on the direct value are not documented (the upstream docs say "20 to max"); the highest target seen on Main_Target_Temp is 59 degC, during DHW.
  • Garbage or empty payloads write 0 degC (see above). Always publish a validated integer with retain: false; a retained command would be replayed by the broker to every reconnecting subscriber.
  • Echo (believed): when the unit reports a different request (for example after a change on the controller), the "Set Z1 Heat selector" automation updates the helper and the "Set Z1 Heat Temperature" automation then publishes the same value back. It is harmless for an identical value but it means every device-side change is re-written once.
  • Writes are persistent in the unit; there is no automatic fallback if Home Assistant or the optimizer stops. A control loop needs a watchdog that restores a safe request (the existing AppDaemon watchdog does this for the operating mode only, see appdaemon_climate.yaml).
  • OSCommand and SendRawValue are unrestricted over MQTT. Anyone with broker credentials can change unit settings; keep the broker credentials and mosquitto network exposure as they are.
  • First write experiment, when approved: write a value equal to the current one, check that Z1_Heat_Request_Temp and Z1_Heat_Curve_Target_High_Temp behave as expected, then step by 1 K, one change at a time, watching Heating_Mode, Z1_Water_Target_Temp and Error.

docs.title: Read-only checks
docs.text:
# state, from the broker pod; the secret is read from the mosquitto-user Secret, never printed
kubectl -n mosquitto exec mosquitto-0 -c mosquitto -- \
  mosquitto_sub -h 127.0.0.1 -u <user> -P <password> -W 330 -C 1 \
  -t 'panasonic_heat_pump/main/Heating_Mode'

Prometheus has the HA entities (hass_sensor_unit_celsius{entity="sensor.aquarea_z1_heat_request_temperature"}), including Heating_Mode as sensor.aquarea_heating_mode since 2026-10-30. The exporter has no entity filter (prometheus: in configuration.yaml), so new numeric sensors and binary sensors appear without further config.

docs.title: Add app to SSO (GitOps with Kaniop)
docs.text: Preferred method. The Kaniop operator manages OAuth2 clients and groups declaratively via CRDs. ArgoCD syncs the resources and the operator creates the client in Kanidm plus a Kubernetes secret with the credentials.

docs.title: 1. Create the group
docs.text:
apps/<name>/templates/kanidm-group.yaml:

---
apiVersion: kaniop.rs/v1beta1
kind: KanidmGroup
metadata:
  name: <app>-users
spec:
  kanidmRef:
    name: kanidm
    namespace: kanidm

Optionally add an <app>-admins group if the app supports admin scope maps.

docs.title: 2. Create the OAuth2 client
docs.text:
apps/<name>/templates/kanidm-oauth2-client.yaml:

---
apiVersion: kaniop.rs/v1beta1
kind: KanidmOAuth2Client
metadata:
  name: <app>
spec:
  kanidmRef:
    name: kanidm
    namespace: kanidm

  displayname: <app>

  origin: https://<app>.grigri.cloud/

  redirectUrl:
    - https://<app>.grigri.cloud/<callback-path>

  scopeMap:
    - group: <app>-users
      scopes:
        - openid
        - profile
        - email

  # Optional: admin scope map
  # supScopeMap:
  #   - group: <app>-admins
  #     scopes:
  #       - admin

  preferShortUsername: true
  strictRedirectUrl: true

Common optional flags:

Flag When to use allowInsecureClientDisablePkce: true App doesn't support PKCE public: true Public client (no secret, e.g. SPA/native) allowLocalhostRedirect: true CLI tools that redirect to localhost jwtLegacyCryptoEnable: true App needs legacy JWT encryption

docs.title: 3. Consume the secret
docs.text:
The operator creates a secret named <app>-kanidm-oauth2-credentials with keys CLIENT_ID and CLIENT_SECRET. Reference it in your chart's env vars:

env:
  - name: OIDC_CLIENT_ID
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: <app>-kanidm-oauth2-credentials
        key: CLIENT_ID
  - name: OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: <app>-kanidm-oauth2-credentials
        key: CLIENT_SECRET

The OIDC issuer URL follows this pattern:

https://idm.grigri.cloud/oauth2/openid/<app>

docs.title: 4. Add users to the group
docs.text:
Users must be added manually by an admin after the group is created:

kanidm group add-members <app>-users ${USER} -D idm_admin

docs.title: 5. Verify
docs.text:
After ArgoCD syncs, check the client is ready:

kubectl --context=grigri get kanidmoauth2client <app> -n <namespace>
kubectl --context=grigri get secret <app>-kanidm-oauth2-credentials -n <namespace>

The status should show ready: true and all conditions True.

docs.title: Manual CLI method (legacy)
docs.text:
Example with Grafana:

kanidm system oauth2 create grafana grafana  https://grafana.grigri.cloud/login/generic_oauth -D admin
kanidm group create grafana-users -D admin
kanidm group add-members grafana-users ${USER} -D admin
kanidm system oauth2 update-scope-map grafana grafana-users openid profile email -D admin
kanidm system oauth2 show-basic-secret grafana -D admin
kanidm group create grafana-admins -D admin
kanidm group add-members grafana-admins ${USER} -D admin
kanidm system oauth2 update-sup-scope-map grafana grafana-admins admin -D admin
kanidm system oauth2 prefer-short-username grafana -D admin
kanidm system oauth2 set-landing-url grafana https://grafana.grigri.cloud/login/generic_oauth

If PKCE needs to be disabled:

kanidm system oauth2 warning-insecure-client-disable-pkce ${CLIENT}

docs.title: Use groups in SSO
docs.text:
To pass groups in JWT you need to ask for openid groups scopes.

After next login, you will receive groups uuid and groups spn in the token:

    ...
  "scopes": [
    "email",
    "groups",
    "openid",
    "profile"
  ],
  "groups": [
    "idm_all_persons@idm.grigri.cloud",
    "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000035",
    "idm_all_accounts@idm.grigri.cloud",
    "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000036",
    "XXXXXX@idm.grigri.cloud",
    "XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX",
    ...
  ]
}

Note: When groups scope is activated your header size will be above 4k so you will need to add this annotation to your ingress:

nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffer-size: "16k"

docs.title: Kubernetes upgrade
docs.text:
Update k3s_version to desired version and then run:

cd metal
ANSIBLE_EXTRA_ARGS="-t k3s-upgrade -e serial=1" make cluster

Note: it worked perfectly with serial=100% or running it by default.

Stale tag: no task or role in metal/ is tagged k3s-upgrade, so -t k3s-upgrade selects nothing. The k3s role is tagged k3s (metal/playbooks/install/cluster.yml:14-16) and deliberately leaves upgrades to the system-upgrade-controller Plans (system/system-upgrade/k3s/) — see the comment in metal/roles/k3s/tasks/main.yml:12. K3s version bumps stay human-only per AGENTS.md, and agents may apply only a committed, config-only -t k3s --limit <node> change.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: The deployment of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) application was carried out in k8s using the Fedora guide for OpenShift as reference.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
The migration process involved recreating the backend and suffix, as follows:

dsconf localhost backend create --suffix dc=grigri,dc=cloud --be-name userroot --create-suffix

To import current values, LDIF files were utilized. First, the current LDIF files were exported using the following command:

ldapsearch -w 'XXXXXXX' -D 'cn=Directory Manager' -H ldaps://ldap.grigri -b dc=grigri,dc=cloud -LLL "(objectclass=*)"

Next, Apache Directory Studio was used for importing the exported files.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The permissions for the LDAP deployment were set in accordance with the guidelines provided by Red Hat's official documentation. The following commands were executed:

ldapmodify -w 'XXXXXXX' -D 'cn=Directory Manager' -H ldaps://ldap.grigri -b dc=grigri,dc=cloud -x
dn: dc=grigri,dc=cloud
changetype: modify
add: aci
aci: (targetattr!="userPassword || aci")(version 3.0; acl "Enable anonymous ac
 cess"; allow (read, search, compare) userdn="ldap:///anyone";)

ldapmodify -w 'XXXXXXX' -D 'cn=Directory Manager' -H ldaps://ldap.grigri -b dc=grigri,dc=cloud -x
dn: ou=People,dc=grigri,dc=cloud
changetype: modify
add: aci
aci: (targetattr="userpassword")(version 3.0; acl "read password access"; allo
 w(read) userdn =  "ldap:///uid=*,ou=Read,ou=ServiceUsers,dc=grigri,dc=cloud";
 )

docs.title: Migrate controller node
docs.text: Based in K3s backup and restore doc.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Take etcd snapshot and stop k3s in old controller.
  2. Copy /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server and etcd snapshot to new controller.
  3. Update Ansible inventory controller node and start new controller.
  4. Check API is working and there are no agents.
  5. Start all agents with make cluster.

Example:

# k8s-amd64-1
k3s etcd-snapshot save
systemctl stop k3s

rsync -av --delete /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/ backup@prusik:/datasets/backups/k3s/server

# grigri
k3s server --cluster-reset --cluster-reset-restore-path=/datasets/backups/k3s/server/db/snapshots/on-demand-grigri-1716963887 --token /datasets/backups/k3s/server/token

# change inventory with new controller and move controller to worker

# localhost
cd metal
ANSIBLE_EXTRA_ARGS="--limit prusik" make cluster
kubectl get nodes
make cluster

# remove labels

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
In ZFS server:

# variables
PVC=datasets/k8s/l/v/pvc-0f17e0bf-6741-44fa-9e37-e5ed394ff56b
NAME=transcoder-rabbit
SIZE=1G
NAMESPACE=transcoder

NEW_DATASET=${DATASET}/${NAME}

zfs snapshot ${PVC}@clone
zfs clone ${PVC}@clone ${NEW_DATASET}
zfs promote ${NEW_DATASET}
zfs unmount ${NEW_DATASET}
zfs set mountpoint=legacy ${NEW_DATASET}
zfs set quota=${SIZE} ${NEW_DATASET}

cat << EOF > /tmp/pv.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: ${NAME}
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  capacity:
    storage: ${SIZE}i # size of the volume
  claimRef:
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
    name: ${PVC_NAME}
    namespace: ${NAMESPACE}
  csi:
    driver: zfs.csi.openebs.io
    fsType: zfs
    volumeAttributes:
      openebs.io/poolname: ${DATASET}
    volumeHandle: ${NAME}
  nodeAffinity:
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: kubernetes.io/hostname
          operator: In
          values:
          - grigri
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Delete
  storageClassName: openebs-zfspv
  volumeMode: Filesystem
EOF
k3s kubectl apply -f /tmp/pv.yaml

cat << EOF > /tmp/zfs-volume.yaml
apiVersion: zfs.openebs.io/v1
kind: ZFSVolume
metadata:
  finalizers:
  - zfs.openebs.io/finalizer
  name: ${NAME}
  namespace: zfs-localpv
spec:
  capacity: "$(echo "(${SIZE::-1} * 1024 * 1024 * 1024) / 1" | bc)" # size of the volume in bytes
  fsType: zfs
  ownerNodeID: grigri
  shared: "yes"
  poolName: ${DATASET}
  volumeType: DATASET
status:
  state: Ready
EOF
k3s kubectl apply -f /tmp/zfs-volume.yaml

docs.title: Library
docs.text:
We have two different libraries:

  • Main library: /music/ (mounted from navidrome-music PVC)
  • Lidarr library: /music/lidarr/ (mounted from /datasets/music on the host)

Main library is backuped by Velero. Lidarr library is not backed up. If you want to move something from Lidarr library to main library, you need to copy files from /music/lidarr/ to /music/ in the proper directory and adjust the metadata accordingly.

Note: Lidarr does not know about files in the main library.

docs.title: Update music metadata
docs.text:
# Explore pod
kubectl --context=grigri -n navidrome exec -it $(kubectl -n navidrome get pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=navidrome -o jsonpath="{.items[0].metadata.name}") -- /bin/sh

# Copy files to local
kubectl --context=grigri -n navidrome cp $(kubectl -n navidrome get pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=navidrome -o jsonpath="{.items[0].metadata.name}"):/music/path/ /tmp/path/

# Change metadata with local tools
easytag /tmp/path/

# Copy files back to pod
kubectl --context=grigri -n navidrome cp /tmp/path/ $(kubectl -n navidrome get pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=navidrome -o jsonpath="{.items[0].metadata.name}"):/music/path/

After updating the metadata, you may need to rescan the music library from the Navidrome web interface and remove missing files: https://navidrome.grigri.cloud/app/#/missing.

KUBECONFIG=/tmp/kubeconfig.yaml kubectl -n nextcloud cp config/www/nextcloud/apps/ $POD_NAME:/tmp/

docs.title: data
docs.text:
POD_NAME=$(KUBECONFIG=/tmp/kubeconfig.yaml kubectl -n nextcloud get pod -l app.kubernetes.io/component=app --no-headers -o custom-columns=":metadata.name")
# Skip the user directories that already live on their own ZFS volume (one -not -path per user).
for DIR in $(find /datasets/nextcloud/ -maxdepth 1 -mindepth 1 -not -path '*/<user-a>' -not -path '*/<user-b>'); do
    echo $DIR;
    KUBECONFIG=/tmp/kubeconfig.yaml kubectl -n nextcloud cp --retries=5 $DIR $POD_NAME:/var/www/html/data/
done
#KUBECONFIG=/tmp/kubeconfig.yaml kubectl -n nextcloud cp --retries=5 /datasets/fotos $POD_NAME:/var/www/html/data/<user>/files/
KUBECONFIG=/tmp/kubeconfig.yaml kubectl -n nextcloud exec -it $POD_NAME -- bash
chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html/data

Alternative using rsync:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: rsync
  namespace: nextcloud
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      name: rsync
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: rsync
          image: instrumentisto/rsync-ssh
          command:
            - rsync
            - -avz
            - --numeric-ids
            - --delete
            - --progress
            - /src/
            - /dest/data/
          volumeMounts:
            - name: src
              mountPath: "/src/"
            - name: dest
              mountPath: "/dest/"
      volumes:
        - name: src
          hostPath:
            path: /datasets/nextcloud/
            type: Directory
        - name: dest
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: nextcloud-nextcloud-data
      restartPolicy: Never
      nodeSelector:
        name: grigri

docs.title: Restoring to a Different Node
docs.text:
To restore to a different node, create a ConfigMap with the following YAML:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  # any name can be used; Velero uses the labels (below)
  # to identify it rather than the name
  name: change-pvc-node-selector-config
  # must be in the velero namespace
  namespace: velero
  # the below labels should be used verbatim in your
  # ConfigMap.
  labels:
    # this value-less label identifies the ConfigMap as
    # config for a plugin (i.e. the built-in restore item action plugin)
    velero.io/plugin-config: ""
    # this label identifies the name and kind of plugin
    # that this ConfigMap is for.
    velero.io/change-pvc-node-selector: RestoreItemAction
data:
  # add 1+ key-value pairs here, where the key is the old
  # node name and the value is the new node name.
  grigri: prusik

Warning: ArgoCD labels are going to be restored too. If you are doing the restore into other namespace as in the example, disable ArgoCD or modify the labels.

docs.title: Restoring with a Different Storage Class
docs.text:
To restore with a different storage class, create a ConfigMap with the following YAML:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  # any name can be used; Velero uses the labels (below)
  # to identify it rather than the name
  name: change-storage-class-config
  # must be in the velero namespace
  namespace: velero
  # the below labels should be used verbatim in your
  # ConfigMap.
  labels:
    # this value-less label identifies the ConfigMap as
    # config for a plugin (i.e. the built-in restore item action plugin)
    velero.io/plugin-config: ""
    # this label identifies the name and kind of plugin
    # that this ConfigMap is for.
    velero.io/change-storage-class: RestoreItemAction
data:
  # add 1+ key-value pairs here, where the key is the old
  # storage class name and the value is the new storage
  # class name.
  openebs-zfspv: backup

Warning: Ensure that the original parent zfs volume exists in the target storage class (e.g., datasets/openebs).

velero restore create --from-backup ${BACKUP_NAME} --include-namespaces ${NAMESPACE} --restore-volumes=true --namespace-mappings ${NAMESPACE}:${TARGET_NAMESPACE}

Note: ArgoCD labels will also be restored. If restoring to a different namespace, consider disabling ArgoCD or modifying the labels accordingly.

Example filtering by resource and labels:

velero restore create --from-backup retain-quaterly-20240910023040  --include-namespaces mintpsicologia --restore-volumes=true --namespace-mappings mintpsicologia:mintpsicologia --include-resources persistentvolumes,persistentvolumeclaims --selector app.kubernetes.io/name=mariadb

Get the firmware from the dustbuilder and download it to the robot.

Go to Dreame L10S Ultra section.

Email: anonymous

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
You need to have your robot already rooted to use this firmware! The robot needs to be in its docking station and fully charged!

  1. Connect to robot via SSH using your SSH key
ssh root@tanque.iot.grigri
  1. Download firmware update to /tmp
cd /tmp
wget --no-check-certificate {url-of-firmware.tar.gz}
  1. Unpack firmware package
tar -xzvf {name-of-firmware.tar.gz}
  1. Run installer
./install.sh

The robot should install the firmware and reboot. This steps will update the Kernel, Rootfs and MCU firmware

Note: It takes like 3 minutes to install and reboot since {"ret":"ok"} is shown.

docs.title: Vault Migration: File to Raft Storage
docs.text: Step-by-step guide to migrate Vault from file storage to raft storage using vault operator migrate.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The vault operator migrate command converts data in-place from file to raft format, preserving everything:

  • KV secrets
  • PKI root CA keys
  • Auth methods
  • Policies

docs.title: 1. Backup Data
docs.text:
Stop Vault and backup the PVC data (guarantees consistency):

# Scale down vault to stop writes
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault scale statefulset vault --replicas=0

# Wait for pod to terminate
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault wait --for=delete pod/vault-0 --timeout=120s

# Create backup pod mounting the PVC
cat <<EOF | kubectl --context=grigri apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: vault-backup
  namespace: vault
spec:
  containers:
  - name: backup
    image: busybox
    args: [sleep, "1000000"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: vault-data
      mountPath: /data-source
  volumes:
  - name: vault-data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: vault-file-vault-0
EOF

# Wait for backup pod
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault wait --for=condition=ready pod/vault-backup --timeout=60s

# Create backup tarball
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault exec vault-backup -- tar czf /tmp/vault-backup.tar.gz -C /data-source .

# Copy backup to local machine
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault cp vault-backup:/tmp/vault-backup.tar.gz ./vault-backup.tar.gz

# Cleanup backup pod
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault delete pod vault-backup

docs.title: 2. Migrate Data Format
docs.text:
Start Vault temporarily to run the migration:

# Scale vault back up
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault scale statefulset vault --replicas=1
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault wait --for=condition=ready pod/vault-0 --timeout=120s

# Get root token
TOKEN=$(kubectl --context=grigri -n vault get secret vault-unseal-keys -o jsonpath='{.data.vault-root}' | base64 -d)

# Create migration config and run migration
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault exec vault-0 -- sh -c "
  cat > /tmp/migrate.hcl << 'EOF'
storage_source \"file\" {
  path = \"/vault/file\"
}
storage_destination \"raft\" {
  path = \"/vault/file\"
  node_id = \"vault-0\"
}
cluster_addr = \"https://vault.vault:8201\"
EOF

  VAULT_SKIP_VERIFY=true VAULT_TOKEN=$TOKEN \
  vault operator migrate -config=/tmp/migrate.hcl
"

Expected output:

Migration successfully completed!

docs.title: 3. Update Vault Configuration
docs.text:
Edit platform/vault/templates/vault.yaml:

config:
  storage:
    raft:
      path: "${ .Env.VAULT_STORAGE_FILE }"
      node_id: "vault-0"
  listener:
    tcp:
      address: "0.0.0.0:8200"
      tls_cert_file: /vault/tls/server.crt
      tls_key_file: /vault/tls/server.key
      cluster_address: "0.0.0.0:8201"
  api_addr: "https://vault.vault:8200"
  cluster_addr: "https://vault.vault:8201"
  ui: true

Commit and push (ArgoCD will sync):

git add platform/vault/templates/vault.yaml
git commit -m "feat(vault): migrate from file to raft storage"
git push

docs.title: 4. Redeploy Vault
docs.text:
# Delete pod to pick up new config
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault delete pod vault-0

# Wait for vault to be ready
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault wait --for=condition=ready pod/vault-0 --timeout=120s

docs.title: 5. Verify Migration
docs.text:
TOKEN=$(kubectl --context=grigri -n vault get secret vault-unseal-keys -o jsonpath='{.data.vault-root}' | base64 -d)

kubectl --context=grigri -n vault exec vault-0 -- sh -c "
  export VAULT_SKIP_VERIFY=true VAULT_TOKEN=$TOKEN

  echo '=== Vault Status ==='
  vault status

  echo ''
  echo '=== KV Secrets ==='
  vault kv list secret/

  echo ''
  echo '=== PKI Mounts ==='
  vault secrets list | grep pki

  echo ''
  echo '=== Raft Snapshot Test ==='
  vault operator raft snapshot save /tmp/test.snap && echo 'Raft snapshot OK'
"

Expected status output:

Storage Type             raft
HA Enabled               true
Raft Committed Index     XXX
Raft Applied Index       XXX

docs.title: ArgoCD Considerations
docs.text:
Vault modifies pod labels dynamically (vault-active, vault-sealed, etc.). ArgoCD may try to sync these back. Add to your Application manifest:

spec:
  ignoreDifferences:
    - kind: Pod
      name: vault-0
      jsonPointers:
        - /metadata/labels/vault-active
        - /metadata/labels/vault-sealed
        - /metadata/labels/vault-initialized

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
# Get root token
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault get secret vault-unseal-keys -o jsonpath='{.data.vault-root}' | base64 -d

# Check Vault status
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault exec vault-0 -- vault status

# Create raft snapshot
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault exec vault-0 -- sh -c "
  VAULT_SKIP_VERIFY=true VAULT_TOKEN=<token> \
  vault operator raft snapshot save /vault/file/backup.snap
"

# Restore raft snapshot
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault exec vault-0 -- sh -c "
  VAULT_SKIP_VERIFY=true VAULT_TOKEN=<token> \
  vault operator raft snapshot restore /vault/file/backup.snap
"

# Force leader step-down (for HA)
kubectl --context=grigri -n vault exec vault-0 -- sh -c "
  VAULT_SKIP_VERIFY=true VAULT_TOKEN=<token> vault operator step-down
"

docs.title: Kivi voice assistant
docs.text:
"Kivi" is the household voice assistant. In Home Assistant the Assist pipeline is named "Kiwi" and the name is pronounced "kivi"; the assistant spells it "Kivi". The satellite hardware and software are developed in pando85/webos-voice-satellite; this section keeps the homelab side: which conversation agent ("brain") answers, measured against the cluster services.

  • Kivi plan: goal, live architecture, decisions, workstreams (wake word, Whisper, real-usage validation, decision model, fine-tuning) and the open decisions for the owner.
  • Conversation agent evaluation: Kiais gateway metrics, the dry-run harness in scripts/voice-assistant/agent_eval/, Spanish test phrases, and which requests Home Assistant's built-in intents already handle.
  • Kiais as the conversation agent: core (llama_cpp, litellm), HACS and own-component options verified on a throwaway Home Assistant 2026.10.4 with prefer_local_intents, the Kiais streamed tool-call quirk, and the deployment (core llama_cpp, UI only, deployed 2026-11-05 as conversation.fast) and rollback steps.
  • Small local models: the GTX 1060 budget, small models as router, STT corrector and home agent, Whisper prompt, model size and CPU options, measured on synthetic Spanish audio; ranked additions in Conversation agent design.
  • Kivi decider PoC: headroom of a small decision model behind the built-in intents, measured before building one; the synthetic dataset kivi-fake-v1 (four fake homes, phrasing styles, TV-dialogue negatives, local-LLM paraphrases, audio subset) and what custom sentences already cover.
  • Decision models: whether a small non-generative decision model (Laya, Quyet) or an embedding and fuzzy-matching baseline can execute, offline and without wrong actions, the home commands the built-in intents miss, before they go to Kiais; zero-shot on the synthetic corpus, the kivi-fake-v1 fake homes and the real names (counts only).
  • Whisper GPU benchmark: compute type and beam size of the live Whisper on the GTX 1060 with synthetic Spanish commands (partial: no setting beats the current one on a quiet GPU, beam 1 saves 26 ms; the benchmark pod disturbed the live service, see the incident section; --vad-clip not measured).
  • STT hint list and learning from usage: biasing the Spanish Whisper STT towards the home's names (upstream --hass-token), a privacy-bounded loop that turns misrecognitions into reviewed hint, alias and correction proposals, and a phased plan.
  • Data register: what the assistant collects (Whisper transcripts in Loki for 180 days under a temporary exception, derived replay datasets, names list, Kiais requests, no audio), where it lives, who reads it, how to stop or delete it, and the usage rules.

  • Building the Whisper STT image on Forgejo: summary and the cluster side (canary, ExternalSecret, prompt ConfigMap, values.yaml cutover, rollback to 2.4.0). The build itself (Dockerfile, Forgejo workflow, Pascal sm_61 checks, runner disk, risks) lives in agil/wyoming-whisper on git.grigri.cloud (private).

  • Custom wake word "kivi": openWakeWord model for the lone word "kivi", trained on synthetic Spanish voices, measured against alexa with the server's exact features (recall, false accepts per hour, near-words), deployment notes (--custom-model-dir, calibrated threshold, rollback to alexa) and the owner's real-voice test. Not deployed. Scripts in scripts/voice-assistant/wakeword/.

  • Model registry: one row per model (STT, wake words alexa and kivi, conversation agent, decision models) with version, short sha256, where it runs, whether it is deployed, threshold, measured scores, licence and storage (the licence-restricted kivi model is in the private Forgejo repository agil/kivi-models), and how to register a model.
  • Lessons learned: pitfalls met so far, each with symptom, root cause, detection, fix and guard.

Results of evaluation runs (per-phrase JSON) are private and never committed; the harness writes them outside this repository.

docs.title: Kivi conversation agent: where small local models fit
docs.text: Status: design, ranked additions for the owner's decision. Since 2026-11-05 (about 15:50) Kivi runs on Kiais fast through Home Assistant's core llama_cpp integration with prefer_local_intents on (deployed); this note ranks what to add to that. This study changed nothing in Home Assistant, the cluster or GitOps state. Date: 2026-11-05 Evidence: small local models study (this design's measurements), conversation agent evaluation (Kiais), Kiais integration, STT hint list. Labels as in those documents: documented, observed, measured (on the workstation), inferred, hypothesis.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Owner's target: home commands handled in the house, fast and accurately; general and live questions answered by the Kiais gateway. Constraint: the cluster's GTX 1060 has about 1.0 GiB left for anything new once Whisper's transcription peak and a possible Jellyfin transcode are reserved.

docs.title: What the measurements say
docs.text:
1. A model that fits 1.0 GiB cannot be the home agent. With Home Assistant's own tool schema, every model from 270 M to 1.5 B parameters passed 0 to 16 % of the control phrases; the first usable size was qwen3:4b-instruct (2.5 GB), which handled 10 of the 13 graded phrases that Home Assistant's built-in intents miss (Kiais fast: 11 of 13).
  2. The best "router" already exists. With prefer_local_intents, Home Assistant's strict built-in matching answers the plain commands locally and never claims a general question. What it misses (colloquial phrasing, state questions, "pon ... a N" forms, STT errors) is exactly what needs a capable agent. A sentence-embedding classifier (278 M, about 10 ms) separates home from general requests well (92 % on Whisper output at +5 dB of TV noise) and is cheaper and as accurate as any small LLM router, but it only pays off if a local agent exists to send the home part to.
  3. Small LLMs do not fix Whisper's errors. As transcript correctors they recovered about as many commands as they broke, and they rewrote non-command questions (section 7 of the study).
  4. The useful non-LLM fix is the Whisper prompt, and the verbs carry it. The generic command verbs as initial_prompt (with or without the home's names) raised built-in intent success from 82 to 88 % on clean synthetic audio and from 65 to 74 % at +5 dB of TV noise; names alone gave less (70 % at +5 dB, nothing on clean audio). Whisper small, medium and large-v3 are not better than the deployed large-v3-turbo.
  5. Whisper itself costs 0.86 s on the 1060 (observed), almost independent of how long the command is.

docs.title: Candidate configurations, ranked
docs.text:
Latency is from the end of the user's speech to the first audio of the answer, at the median, excluding end-of-speech detection and audio transport (the same for every option). Components: Whisper on the 1060 0.86 s (observed); built-in intent match about 0.01 s (measured) plus the action; Piper first audio 0.02 to 0.19 s for one sentence (measured, workstation CPU); Kiais fast time to first speech 3.06 s for a home command with a tool call and 1.20 s for a general question (observed by the conversation agent evaluation from the workstation); qwen3:4b-instruct on the prusik CPU about 2.7 s for a tool round plus the answer's first sentence with a warm prompt cache (inferred from the workstation benchmark, where it is 3.7 s; study section 10). Command accuracy is on the fake home's 44 control phrases (reference text), which is optimistic for real audio (study section 5).

Rank Configuration Home commands: accuracy / latency General and live New VRAM / CPU Privacy Effort live A. Built-in first, Kiais fast behind it (prefer_local_intents on; deployed), plus the Whisper prompt with the command verbs (the addition ranked first) 41 of 43 graded (95 %: 30 by built-in intents, 11 of the other 13 by Kiais); about 1.0 s when the built-in intents match (30 of 44 reference texts; 56 % of the control clips of clean synthetic audio without the prompt, 44 % at +5 dB of TV noise), about 4.1 s when Kiais handles it Kiais: 100 % on the set, about 2.3 s none the unmatched third of commands and all general questions leave the house, with the exposed names in the system prompt agent and settings done; the Whisper prompt is low effort (hint list) 2 B. A, plus a local qwen3:4b-instruct on the prusik CPU for home requests the built-in intents miss; an embedding router sends the rest to Kiais 40 of 43 (93 %: 30 built-in, 10 of 13 local); about 1.0 s matched, about 3.7 s local fallback (4.7 s at the workstation's speed), plus 16 to 35 s once after every model load or prompt change Kiais, as in A, plus about 0.01 s for the router (built-in match first, then the embedding centroid: 4 % of general questions misrouted to the local model and 7 % of home phrases sent to Kiais, on Whisper output of clean audio) 0 VRAM; 4 to 6 GiB RAM and bursts of 8 to 16 cores on prusik home commands stay in the house high: a router component (custom conversation agent or inside Kiais), an Ollama on CPU, cache care 3 B with the model split between CPU and the 1060 (about 11 of 36 layers in 1.0 GiB) as B, decode about 20 % faster (inferred) as B 1.0 GiB VRAM as B as B plus the VRAM guard; risks Whisper's burst; not worth it 4 A small LLM (≤ 1.0 GiB) on the 1060 as router or STT corrector router: no gain over the embedding model on CPU; corrector: net loss or wrong targets for every model that fits 0.4 to 1.0 GiB as A medium; not recommended 5 A small LLM (≤ 1.0 GiB) as the home agent 0 to 16 % 0 to 85 % 0.4 to 1.0 GiB local rejected 6 Whisper on CPU, the whole 1060 for an LLM every command +2.8 s (Whisper large-v3-turbo takes 3.6 s on 16 CPU threads, measured), and the only agent that fits 3 GB (qwen2.5:3b) passed 37 % 0 / 16 cores per request local rejected 7 Smaller Whisper (small, medium) to free VRAM built-in intent success drops 6 to 24 points (measured) frees 0.3 to 0.8 GiB rejected

Recommendation, as additions to the live setup:

  1. Add the Whisper prompt with the command verbs now (a static --initial-prompt, below), and the home's names later with the hint list plan. It moves more commands onto the 1 s built-in path: built-in intent success from 82 to 88 % on clean synthetic audio and from 65 to 74 % at +5 dB of TV noise (measured), with no measurable latency and no VRAM. The rest of the live setup stays as it is.
  2. Optional: a local fallback agent (B: qwen3:4b-instruct on the prusik CPU, an embedding router in front). Worth it only if home commands should not leave the house, or as resilience: Kiais fast returned 783 errors in two days of October (conversation agent evaluation), and the live pipeline has no second agent. It costs about the same latency as Kiais for those commands, a custom routing component and RAM and CPU on prusik.
  3. Do not add a small model on the 1060 as router, corrector or agent (rows 4 and 5), and keep Whisper large-v3-turbo on the GPU (rows 6 and 7).

docs.title: Decisions 2026-11-05
docs.text:
1. The verbs prompt ships with the custom image rollout, not before. The Whisper prompt (static --initial-prompt, verbs first, then the names via --hass-token) goes live with agil/wyoming-whisper 3.8.1 (image build, hint list). apps/home-assistant/values.yaml stays on pando85/wyoming-whisper:2.4.0 without the prompt for now.
  2. Fallback if the custom image canary fails: apply the verbs-only prompt on 2.4.0 with the diff below, unchanged. Checked on 2026-11-05 against the image itself (pulled, then removed): pando85/wyoming-whisper:2.4.0 contains wyoming-faster-whisper 2.4.0, whose --help lists --initial-prompt INITIAL_PROMPT ("Optional text to provide as a prompt for the first window"). The entrypoint is bash /run.sh, which forwards the container args as a quoted "$@", and helm template renders the prompt as one list item (10 args in total: the existing 8 plus --initial-prompt and the quoted text; the text has commas and spaces but no quotes or accents), so it arrives as a single argument. Rollback: remove the two lines (or revert the commit).
  3. The local fallback agent (option B: qwen3:4b-instruct on the prusik CPU with an embedding router) is rejected by the owner. Kiais availability is considered the same as Home Assistant's, so there is no separate local fallback. Option 3 stays unchosen as well; the idle in-cluster Ollama question (open question 4) is unaffected by this decision.
  4. Zero-shot decision models between the built-in intents and Kiais: not recommended (study result, for the owner's decision). Laya, Quyet-1.0-Tiny and Quyet-1.0-Small, used zero-shot with typed questions over the home's options, rescued at most 8 % of the missed commands at a wrong-action rate of about 1 % on the synthetic corpus, and fewer than an embedding and fuzzy-matching baseline on the kivi-fake-v1 homes (11 %). Their confidence threshold did not transfer between phrase sets, and none rescued more than 1 of 27 missed commands built from the real names (decision models). A decider needs training on the home's own commands (decider PoC) before it can be wired in.

docs.title: Proposed GitOps change for approval
docs.text:
For the first addition (Whisper prompt): no Ollama change. The pipeline settings and the Kiais agent are already deployed (integration note). The verbs-only prompt works on the deployed image (--initial-prompt exists in wyoming-faster-whisper 2.4.0, documented) and contains no home data, so it can go into apps/home-assistant/values.yaml as it is (coordinate with the hint list's image change, which keeps a static prompt before the names):

           args:
             - --model
             - large-v3-turbo
             - --language
             - es
             - --device
             - cuda
             - --compute-type
             - int8
+            - --initial-prompt
+            - "Enciende, apaga, sube, baja, abre, cierra, para, pausa, reanuda, silencia, quita el silencio, pon, temporizador, minutos, volumen, brillo, por ciento, grados."

Rollback: revert the commit; ArgoCD restarts the Whisper pod either way (about 30 s without STT, model already on the volume). Check after the change: Whisper's per-request time in Loki stays at about 0.86 s, and the share of "no intent matched" answers does not rise. The in-cluster Ollama stays as it is (idle, no model, GPU reserved but unused); removing it is a separate decision.

For B (only if chosen): Ollama on the prusik CPU, the GPU left to Whisper and Jellyfin. Proposed diff to apps/ollama/values.yaml (inferred sizes: qwen3:4b-instruct Q4_K_M is 2.5 GB on disk; resident about 3 GB plus 1.2 GB of KV cache at 8192 tokens; the embedding model 0.6 GB):

 ollama:
   ollama:
     gpu:
-      enabled: true
+      enabled: false
       type: 'nvidia'
     models:
-      pull: []
-        # - qwen2.5:3b
+      pull:
+        - qwen3:4b-instruct
+        - granite-embedding:278m
       run: []

   extraEnv:
-    - name: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
-      value: all
     - name: TZ
       value: Europe/Madrid
     - name: OLLAMA_DEBUG
       value: "0"
+    - name: OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE        # no cold load (16 to 35 s of prompt prefill) between requests
+      value: "-1"
+    - name: OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL      # one cache slot: keeps the agent's system prompt cached
+      value: "1"
+    - name: OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS # agent and embedding model resident together
+      value: "2"
+    - name: OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH
+      value: "8192"
   ...
   resources:
     requests:
-      cpu: 10m
-      memory: 20Mi
+      cpu: "1"
+      memory: 4Gi
     limits:
-      memory: 2Gi
-      nvidia.com/gpu: 1
+      memory: 6Gi

-  runtimeClassName: nvidia
+  nodeSelector:
+    kubernetes.io/hostname: prusik

No CPU limit, so a request can use the idle cores of prusik (about 1 of 32 busy, observed); prusik had about 17 GB of RAM free (observed). Rollback: git revert of the commit and an ArgoCD sync; the pulled models stay on the ollama-data volume until removed with ollama rm.

If the owner prefers to keep a GPU option open, the guard for a model on the 1060 next to Whisper is OLLAMA_GPU_OVERHEAD: "943718400" (900 MiB reserved: with Whisper idle Ollama then sees about 1.0 GiB, and less while Whisper or Jellyfin run) plus OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL: "1" and a context cap; the variable exists in Ollama 0.35.1 (documented, ollama serve --help) and must be checked on 0.40.13.

docs.title: Owner-approval experiment on the real cluster
docs.text:
Only needed if B (or a GPU model) is pursued; A needs no model measurement. Nothing below has been run.

  • Question: do the workstation-derived figures hold on prusik: qwen3:4b-instruct speed on its CPU (inferred 20 to 23 tokens per second generated, 200 to 230 per second of prompt), the time to first speech with a warm prompt cache, and no effect on Whisper?
  • Prerequisites: the owner's approval of the B diff above (commit, push, ArgoCD sync); the model pulls by the chart's models.pull (about 3.1 GB on the ollama-data volume).
  • Steps (read-only after the sync, over the existing ingress, no kubectl exec):
  • Baseline for 10 minutes: DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED, node_cpu_seconds_total of prusik, and Whisper's per-request time from its Loki lines (as in study section 2).
  • Speed: five POST https://ollama.internal.grigri.cloud/api/generate with num_predict 64 and options.num_ctx 8192; read prompt_eval_count, prompt_eval_duration, eval_count, eval_duration from the responses.
  • Agent: scripts/voice-assistant/agent_eval/run.py run --base-url https://ollama.internal.grigri.cloud/v1 --model qwen3:4b-instruct --categories control,followup --repeat-control 2 --warmup --extra-body '{"reasoning_effort":"none"}' (synthetic phrases, dry run, nothing executed in Home Assistant). Record the time to first speech of the second and later requests (warm cache) separately from the first.
  • Router: small_models/router_eval.py --server https://ollama.internal.grigri.cloud --methods emb:granite-embedding:278m.
  • Repeat step 1 while step 3 runs: Whisper latency and VRAM must not change; prusik CPU stays below about 50 % on average.
  • Expected: decode at least 15 tokens per second, warm time to first speech under 4 s, Whisper p50 still about 0.86 s.
  • Failure interpretation: slower than 10 tokens per second or Whisper affected means B is not viable on this node; keep A.
  • Duration: about 30 minutes plus the pull. Rollback: git revert of the values change and an ArgoCD sync; remove the models with ollama rm through the API if the space is needed.

A GPU variant (a model on the 1060 next to Whisper) is not proposed: no role in this study needs it. If the owner wants the real 1060 numbers anyway, add OLLAMA_GPU_OVERHEAD: "943718400" and OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL: "1", keep gpu.enabled, pull qwen2.5:0.5b (0.4 GB), and measure as in step 2 while watching DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED stay below about 2.6 GiB during a transcription.

docs.title: Wiring in Home Assistant 2026.10 (feasibility)
docs.text:
Piece Where it can live Status Effort Built-in intents first pipeline option prefer_local_intents (since 2024.12); strict matching only, no fuzzy matching for Spanish (the 2026.10 gazetteer fallback is English only and not on this path) documented, 2026.10.4 source a UI setting (owner's yes) Kiais as the agent core llama_cpp integration with Kiais' base URL (integration note) deployed 2026-11-05 done Whisper prompt --initial-prompt exists in the deployed wyoming-faster-whisper 2.4.0; 3.6.0 and later add --hass-token (names fetched from Home Assistant); the command verbs need the static part documented low (hint list) Local agent (B) core ollama integration against the in-cluster Ollama (num_ctx default 8192, keep_alive default -1, think off) documented low once Ollama runs Router (B) Home Assistant has one agent per pipeline and no fallback chain (documented). Options: a small custom conversation agent that embeds the text and calls conversation.async_converse with the local or the Kiais agent id (the function is exported, documented); or a "kivi" model inside the Kiais gateway that forwards home requests to the local model (hypothesis: depends on Kiais' code) design only about 200 lines plus tests, or a Kiais change STT corrector a Wyoming STT proxy in front of Whisper that rewrites the transcript (Wyoming RapidFuzz Proxy does this without an LLM, unverified), or a wrapping custom conversation agent not recommended by the measurements medium

Cache care for B (inferred from Home Assistant 2026.10.4's chat_log.py, documented): the system prompt is the instructions, the Assist API prompt with the static list of exposed names, and the date and time only when no GetDateTime tool is offered. With the Assist API it is stable between requests, so llama.cpp's prefix cache keeps prompt processing to the new turn (tens of tokens). Anything else that uses the same model and slot with a different prompt (a router call, another client) evicts the cache, and the next command pays the full prefill (about 3600 tokens for the fake home: 16 to 47 s on a CPU). Use a separate model for the router (the embedding model is) and no other clients on the agent model.

docs.title: Open questions for the owner
docs.text:
1. Privacy and resilience: is it acceptable that home commands the built-in intents miss (about a third on clean audio, more under TV noise) go to Kiais together with the exposed names, and that Kivi cannot answer them when Kiais is down, or should a local fallback (B) be added?
  2. Latency: is about 4 s acceptable for those commands? Neither A nor B gets them under 3 s on this hardware; only the built-in path (about 1 s) does.
  3. Whisper prompt: approve the verbs-only --initial-prompt change now (generic text, no home data)? The names can follow with --hass-token (they stay in the cluster).
  4. Ollama: keep the idle in-cluster Ollama (it holds a GPU slot and a volume but no model), move it to CPU for B, or remove it?
  5. Real names: the built-in hit rate depends on the real entity names, aliases and exposure; may an agent check the owner's phrases against Home Assistant's read-only recognition endpoint (conversation/agent/homeassistant/debug, executes nothing) to replace the fake-home figures?
  6. B's cost: if B is wanted, approve the Ollama-on-CPU diff and the experiment above (4 to 6 GiB RAM and CPU bursts on prusik).

docs.title: Usage rules
docs.text:
• Consent for voices. A person's voice is imported into the real-voice dataset (datasets 8, 9) only after that person agreed. Speakers are pseudonymous ids (spk01...) in every file and manifest; the mapping is the owner's, outside the repository. Household wake-stage audio (dataset 5) may be extracted as training negatives (dataset 10) under the same local-only rules.
  • Purpose limited to improving Kivi: speech-to-text, the hint list, aliases, custom sentences and the decision between the local and the LLM path. No other use.
  • Local analysis. Replay and statistics run on the workstation with scripts. Agents work from aggregates: counts, miss rates, category totals. Transcript text is never pasted into an AI session and never sent to a cloud or LLM API for analysis.
  • Samples for manual review are shown to the owner only.
  • Nothing private in git. No transcripts, samples, recordings or tokens in any repository, commit message, issue or pull request. Documents carry counts and shapes only.
  • Summary on use. When the data is used, the owner gets a summary of what was collected (period, number of utterances, kinds of sources) and what was done with it.
  • False wakes. Because the wake word is server-side, speech that did not address Kivi can be transcribed and stored. The household should know that the assistant's microphones feed this while the exception lasts.
  • Ending. The exception ends when the replay study is done, or earlier on the owner's decision: revert the commit, delete dataset 2, and decide whether to purge dataset 1 before it ages out.

docs.title: Kiais as the Kivi conversation agent in Home Assistant
docs.text:
Status: VERIFIED on a throwaway local Home Assistant 2026.10.4 (same image as production); DEPLOYED to production on 2026-11-05 with the owner's approval (see Deployed 2026-11-05). Date: 2026-11-05 Scope: how the production Home Assistant (2026.10.4, apps/home-assistant/) should talk to the Kiais gateway (fast tier) as the agent behind the "Kiwi" pipeline, with built-in intents first. Risk of the work done: nothing changed in the production Home Assistant, the cluster or git-applied state. Read-only checks on production: the custom components folder, the agent config entries and pipelines (domains and names only), and one unauthenticated GET /v1/models from the Home Assistant pod. Two local sessions sent about 190 chat requests with synthetic Spanish text to Kiais fast over the public URL; the key was the owner's existing client key, loaded into an environment variable for the run only.

Evidence labels: documented (read in source code at the version named), observed (seen on the live system or the gateway on the date above), verified (run end to end on the throwaway Home Assistant), inferred (reasoned from the above, not run).

Correction: the first version of this page said Home Assistant 2026.10.4 has no core OpenAI-compatible conversation integration. That was wrong: core ships litellm and llama_cpp, both of which take a base URL and speak /v1/chat/completions. Both were tested in a second session and the recommendation changed.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
1. Use the core llama_cpp integration ("llama.cpp", in core at 2026.10.4, quality scale bronze) pointed at Kiais. Verified on 2026.10.4 against Kiais fast: it streams, uses Home Assistant's Assist LLM API (intent tools and GetLiveContext), keeps follow-ups, and every control turn changed the right entity. Its stream parser is not affected by the Kiais quirk (see below). It needs no code, no HACS and no GitOps change: only UI configuration. Its latency matched our own component's within noise.
  2. Pipeline "Kiwi": agent llama.cpp "Fast" (model fast), "Prefer handling commands locally" on (prefer_local_intents), Spanish prompt below, Assist API on, temperature 0.2, maximum tokens 300.
  3. The same integration can later point at a local llama.cpp server (for example a small model on the GTX 1060 that another study is looking at) as a second entry, with no change to the approach (inferred: same OpenAI-compatible API; the integration was written for llama.cpp's server).
  4. Keep kiais_conversation (our prototype, in scripts/voice-assistant/custom_components/kiais_conversation/) only as a reference and fallback, not deployed. It would be worth deploying only if a gap below starts to matter (timeouts, history trimming, a Spanish error message).

Gaps of llama_cpp to accept (documented, 2026.10.4 source):

  • Timeouts and retries are the OpenAI SDK defaults (openai 3.10.0: read timeout 600 s, 2 retries) and have no option; a hung backend would keep a voice turn open until Kiais' own stream idle timeout (300 s) or the satellite gives up.
  • No history limit: the whole chat log of the conversation is sent (Home Assistant drops idle conversations after a few minutes, so voice conversations stay short; inferred).
  • Streaming support is detected once in the config flow (a streamed test request with tools); it was detected as supported for Kiais (observed).
  • On a gateway error the pipeline gets a generic Home Assistant error, not a spoken Spanish fallback.

Confidence: high that it works (verified end to end on the production image with the real gateway, 68 turns per agent over the two runs); medium on latency (one afternoon, one gateway backend).
