docs.title: Small local models for Kivi: GPU budget, router, STT corrector, local agent, and non-LLM fixes
docs.text:
Status: DONE for the PC-only measurements; the real GTX 1060 measurement needs the owner's approval (proposal in the design note) Date: 2026-11-05 Systems: homelab node prusik (GTX 1060 3 GB, Pascal sm_61) read-only; measurements on the workstation z800 (RTX 4060 Ti 16 GB, Ryzen 9 5950X 16 cores / 32 threads, DDR4) Related: conversation agent evaluation (Kiais metrics and the harness reused here), STT hint list (uses the prompt numbers of section 5), satellite-side backlog section 12 (formerly EXP-019 of that repository) Risk: read-only on the cluster and Home Assistant; no TV, no sound, no microphone. Nothing was pulled into the cluster Ollama. Kiais received no requests from this study. Scripts: scripts/voice-assistant/small_models/ (this study) on top of scripts/voice-assistant/agent_eval/ (phrases, fake home, built-in intent matcher, chat harness)

Evidence labels: documented (read in source, a manifest or a model card, version named), observed (read from the cluster, Prometheus or Loki on the date above), measured (run on z800 in this study), inferred (computed from the above, not run on the target), hypothesis.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Can a small model on the cluster's GTX 1060 (or on a node CPU) make the Spanish pipeline "Kiwi" better, as a router (home command or general question), as a corrector of Whisper transcripts, or as the home-control agent itself, and how does that compare with non-LLM fixes (Whisper prompt, model size, Home Assistant's built-in intents)? Owner's target: commands handled locally, fast and accurate; general and live questions routed to the Kiais gateway.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. VRAM budget (observed): Whisper large-v3-turbo int8 holds 1140 MiB on the 1060 and peaks at 1556 MiB while transcribing; Jellyfin may also use the GPU. The owner set the LLM budget to 1.0 GiB, guarded so it can never take Whisper's burst.
  2. No model that fits 1.0 GiB is a usable Home Assistant agent (measured). Nine models of 270 M to 1.5 B parameters passed 0 to 16 % of the control phrases with Home Assistant's tool schema; the first usable size is qwen3:4b-instruct (65 % of all control phrases, and 10 of 13 of the phrases the built-in intents miss, against 11 of 13 for Kiais fast). It needs about 2.5 GB plus cache, so on this cluster it would run on the prusik CPU or split CPU/GPU.
  3. The router does not need an LLM. Home Assistant's own strict matching (prefer_local_intents) already sends every general and live question away (21 of 21) and keeps 32 of 47 home phrases local. A multilingual sentence-embedding model (278 M) with 3 nearest neighbours, behind the built-in match, reaches 66 of 68 (97 %) on the reference texts in tens of milliseconds on a CPU. Small LLM routers were worse (section 6).
  4. The Whisper prompt is the cheapest accuracy gain (measured): area and device names as initial_prompt raised built-in intent success from 65 % to 70 % at +5 dB of TV content (no gain on clean audio); the generic command verbs, with or without the names, raised it to 85 to 88 % clean, 74 to 75 % at +5 dB and 57 % at 0 dB (from 82, 65 and 46 %; verbs only: 52 phrases fixed and 3 broken over the four conditions). A static verbs-only prompt works on the deployed image today. hotwords gave output identical to initial_prompt. Whisper small and medium were significantly worse than the deployed large-v3-turbo, and large-v3 was not better.
  5. LLM transcript correctors do not pay off (measured): every model that fits broke about as many commands as it fixed, or more, and some rewrote a command to a different device; the only clearly positive one (qwen2.5:3b, 1.9 GB) gained less than the Whisper prompt.
  6. Latency on the 1060 (observed from its logs): Whisper takes 0.78 s plus 0.03 s per second of audio (p50 0.86 s), almost independent of the command length, because the encoder always runs a 30 s window.

docs.title: 1. GPU budget on prusik (observed 2026-11-05)
docs.text:
Item Value Source GPU GTX 1060 3 GB, 3072 MiB, driver 580.159.03, Pascal sm_61 DCGM exporter, nvidia-smi Sharing time-slicing, 8 replicas, no memory isolation (failRequestsGreaterThanOne: false) system/gpu-operator/time-slicing-config.yaml GPU pods home-assistant-whisper, jellyfin-0, ollama (each nvidia.com/gpu: 1) kubectl get pods Resident now one process, 1138 MiB: Whisper. Ollama has no model loaded (ollama list empty, 0.40.13); Jellyfin idle nvidia-smi in the DCGM pod Used, 7 and 30 days min 1118, p95 1140, max 1556 MiB DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED Peaks 1556 MiB only during transcriptions; encoder and decoder utilisation of NVENC/NVDEC 0 for 30 days DCGM_FI_DEV_ENC_UTIL, DEC_UTIL Ollama chart ollama/ollama:0.40.13, chart 1.94.0, limits.memory: 2Gi, nvidia.com/gpu: 1, models.pull: [] apps/ollama/values.yaml Whisper pando85/wyoming-whisper:2.4.0, --model large-v3-turbo --language es --device cuda --compute-type int8; beam size default 5, no prompt, no VAD filter apps/home-assistant/values.yaml; wyoming-faster-whisper 2.4.0 source

Budget (inferred): 3072 MiB minus Whisper's peak (1556 MiB) leaves 1516 MiB. A Jellyfin transcode reserves roughly 250 to 300 MiB (hypothesis, not observed here), and a CUDA context of a second process costs roughly 100 to 150 MiB on Pascal (hypothesis), so about 1.0 GiB remains for an LLM's weights, KV cache and compute buffers. The owner confirmed 1.0 GiB with Jellyfin coexisting.

Whisper large-v3-turbo is not the "small model": it is the second-largest Spanish-capable Whisper and already takes about half of the card. CTranslate2 runs int8 on sm_61 as int8_float32 (documented, CTranslate2 quantization table).

A risk of the current setup (inferred): Ollama sizes its offload against the free VRAM when it loads a model. While Whisper is idle it sees about 1.86 GiB free and can take the 416 MiB that Whisper needs during a transcription, after which Whisper's CUDA allocation fails. The guard is OLLAMA_GPU_OVERHEAD plus a context cap (design note).

docs.title: 2. Whisper latency on the 1060 (observed from the Whisper pod's own logs)
docs.text:
wyoming-faster-whisper logs Processing audio with duration ... before and the transcript after each request at INFO level (documented, handler.py of 2.4.0), so Loki holds a timing per request. Over 2026-10-16 to 2026-11-05, 445 requests (the transcripts themselves are private and were not copied into this repository):

Audio length n STT p50 / p90 (s) under 2 s 132 0.84 / 0.89 2 to 3 s 104 0.85 / 0.90 3 to 4 s 74 0.85 / 0.91 4 to 6 s 35 0.88 / 0.96 6 to 10 s 73 0.93 / 0.99 over 10 s 25 0.89 / 1.06

Least squares: STT = 0.78 s + 0.029 s per second of audio. The fixed part is the encoder over a 30 s window. The same model and settings take 0.19 s per item on the 4060 Ti (measured), so the 1060 is about 4.5 times slower on this compute-bound work; this factor is used below for prefill estimates (inferred). Decoding of an LLM is memory-bound and scales with bandwidth (192 against 288 GB/s, about 1.5 times; inferred).

docs.title: 3. Method
docs.text:
• Phrases and fake home: agent_eval/phrases_es.yaml (44 home control, 15 general, 11 live information, 6 two-turn follow-ups) and agent_eval/inventory_es.yaml (a fake Spanish home). No real data.
  • Built-in intents: agent_eval/builtin_intents.py runs hassil 3.12.1 with home-assistant-intents 2026.10.6 (the pins of HA 2026.10.4) with the default agent's slot lists and the satellite area as context; inferred, not a run of Home Assistant. Of the 44 control reference texts, 29 resolve to the expected call; 15 fall through (5 because Home Assistant hands HassMediaSearchAndPlay to an LLM agent with control, 9 without a match, 1 with no tool twin).
  • Semi-synthetic audio (small_models/stt_corpus.py): the 70 single-turn phrases spoken by the seven Spanish Piper voices of the satellite project's Phase 2 corpus, at -22 dBFS active speech, clean and mixed with random excerpts of its TV content set (Spanish narration, English film dialogue, songs with vocals) at +10, +5 and 0 dB speech-to-content ratio: 1960 clips. The two es_ES-mls_*-low voices are unintelligible even digitally (also found in the satellite's Phase 2 session 2) and are excluded from every figure; 5 voices remain (2 ES male and female, 1 ES male, 2 MX), 350 clips per condition. No room acoustics or echo-canceller residue are modelled.
  • Transcription (small_models/stt_eval.py): faster-whisper 1.2.1 with the call of wyoming-faster-whisper 2.4.0 (language es, beam 5, optional initial_prompt; no VAD, no hotwords) on the 4060 Ti. Scored by WER (the satellite's Phase 2 normalisation v1.1 with numerals spelled on both sides) and by built-in intent success: the share of the 29 handleable control phrases whose transcript still resolves to the right call. Paired differences use the exact McNemar test; items of the same phrase in different voices are not independent, so p-values are indicative.
  • Router (small_models/router_eval.py), corrector (small_models/corrector_eval.py) and agent (agent_eval/run.py against a private Ollama 0.35.1 bound to 127.0.0.1:11500, models from the Ollama library at their default quantisation, num_ctx 8192 as Home Assistant's Ollama integration sets by default, thinking off).
  • Latency: every timing excludes the one-off model load (a warm-up request first; the model store was on a hard disk). The workstation was shared with a wake-word training job (load average 25 to 98) and the GPU with the other runs of this study, so accuracy figures are clean but the timing figures of the routers, corrector and agent runs are upper bounds; the dedicated speed benchmarks are in section 9.

docs.text:
Ollama's own size estimate at load (weights, KV cache and compute graph) on the 4060 Ti, measured; licences from the model pages (documented).

Model (Ollama tag) Quant Download Loaded at 2k / 4k / 8k ctx Tools Licence Fits 1.0 GiB? functiongemma:270m Q8_0 300 MB 321 / 323 / 363 MB yes Gemma Terms of Use yes gemma3:270m Q8_0 291 MB not measured no Gemma Terms of Use yes granite4:350m BF16 708 MB 784 / 845 / 994 MB yes Apache-2.0 yes (to 8k) qwen2.5:0.5b Q4_K_M 397 MB about 0.4 / 481 / 580 MB yes Apache-2.0 yes qwen3:0.6b Q4_K_M 522 MB 693 / 930 MB / 1.4 GB yes Apache-2.0 to 4k qwen3.5:0.8b Q8_0 1.3 GB with vision and draft parts 554 / 560 / 597 MB reported, but 1536 / 1737 MiB measured at 1k / 4k yes Apache-2.0 no gemma3:1b Q4_K_M 806 MB 875 / 877 / 952 MB no Gemma Terms of Use yes, barely lfm2.5-thinking:1.2b Q4_K_M 731 MB 814 / 841 / 963 MB yes LFM Open License 1.0 (revenue cap, not OSI) yes, barely qwen2.5:1.5b Q4_K_M 986 MB 1.1 / 1.2 / 1.4 GB yes Apache-2.0 no qwen3:1.7b Q4_K_M 1.4 GB 1.5 / 1.7 / 2.2 GB yes Apache-2.0 no llama3.2:1b Q8_0 1.3 GB 1.4 / 1.5 / 1.7 GB yes Llama 3.2 Community Licence no qwen2.5:3b Q4_K_M 1.9 GB (not loaded on the 1060) yes Qwen Research Licence (non-commercial) no qwen3:4b-instruct Q4_K_M 2.5 GB (not loaded on the 1060) yes Apache-2.0 no granite-embedding:278m, paraphrase-multilingual F16 562 MB each embedding only n/a Apache-2.0 yes

Measured VRAM deltas on an otherwise idle card (nvidia-smi before and after loading, so they include the runner's CUDA context): granite-embedding:278m 313 MiB, gemma3:1b 987 / 1003 MiB at 1k / 4k context, qwen2.5:1.5b 1175 / 1261 MiB, qwen3.5:0.8b 1536 / 1737 MiB. Ollama's own estimate is low for qwen3.5:0.8b (its hybrid attention and extra parts), so check the real footprint before trusting an estimate on the 1060. Of the LLMs, only those up to about 0.6 B parameters at a short context clearly fit 1.0 GiB.

The Home Assistant style system prompt plus the 26 tool definitions of the fake home is 3633 tokens (measured with qwen2.5:1.5b's tokenizer), so a tool agent needs num_ctx of at least 4096, and Home Assistant's Ollama integration uses 8192 by default (documented). A real home with more exposed entities needs more.

Runtimes (documented unless marked): llama.cpp (the engine inside Ollama) supports sm_61 with integer dp4a kernels and partial offload (-ngl) and AVX-512 on Zen 4; Ollama adds model management and the API Home Assistant's ollama integration speaks; Home Assistant 2026.10.4 also has a core llama_cpp integration (base URL of a llama-server) and a core litellm integration (URL plus key, OpenAI client) (documented, config_flow.py at tag 2026.10.4). CTranslate2 already runs Whisper; its LLM support is narrower (hypothesis that it brings nothing over llama.cpp here). ExLlamaV2, vLLM and TensorRT-LLM rely on FP16 tensor maths; Pascal consumer cards run FP16 at a small fraction of FP32 speed and lack tensor cores, so they are not realistic on the 1060 (inferred). ONNX Runtime GenAI could run small models on CPU (hypothesis; not measured).

docs.title: 5. Whisper: prompt, hotwords, beam and model size
docs.text:
Built-in intent success on the 29 handleable control phrases (145 clips per condition) and WER over all 70 phrases (350 clips per condition), 4060 Ti, measured.

Configuration Clean +10 dB +5 dB 0 dB WER clean / +5 / 0 dB large-v3-turbo int8, beam 5 (as deployed) 119/145 (82 %) 103 (71 %) 94 (65 %) 67 (46 %) 0.044 / 0.117 / 0.341 same + initial_prompt (areas and device names) 117 (81 %) 108 (74 %) 102 (70 %) 76 (52 %) 0.044 / 0.111 / 0.296 same + hotwords (same text) identical to the prompt row same + initial_prompt names and command verbs 123 (85 %) 114 (79 %) 109 (75 %) 82 (57 %) 0.035 / 0.102 / 0.271 same + initial_prompt command verbs only (no names) 128 (88 %) 113 (78 %) 108 (74 %) 83 (57 %) 0.033 / 0.103 / 0.279 same + verbs first, then names (the order of wyoming-faster-whisper 3.8.1: static prompt, then --hass-token names) 122 (84 %) 111 (77 %) 107 (74 %) 80 (55 %) 0.035 / 0.097 / 0.284 large-v3-turbo, beam 1 116 (80 %) 104 (72 %) 89 (61 %) 59 (41 %) 0.051 / 0.138 / 0.380 small int8, beam 5 102 (70 %) 80 (55 %) 59 (41 %) 42 (29 %) 0.079 / 0.201 / 0.438 small + names prompt 107 (74 %) 83 (57 %) 71 (49 %) 48 (33 %) 0.068 / 0.176 / 0.415 medium int8, beam 5 110 (76 %) 82 (57 %) 71 (49 %) 52 (36 %) 0.050 / 0.149 / 0.406 medium + names prompt 112 (77 %) 96 (66 %) 84 (58 %) 63 (43 %) 0.042 / 0.112 / 0.323 large-v3 int8 + names prompt 122 (84 %) 109 (75 %) 91 (63 %) 76 (52 %) 0.036 / 0.099 / 0.271

Paired, prompt against no prompt (fixed / broken phrases, exact McNemar): clean 1 / 3 (p 0.63), +10 dB 7 / 2 (p 0.18), +5 dB 12 / 4 (p 0.08), 0 dB 12 / 3 (p 0.035); pooled over the three noisy conditions 31 / 9. Model size, paired against large-v3-turbo with the same prompt setting: small breaks 18 to 38 phrases per condition and fixes 1 to 7 (p < 0.001 everywhere); medium breaks 14 to 31 and fixes 3 to 9 (p < 0.07); large-v3 (with the names prompt, against turbo with it) is level on clean, +10 and 0 dB and worse at +5 dB (6 fixed, 17 broken, p 0.035), and the largest new process during its run peaked at about 2.4 GiB on the 4060 Ti, so on the 1060 it would leave no room for anything else. Names and command verbs against no prompt: clean 4 / 0 (p 0.13), +10 dB 13 / 2 (p 0.007), +5 dB 17 / 2 (p 0.001), 0 dB 18 / 3 (p 0.001), pooled noisy 48 / 7; against names only: 29 fixed and 4 broken over the four conditions. Beam 1 against beam 5: pooled noisy 4 / 16 (worse). The names prompt was "Kivi, asistente de casa. " followed by the 32 distinct area and device names and aliases of the fake home (about 80 tokens); it made Whisper write "Kivi" into 3 of 1400 transcripts whose audio has no "Kivi" (keep the assistant's name out of the prompt). hotwords in faster-whisper fills the same prompt slot, which explains the identical output.

What still fails with the prompt on clean audio is mostly the command verb at the start of a short utterance ("Reanuda la tele" heard as "Renuda la tele", "Apaga la tele" as "Hasta acá la tele", "Pausa la tele" as "Pops a la tele", "Apaga la luz" as "Para la luz") and words outside the names list ("temporizador" as "Tiempoizador", "toldo" as "tolo"). Names alone cannot fix verbs, so a third variant appends the generic command vocabulary of Home Assistant's Spanish intents ("Enciende, apaga, sube, baja, abre, cierra, para, pausa, reanuda, silencia, quita el silencio, pon, temporizador, minutos, volumen, brillo, por ciento, grados.", no test sentence, about 40 more tokens; VERBS_ES in stt_eval.py). The rows in bold, with and without the names, are the largest gain of the study. Caveat: the verbs are the same generic verbs the test phrases use, as real commands do; the gain on the owner's own phrasing is to be confirmed with real transcripts (hint-list phase 2).

Verbs only against no prompt: clean 9 / 0 (p 0.004), +10 dB 11 / 1 (p 0.006), +5 dB 15 / 1 (p 0.001), 0 dB 17 / 1 (p < 0.001). Verbs first then names against no prompt: 4 / 1, 10 / 2, 14 / 1, 16 / 3. Against names then verbs, neither variant differs significantly (p 0.06 to 1.0). So on this fake home the verbs carry the gain; the names add nothing measurable, probably because the fake home's names are common Spanish words that Whisper already knows (real names may differ). Neither verbs variant leaked "Kivi" (0 of 1400 each).

For the hint list: put the command verbs in the prompt, not only names; a static verbs-only --initial-prompt already works on the deployed 2.4.0 image and needs no home data; the 3.8.1 order (verbs first, then the names) is as good. Keep "Kivi" out (it leaked into 3 of 1400 transcripts in every run whose prompt started with it); the prompt's latency cost is in section 9.

docs.title: 6. Router
docs.text:
Task: label a transcript "casa" (handled in the house: built-in intents or a local agent) or "kiais" (general knowledge, chat, open-world live information). Labels: all 44 control phrases plus "¿Qué tiempo hace fuera?", "¿Qué hora es?" and "¿Qué día es hoy?" are "casa" (47); the 15 general and the other live phrases are "kiais" (21); the two calendar phrases are not scored. Methods:

  • builtin: "casa" when Home Assistant's strict built-in matching resolves an intent (what prefer_local_intents does; HassMediaSearchAndPlay and HassGetState count as not matched, as Home Assistant hands them to an LLM agent with control).
  • embedding: granite-embedding:278m or paraphrase-multilingual (both multilingual, Apache-2.0), nearest class centroid or 3 nearest neighbours over 80 synthetic training phrases written for this study (40 per class, no sentence shared with the test set; in router_eval.py).
  • LLM: JSON-schema constrained {"ruta": "casa" | "kiais"} with a Spanish instruction, the area and device names and four few-shot pairs; about 400 prompt tokens.
  • builtin + X: built-in match first, X only for the rest (how X would sit behind prefer_local_intents).

Reference texts (68 items), measured:

Method Accuracy Home kept local General/live to Kiais p50 ms builtin 53 (78 %) 32/47 21/21 10 granite-embedding, 3-NN (with or without builtin) 66 (97 %) 47/47 19/21 9 to 89 builtin + granite-embedding, centroid 66 (97 %) 45/47 21/21 paraphrase-multilingual, centroid, + builtin 64 (94 %) 45/47 19/21 qwen3.5:0.8b (with or without builtin; 1.5 GiB, does not fit) 67 (99 %) 47/47 20/21 153 builtin + qwen3:0.6b 65 (96 %) 44/47 21/21 77 gemma3:1b 63 (93 %) 47/47 16/21 126 qwen2.5:1.5b 60 (88 %) 47/47 13/21 100 qwen2.5:0.5b 56 (82 %) 47/47 9/21 73 builtin + granite4:350m 53 (78 %) 44/47 9/21 74

Without the few-shot pairs and without quoting the transcript, every small LLM answered the question instead of classifying it, and the constrained output fell to the first label for all 68 items: the prompt format matters more than the model at this size.

Whisper transcripts of the same phrases (5 voices, 340 items per condition, large-v3-turbo as deployed, no prompt), measured:

Reading: built-in matching is a perfect "send away" filter (it never claims a general question) but loses a third to two thirds of the home phrases under STT errors, which then go to the fallback agent. The embedding router keeps nearly all home phrases local and costs about 10 ms on the workstation GPU (the CPU figure is in section 9), with errors leaning towards "casa" for general questions. Which error is cheaper depends on the fallback (design note). Timings are from a shared GPU and include the HTTP round trip to Ollama.

docs.title: 7. STT corrector
docs.text:
Task: rewrite a Whisper transcript into the intended command using only the area and device names of the home, and return anything that is not about the home unchanged. JSON-constrained output, Spanish instruction, the name lists, three few-shot pairs (one verb fix, one name fix, one question left alone). Input: the deployed Whisper's transcripts at +5 and 0 dB (700 items: 290 handleable control items, 260 general and live items, the other control phrases ignored). Scored by Home Assistant's built-in matching on the corrected text, measured:

Corrector Control pass raw -> corrected Recovered Broken False commands on general/live General/live text changed p50 ms (4060 Ti, shared) Fits 1.0 GiB none 161 -> 161 0 0 0 0 0 granite4:350m 161 -> 165 4 0 0 28 150 yes qwen2.5:0.5b 161 -> 115 6 52 1 29 139 yes qwen3:0.6b 161 -> 143 14 32 1 73 166 to 4k qwen3.5:0.8b 161 -> 131 13 43 2 115 310 no (1.5 GiB) gemma3:1b 161 -> 145 18 34 1 158 244 barely qwen2.5:1.5b 161 -> 165 11 7 1 40 232 no qwen2.5:3b 161 -> 174 17 4 1 18 162 no for comparison: Whisper initial_prompt, names (section 5) 161 -> 178 24 7 +0 (inside STT) no VRAM for comparison: Whisper initial_prompt, verbs only (section 5) 161 -> 191 32 2 +0 (inside STT) no VRAM

Observed behaviour: real fixes ("Apara todas las luces" to "Apaga todas las luces", "pesiana" to "persiana") come with wrong-target rewrites ("Pon la luz de la encimera al máximo" became "Pon la luz del techo al máximo", which would operate a different device) and with rewrites of ordinary requests ("Cuéntame un chiste corto" became "¿Te gustaría que te cuente un chiste corto?"). A corrector sits in front of every request, so its broken and wrong-target cases cost more than the misses it fixes. The only clearly positive model, qwen2.5:3b (+13 net), does not fit the budget and gains less than the Whisper prompt, which costs no VRAM.

docs.title: 8. Local tool agent
docs.text:
The agent_eval harness (26 Home Assistant style tools, dry run, fake home, automatic grading), every category once, against the private Ollama with num_ctx 8192 and thinking off, measured. Pass % excludes "review" phrases. Kiais fast from the conversation agent evaluation for comparison (control twice there).

Model Control Control, action Follow-ups General Live Fall-through 13 Fits 1.0 GiB functiongemma:270m 0 % 0 % 0 % 0 % 0 % yes granite4:350m 14 % 6 % 8 % 8 % 0 % yes qwen2.5:0.5b 14 % 10 % 0 % 15 % 36 % yes qwen3:0.6b 0 % 0 % 0 % 46 % 18 % 4k only qwen3.5:0.8b 14 % 3 % 50 % 38 % 55 % no (1.5 GiB) lfm2.5-thinking:1.2b 7 % 3 % 25 % 46 % 36 % barely qwen2.5:1.5b 16 % 13 % 33 % 85 % 64 % no qwen2.5:3b 37 % 29 % 50 % 85 % 64 % 7 of 13 no qwen3:4b-instruct 65 % 58 % 83 % 100 % 64 % 10 of 13 no (2.5 GB) Kiais fast 93 % 94 % 100 % 100 % 100 % 11 of 13 cloud

"Fall-through 13" are the control phrases Home Assistant's built-in intents do not handle and that are graded (c05, c13 to c16, c26, c36 to c41, c44): the phrases a fallback agent behind prefer_local_intents actually receives. qwen3:4b-instruct passed the colloquial ("Está muy oscuro aquí", "Quita la tele", "Ponme la tele más bajita", "Apágalo todo en la cocina"), state and missing-target phrases, and failed "Pon la luz del salón al cuarenta por ciento", "Para el toldo" and "Pon la siguiente canción en el altavoz de la cocina".

Failure modes of the small models (measured, from the stored calls): they fill every optional slot (floor, device_class: light, colour, temperature), so the target no longer resolves, or they answer in text without calling a tool (qwen2.5:1.5b once answered in Chinese). This is not a prompt-format problem that a few-shot fix removes: the tool schema is Home Assistant's own and cannot be slimmed without a custom LLM API. Timings of these runs (TTFS p50 0.1 to 1.1 s on the 4060 Ti) are not representative of the 1060 or a CPU; see section 9.

docs.title: CPU (measured on the workstation, inferred for prusik)
docs.text:
llama-bench (llama.cpp CPU build) on the exact GGUF files Ollama downloaded, 2 repetitions, in a window when the wake-word training was paused (load average 7.6 to 9.5 from other sessions, recorded per run). Tokens per second; pp is prompt processing, tg generation.

Model 16 threads: pp64 / pp512 / tg 8 threads: pp64 / pp512 / tg pp3600 (16 threads) granite-embedding:278m (F16) pp16 1761, pp64 2533 pp16 1390, pp64 1803 qwen2.5:0.5b 685 / 742 / 96 438 / 440 / 98 581 gemma3:1b 376 / 402 / 46 231 / 247 / 45 352 qwen2.5:1.5b 397 / 356 / 36 268 / 270 / 39 189 (load 18 to 29) qwen2.5:3b 200 / 204 / 20 130 / 128 / 20 qwen3:4b-instruct 152 / 156 / 15.3 100 / 98 / 15.6 77 ± 17 (load 18 to 29)

The pp3600 column was measured after the training resumed (load in brackets): long prompts are also slower per token because attention grows with the context. Generation is memory-bound (8 threads are as fast as 16); prompt processing scales with cores. prusik's Zen 4 with DDR5 should generate about 1.4 to 1.6 times faster if its memory runs at 4800 MT/s or more (bandwidth ratio; inferred, memory speed not read) and process prompts 1.3 to 1.5 times faster (AVX-512, newer cores; inferred).

Other CPU figures (measured, same window): Whisper large-v3-turbo int8 on 16 threads takes 3.6 s p50 for 2.7 s of audio (40 clean clips; load 16), against 0.86 s on the 1060; Piper es_ES-sharvard-medium synthesises one sentence in 18 ms ("Hecho.") to 187 ms (76 characters), and the embedding of a 16-token sentence takes about 9 ms on 16 threads (11.5 ms on 8).

docs.title: GPU
docs.text:
Ollama's own timing fields on the 4060 Ti (about 3600-token prompt with no cached prefix, 64 generated tokens, median of 3), measured while the card was shared with the wake-word training and one Whisper run, so these are lower bounds; the 1060 columns divide prompt processing by the observed 4.5 (compute-bound) and generation by 1.5 (bandwidth ratio), inferred:

Model 4060 Ti pp / tg (tokens/s) 1060 pp / tg (inferred) 1060: 3600-token prompt / 35-token call (inferred) qwen2.5:0.5b 28 700 / 291 about 6 400 / 190 0.6 s / 0.2 s gemma3:1b 15 200 / 186 about 3 400 / 124 1.1 s / 0.3 s qwen3.5:0.8b 9 300 / 170 about 2 100 / 113 1.7 s / 0.3 s qwen2.5:1.5b 8 800 / 67 (contended) about 2 000 / 45 or more 1.8 s / 0.8 s qwen3:4b-instruct 3 400 / 37 (contended) does not fit

granite4:350m stopped after one token in this test and is left out. A small router on the 1060 (about 20 new tokens after a cached few-shot prefix and 8 generated) would take roughly 0.05 to 0.1 s (inferred), against about 0.01 s for the embedding model on the CPU.

docs.title: Whisper prompt cost
docs.text: Back to back on the 4060 Ti (100 clean clips each; the GPU was shared with the wake-word training at 100 % utilisation at the start, so absolute times are upper bounds): p50 / p90 0.192 / 0.227 s without a prompt, 0.187 / 0.198 s with the names, 0.189 / 0.201 s with names and verbs. No measurable cost; on the 1060 the prompt adds well under 0.05 s (inferred: the 120 prompt tokens are processed once per beam in the decoder, which is small next to the 30 s encoder pass). The doubled times in the section 5 runs came from GPU contention, not from the prompt.

docs.title: Hybrid CPU and 1060 (inferred)
docs.text: With 1.0 GiB of the 1060, about 11 of the 36 layers of qwen3:4b-instruct Q4_K_M (2.3 GiB of weights) fit next to their share of the KV cache and the compute buffers. Generation time per token is roughly the sum over layers of bytes over bandwidth: about 70 % of the weights still come from system memory, so generation would be about 20 % faster than CPU-only, and prompt processing gains a little more. That does not justify the risk to Whisper's transcription peak.

docs.title: 10. End-to-end latency budgets
docs.text:
From the end of speech to the first audio of the answer, p50, for the components that differ between options (end-of-speech detection, audio transport and playback are the same for all and excluded). Sources: Whisper on the 1060 0.86 s (observed); prompt +0 to 0.05 s (inferred); built-in match 2 to 10 ms (measured, hassil) plus the action (tens of ms, inferred); Piper 0.02 to 0.19 s (measured, workstation); Kiais fast time to first speech 3.06 s with a tool call and 1.20 s for a general question (observed by the conversation agent evaluation from the workstation; from the cluster it should be similar).

Local qwen3:4b-instruct with a warm prompt cache (inferred from the CPU table): a tool round is about 30 new prompt tokens (0.2 s) and about 35 generated tokens for the call (2.3 s at 15 tokens per second), then about 60 tokens of tool result (0.4 s) and the first answer token; the first sentence (about 12 tokens, 0.8 s) can go to TTS while the rest streams. Workstation: about 3.7 s to the first sentence; prusik: about 2.7 s. Cold (first request after a model load or after the system prompt changed): add the full prompt, about 3600 tokens for the fake home: 23 s at the pp512 rate to 47 s at the measured pp3600 rate on the workstation, about 16 to 35 s on prusik.

Path STT Routing Agent / intent TTS first audio Total p50 Built-in intent matched 0.86 0.01 0.05 0.05 about 1.0 s Command through Kiais fast 0.86 0.01 3.06 + first sentence 0.1 0.1 about 4.1 s General question through Kiais fast 0.86 0.01 1.20 + 0.1 0.1 about 2.3 s Command through local qwen3:4b on prusik CPU (warm) 0.86 0.02 about 2.7 0.1 about 3.7 s (16 to 35 s cold) Any path with Whisper on CPU instead of the 1060 3.6 +2.8 s on each row Small model (≤ 1.0 GiB) as agent on the 1060 0.86 about 0.5 to 1.0 (inferred) 0.1 about 1.5 to 2 s, but 0 to 16 % correct

docs.title: Conclusion and confidence
docs.text:
• No small model on the 1060 earns its VRAM. As the home agent the models that fit fail (0 to 16 %); as a router an embedding model on the CPU is as good and faster; as an STT corrector they break as much as they fix. Confidence high for this fake home and tool schema (the failure modes are structural: slot over-filling and no tool call), medium for other homes.
  • The best accuracy gain is the Whisper prompt with the generic command verbs (names added nothing measurable on this fake home; a static verbs-only prompt works on the deployed image). Measured on synthetic voices and TV-content mixes: confidence medium that the size of the gain carries over to real voices in the room, high that it does not cost latency.
  • A local agent needs at least about 4 B parameters (qwen3:4b-instruct), which on this cluster means the prusik CPU: about as accurate and about as fast as Kiais fast for the commands the built-in intents miss, with a cold-start cost of tens of seconds (inferred from the workstation; the owner-approval experiment in the design note would measure it).
  • The ranked options and the proposed GitOps change are in the design note.

docs.title: Rollback and cleanup
docs.text: Nothing was changed in the cluster or Home Assistant. Read-only kubectl exec was used three times before the coordinator asked for none (nvidia-smi in the DCGM exporter pod, ollama list and ollama --version in the Ollama pod); no other command ran in the cluster. Local: the private Ollama on 127.0.0.1:11500 was stopped and its model store and the Python environment deleted; the generated audio, the per-item results and the private copy of the Whisper log lines stay outside this repository.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• The fake home's names were chosen to be natural; the owner's real names, aliases and exposure decide the real built-in hit rate. Recheck with the owner's phrases against Home Assistant's read-only recognition endpoint.
  • Real voices in the room (reverberation, echo-canceller residue, distance) are not modelled; the satellite project's real-voice set would confirm the Whisper prompt gain.
  • prusik's real CPU speed for qwen3:4b-instruct and the cold-start time (owner-approval experiment in the design note).
  • Whether a router should err towards the local agent or towards Kiais depends on whether a local agent is added at all.

docs.title: Whisper decoding settings on the GTX 1060: compute type, beam size, VAD
docs.text:
Status: PARTIAL, aborted by the experimenter at 2026-11-05 about 19:17 UTC after the benchmark pod caused CUDA out-of-memory errors in the live Whisper (see Incident). Compute type and beam size were measured; --vad-clip and --vad-endpointing were not. Date: 2026-11-05 Systems: node prusik (GTX 1060 3 GB, sm_61, driver 580.159.03), image git.grigri.cloud/agil/wyoming-whisper:3.8.1.1 (wyoming-faster-whisper 3.8.1, faster-whisper 1.2.1, CTranslate2 4.8.5), model large-v3-turbo revision 0a363e91. Nothing ran on a TV or in Home Assistant. Related: Whisper image build, small local models (prompt, GPU budget), Kivi decider PoC (the audio set) Scripts: scripts/voice-assistant/whisper_bench/

Evidence labels: documented (help text, source of the image), measured (this run), inferred, hypothesis.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: For Spanish home commands on this GPU, which wyoming_faster_whisper settings give the best latency (audio end to transcript) without losing accuracy? Matrix: --compute-type int8 vs int8_float32, --beam-size 0 (auto, current) / 1 / 5, then --vad-clip off vs on at the best combination.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. On an undisturbed GPU every configuration is within about 30 ms of the others (measured). p50 audio-end to transcript is 0.85 to 0.88 s and p90 0.88 to 0.93 s for all five completed configs. That matches the production p50 of about 0.91 s.
  2. --beam-size 0 is exactly 5 (documented and measured): __main__.py maps <= 0 to 5 on x86. The two runs gave identical text on 480 of 480 clips.
  3. int8 and int8_float32 gave identical text on 480 of 480 clips and the same latency (+3 ms, measured). Hypothesis: on sm_61, which has no fp16, CTranslate2 resolves int8 to int8 weights with float32 activations, i.e. the same compute as int8_float32. Not verified in the CT2 source.
  4. --beam-size 1 is the only setting that differs: 26 ms faster at p50 (paired, 95 % CI 21 to 28 ms, 98 uncontended clips), 3 % of the request time. Accuracy is not worse within the noise of this set: command exact match 222/384 vs 219/384 (McNemar p = 0.58), WER 13.6 % vs 14.1 %. 57 of 480 transcripts differ from beam 5 (3 clean, 19 at +5 dB, 35 at 0 dB), in both directions.
  5. The big latency effect was not a setting but GPU sharing. Another client was sending the live Whisper a request about every 15 s (about 7 s each) during this run. Clips that overlapped one of those requests had p50 about 1.17 s instead of 0.87 s (+0.3 s) and a maximum of 3.9 s. A first, naive reading of the whole data set would have credited beam 1 or int8_float32 with a 0.25 s gain; that is the contention (the first config ran while 71 % of its clips overlapped live requests, the later ones 41 %).
  6. Not measured: --vad-clip, --vad-endpointing, the float32 out-of-memory confirmation, the reversed second round. See What was not done.

Recommendation: no change to values.yaml for latency. Current settings are on par with every alternative on a quiet GPU. --beam-size 1 is a 26 ms (3 %) optional saving with no measurable accuracy cost; if wanted, see Recommendation. The larger lever is whatever else uses the live Whisper and the shared GPU.

docs.title: Incident: the live Whisper was affected
docs.text:
The owner approved a temporary benchmark pod. Its premise was that the live instance is mostly idle and that a second instance fits next to it (1133 MiB in use of 3072). Both turned out wrong:

  • A second large-v3-turbo instance used 1.77 to 1.83 GiB at peak (1.3 GiB after warm-up, growing with decoding). The card peaked at 2967 of 3072 MiB, leaving about 100 MiB. This is the reason the image build note says not to run two large-v3-turbo instances; it was not followed here.
  • The live Whisper was not idle: from 17:50 UTC (before the pod existed) it handled 30 to 45 requests per 10 minutes with a median of about 7 s each, and it did so again at 19:20 UTC after the pod was deleted. The origin of that load is not known from the logs (and transcripts were deliberately not read).
  • Impact on the live service (from its log, timestamps and error classes only): four requests failed: two with RuntimeError: CUDA failed with error out of memory (18:45:34 and 18:53:51 UTC) and two with cudaErrorInvalidDevice: invalid device ordinal (18:45:34 and 18:54:02 UTC, an after-effect of the first error in the same process). While the pod was running, 67 of 190 live requests took more than 5 s (maximum 47 s). Requests succeeded again in about 0.9 s right after the pod was deleted; the pod has 0 restarts and the GPU is back at 1133 MiB. The live deployment was never scaled, restarted or edited.
  • The benchmark's own server also ran out of memory once (int8f32-b1, at clip 86 of 480). That config and the aborted reversed round are not used.

The run was stopped and the pod deleted as soon as this was seen. A rerun should not share the card with the live Whisper while anything else uses it (see the options at the end).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Pod: pod.yaml (temporary, label app=whisper-bench, activeDeadlineSeconds 3 h), on prusik, runtimeClassName: nvidia, nvidia.com/gpu: 1 (the card is time-sliced 8 ways, so it scheduled). The same image by digest, runs as uid 568. It needs no pull secret (the node already caches the image).
  • Model: the live model volume could not be shared: it is an OpenEBS ZFS dataset and the node refused a second mount ("already mounted"). The pod downloaded the same revision (0a363e91, same model.bin blob) from Hugging Face into an emptyDir. The live pod was only read for ls of the cache.
  • Server: the real python3 -m wyoming_faster_whisper entrypoint per config, with the live --model large-v3-turbo --language es --device cuda and the live verbs --initial-prompt, plus the config's --compute-type and --beam-size. --hass-api was omitted (no token in the benchmark), so the prompt is the static verbs prefix only; the live server appends Home Assistant names after it, which makes the live prompt longer (and possibly slower) than the benchmark's. --local-files-only on; no --debug.
  • Client: wyoming_client.py: Transcribe(es), AudioStart, 1024-sample AudioChunks, AudioStop, wait for Transcript. Latency = AudioStop written to Transcript received (the server only transcribes on AudioStop, so this is the time HA waits after its own end of speech detection). Chunks were sent without real-time pacing. Sequential, one request at a time, 10 unmeasured warm-up requests per config (the model loads lazily on the first one), fixed shuffled clip order, identical for every config.
  • Audio, synthetic only: select_subset.py, seed 20261105, from the kivi-fake-v1 audio set of the decider PoC (Piper voices, TV-content mixes). 160 items stratified by phrasing style (16 per style, 8 styles = 128 commands) and kind (10 questions, 6 out of domain, 6 unclear, 5 unsupported, 5 two-action = 32 non-commands), each in clean, +5 dB and 0 dB = 480 clips, mean 3.2 s. No household recording and no Loki transcript was used.
  • Metrics (metrics.py, analyze.py): word and character error rate after normalisation (numbers_es: "veinte" = "20", "20 %" = "veinte por ciento", "21,5" = "veintiuno y medio"; accents and punctuation removed), command exact match = normalised transcript equals the normalised reference (strict: extra words count), over the 128 commands per condition. Latency p50, p90, max. Paired comparison per (item, condition) clip: exact McNemar on exact match and a 95 % percentile bootstrap (3000 to 10000 resamples over clips) on latency differences. GPU memory is whole-card nvidia-smi, sampled every 0.25 s, minus the 1133 MiB of the live pod.
  • Contention control: the live Whisper logs Completed request in S second(s) per request. live_overlap.py marks a benchmark clip as overlapped when its window (plus 1 s each side) touches a live request's window (end minus S, end). Only timestamps and durations are used. The logs were not read for text. Because S includes the live server's own waiting, the windows are generous: "quiet" clips are really quiet, and many quiet clips were discarded.

Identical for int8-b0, int8-b5, int8f32-b0 and int8f32-b5 (text identical on 480/480 clips).

docs.text:
Subsets differ per config (138 to 282 clips), so the p50 and p90 are close but not paired; the paired test below is the comparison. p90 is tight (0.88 to 0.93 s) because the decoder is short for commands.

Against int8-b1 as the base the others are +0.022 to +0.027 s slower (n = 96 to 170).

docs.title: What was not done
docs.text:
• --vad-clip: not measured. Documented in the image source (models.py, vad_clip_enabled): clipping is "a wash for faster-whisper, which pads audio to 30s internally regardless". The data above agree in spirit: on uncontended clips latency barely depends on clip length (1.3 to 6.3 s, correlation 0.01; medians 0.85 s under 2.5 s, 0.87 s for 2.5 to 3.5 s, 0.89 s above 3.5 s), so shortening the audio should not help. This is a documented expectation, not a measurement here.
  • --vad-endpointing: not measured. Its help text ("End a command and send its transcript after this many seconds of VAD-detected silence (default: wait for audio-stop)") does bear on request latency, but only for a client that keeps streaming after the speaker stops; Home Assistant's own end-of-speech detection ends the stream. A test needs real-time paced streaming (wyoming_client.transcribe(realtime=True) and the limit field of a plan are ready for it) and a risk review: it can cut commands that contain a pause.
  • float32: not tried; 809 M parameters at 4 bytes is more than the card's 3 GiB, and trying it would claim the remaining memory next to the live instance. int8_float32 and int8 are the only usable types (ctranslate2.get_supported_compute_types("cuda") in the pod: float32, int8, int8_float32).
  • Reversed round: planned to cancel order and drift effects; aborted by the incident.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
1. Keep the current arguments (--compute-type int8, --beam-size unset = 5). On a quiet GPU no alternative is meaningfully faster, and none is more accurate. int8_float32 has no effect.
  2. Optional, low value: --beam-size 1 saves about 26 ms per request (3 %) with no measurable accuracy loss on this set. Because 57 transcripts changed (more in noise), it should be judged on real usage (the usage study) before anyone relies on it. If the owner wants it, in apps/home-assistant/values.yaml under whisper.containers.whisper.args, after "int8":
         - --compute-type
         - int8
         - --beam-size
         - "1"

Not applied. Roll back by removing the two lines (the default is 5). 3. Do not expect a latency win from other settings. The measurable latency problem in this run was other work on the GPU, about +0.3 s at p50 and seconds at the tail. Find out which client sends the live Whisper a request every 15 s, and move it or schedule it.

docs.title: Options for a rerun
docs.text:
Needed: --vad-clip on/off and optionally --vad-endpointing, with a reversed round and no contention.

  1. Quiet window, owner-coordinated: pause the other client of the live Whisper, then run the pod. The pod's peak (about 1.8 GiB) still leaves only about 100 MiB next to the live instance, so a live request could still hit an out-of-memory error; run it at a time when nobody uses voice.
  2. Run it on the workstation (RTX 4060 Ti) with the same scripts and image. Latency would not transfer to the GTX 1060 (it would still answer the vad-clip question for accuracy, not for time).
  3. Scale the live Whisper to 0 for the run with the owner's explicit approval (a short voice outage), which is the only way to measure with the card to itself.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
# on the workstation: stage the subset (synthetic audio of the decider PoC)
python3 scripts/voice-assistant/whisper_bench/select_subset.py --data $POC/data/kivi-fake-v1 --out $STAGE
# pod: kubectl apply -f pod.yaml, download the model (faster_whisper.utils.download_model), kubectl cp the
# scripts, plan_stage1.json and $STAGE, then run inside the pod:
python3 run_bench.py --plan plan_stage1.json --manifest /work/data/manifest.csv --root /work/data --out /work/out1 \
    --live tcp://home-assistant-whisper.home-assistant.svc.cluster.local:10300
# analysis, with the live request intervals for the uncontended view:
kubectl logs deploy/home-assistant-whisper --timestamps | python3 live_overlap.py --extract > live.json
python3 analyze.py --results out1 --items $POC/data/kivi-fake-v1/items.jsonl --base int8-b0 --quiet live.json
python3 -m pytest scripts/voice-assistant/whisper_bench

Raw results (synthetic text and timings) stay on the workstation under /work/workspaces/whisper-bench-stage/ and are not committed.

docs.title: Cleanup (done 2026-11-05)
docs.text: The pod whisper-bench and its emptyDir volumes are deleted; no other objects were created (two earlier CPU-only help pods were deleted too). The live home-assistant-whisper pod is Running with 0 restarts and the GPU is back at 1133 MiB.
